results.pageDescription: HOT is a global community of mappers transforming lives using the power of open map data.
results.evidenceText: Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team - HOT Website HOT is a global community of mappers transforming lives using the power of open map data. See Our Work Mapping Chinhoyi: How a Zimbabwean Town Opened Its Map Data Learn how community-led mapping improved Chinhoyi Municipality's infrastructure management, revenue collection, housing regulation, water and sanitation planning, and more. Watch here Next → HOT Portal The platform that leads you to all of our open mapping tools. Fly drones, publish aerial imagery for free, organize mapping projects from home, go the field for easy mapping, free and open for everyone! Discover it here Next → The night the earth shook, strangers started to draw A memorable account of HOT's approach to disaster response, by Akash Wadhwani Read here Next → 1 2 3 ⓘ OpenStreetMap users in HOT's priority regions Our Work Highlighted Programs View all programs HOT implements a range of impactful programs that leverage open map data to address humanitarian challenges globally. Working in 94 countries, we collaborate with local communities, governments, and organizations to create and maintain detailed, accessible maps that aid local communities, NGOs, and governments in making informed decisions and improving lives. 2, }" :style="`order: ${fixedIndex(0) + 1}`" > Conflict & Displacement Our goal is to use open maps and data to strengthen humanitarian efforts in complex emergencies, helping to deliver life-saving aid and support projects for vulnerable communities. 2, }" :style="`order: ${fixedIndex(1) + 1}`" > Learn and Connect Empowering a global network of mappers and community leaders with the skills, knowledge, and connections to drive local humanitarian impact and build long-term resilience 2, }" :style="`order: ${fixedIndex(2) + 1}`" > Disaster Response Disaster response has been at the heart of HOT's mission since its inception. Originating with the Haiti earthquake in 2010, HOT’s responses to major disasters have marked critical milestones in the organization’s history. 2, }" :style="`order: ${fixedIndex(3) + 1}`" > Disaster Risk Reduction Strengthening communities, governments, and partners with open geospatial data and tools to improve disaster mitigation, preparedness, and recovery for informed local decision-making and long-term resilience. 2, }" :style="`order: ${fixedIndex(4) + 1}`" > Urban Development Advancing locally-led open mapping and inclusive urban data production to bring vulnerable and underserved communities into view and strengthen evidence-based urban planning in rapidly growing cities. Impact Areas HOT works to solve local challenges that are global in scale and contribute to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). We work in five core impact areas, and by driving efforts in these key areas work towards our mission to improve well-being, reduce suffering, and increase resilience for people who are systematically underrepresented in countries at high risk of disaster, humanitarian emergency and multidimensional poverty, through making and using open map data. 1 && getRelCar(0) 3 && getRelCar(0) 4, }" :style="`order: ${getRelCar(0) + 1}`" > Disaster Response 1 && getRelCar(1) 3 && getRelCar(1) 4, }" :style="`order: ${getRelCar(1) + 1}`" > Climate Resilience & Sustainability 1 && getRelCar(2) 3 && getRelCar(2) 4, }" :style="`order: ${getRelCar(2) + 1}`" > Public Health 1 && getRelCar(3) 3 && getRelCar(3) 4, }" :style="`order: ${getRelCar(3) + 1}`" > Displacement & Safe Migration 1 && getRelCar(4) 3 && getRelCar(4) 4, }" :style="`order: ${getRelCar(4) + 1}`" > Gender Equality Disaster Response The rising impact and scale of humanitarian emergencies on vulnerable populations make the demand for data-driven disaster response even more pressing. Open geospatial data provides government agencies and first responders with critical information to take more informed and locally appropriate action when a disaster or humanitarian crisis hits. Learn More Climate Resilience & Sustainability Open mapping supports strategies to mitigate potential climate impacts, enhance community preparedness, and ensure that communities grow in environmentally sustainable ways. Through mapping climate hazards and realities in the communities, local players can contribute towards finding sustainable solutions by filling in data gaps and contributing to long-term community resilience and development. Learn More Public Health When communities actively participate in mapping their own areas, they create detailed maps that help identify gaps and plan targeted and effective health interventions, ultimately improving the health and well-being of communities globally. Thus, open geospatial data is invaluable for developing policies that address health disparities, enhance equitable health access, and evaluate the effectiveness of public health programs. Learn More Displacement & Safe Migration Conflict, persecution, violence, and natural disasters have caused a record more than 100 million people worldwide to be displaced . Humanitarian organizations and governments require accurate geospatial data to locate and understand the needs of displaced communities, identify potential risks, enable better coordination and resource allocation, and ensure that assistance reaches those who need it most. Learn More Gender Equality By identifying and addressing gender-specific gaps, open geospatial data provides a more nuanced understanding of how resources, services, and vulnerabilities are distributed across different genders within communities, ensuring an inclusive approach and community ownership in the open mapping process. HOT is committed to fostering inclusivity, and by involving women and gender non-conforming people in mapping initiatives, we ensure their needs are prioritized, enabling targeted and effective interventions to promote gender equity and inclusion. Learn More HOT works around the globe to support the use of OpenStreetMap by local communities and help build a local open mapping movement. HOT works across sectors to provide map data that revolutionizes disaster management, reduces risks, and contributes to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. Who We Are Open Mapping Hubs HOT works through four regional Hubs to support and scale OpenStreetMap communities around the world. Regional Hubs leverage local expertise and resources to create and sustain the open mapping movement. Hubs have a pivotal role in facilitating localized mapping efforts and serve as a vital connection between local communities, NGOs, governments, and international aid organizations, ensuring that mapping initiatives are tailored to regional needs and priorities. Learn more about the Open Mapping Hubs Open Mapping Hubs Asia-Pacific Facilitating collaboration and driving the growth of open mapping ecosystems in Asia-Pacific. Learn More Open Mapping Hubs Eastern & Southern Africa Advancing community development and humanitarian response through open mapping solutions. Learn More Open Mapping Hubs West & Northern Africa The WNA Hub engages with open mapping organizations and communities to facilitate the exchange of ideas and expertise across the region. Learn More Open Mapping Hubs Latin America and the Caribbean Enabling resilient communities through social impact mapping in Latin America and the Caribbean. Learn More Asia-Pacific Facilitating collaboration and driving the growth of open mapping ecosystems in Asia-Pacific. Learn More Eastern & Southern Africa Advancing community development and humanitarian response through open mapping solutions. Learn More West & Northern Africa The WNA Hub engages with open mapping organizations and communities to facilitate the exchange of ideas and expertise across the region. Learn More Latin America and the Caribbean Enabling resilient communities through social impact mapping in Latin America and the Caribbean. Learn More Ready to get started creating and using open data? At HOT, we use a combination of open mapping tools developed by the open-source community to create, access, manage, analyze, and share open map data that serves our partners and local communities. All of these tools and resources are freely available for you to use. Tools & Resources Anyone can get involved in open mapping with HOT! Open mapping helps solve many problems around the world, and the mapping community welcomes you. Join us in making a difference! Your support helps us create impactful change in our community. Get Involved Partner With Us News View all news HOT Announcements No One Left Off the Map: Five Years with HOT in West and North Africa Dr. Ibrahima Cissé, HOT's Regional Director of the West and Northern Africa Open Mapping Hub from 2021 to 2026, shares his farewell words after his five-year tenure. In this piece, he recounts the achievements of his regional team and the impact they've had working hand-in-hand with communities to solve critical issues like climate change, sustainable livelihoods, water and health access, and more, through open mapping. Oct. 26, 2026 Tech and Tools, Blogs Building Africa's Next Drone Workforce: A Q&A with Palesa Thetele. Africa has fewer than 5,000 certified drone pilots. Palesa Thetele, a computing graduate from Botswana, is now one of them. Palesa joined an intensive residency at the African Drone and Data Academy, based at the Malawi University of Science and Technology. She started with zero flight hours. She finished with three remote pilot certifications after using drone mapping, GIS, and AI to tackle public health challenges. Her training is part of Design Thinking for Drone and Data Technology for the Youth Force. The initiative is building a new generation of certified youth drone mappers. It brings together the Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team (HOT), UNICEF, the African Drone and Data Academy, Generation Unlimited, the Lesotho Aviation Authority, and Yoma. We spoke to Palesa about her background, the training, and how she plans to use spatial data to solve problems at home. Subscribe another address Columbia Journalism School will pause its M.A. program (and launch an online degree) The country’s most prestigious journalism school has initiated “a critical evaluation” of the Master of Arts program and is pausing admissions to it. By Sarah Scire Oct. 1, 2026, 3:34 p.m. The Columbia Journalism School will pause admissions for its Master of Arts program, dean Jelani Cobb announced on Thursday. The country’s most prestigious journalism school also announced a new online, part-time degree. In a note to alumni of the M.A. program, Cobb wrote that the administration has “initiat[ed] a critical evaluation” of the M.A. curriculum. “To give this review the focus it deserves, we are temporarily pausing admissions for the upcoming admissions cycle.” The school’s admissions page has been updated with a similar message. Columbia will continue to offer its Master of Science programs in Journalism and Data Journalism. Current M.A. students are not affected by the pause. The estimated cost of attendance for the nine-month M.A. for the 2026-2027 year is roughly $120,000. The M.S. costs around $130,000 and the year-long M.S. in Data Journalism costs about $180,000. According to Columbia, around 80% of students receive some sort of financial aid . The M.A. program is a newer degree — created in 2005 — and was designed for working journalists with three or more years of professional experience “to go deeper into a specialized subject.” The M.S. degree, described as “the foundational program of the Journalism School,” is for students with “zero to three years” of experience. The school also announced it will, for the first time in its history, offer an online degree. The new online Master of Science in Journalism program will be part-time with students earning a degree over two years. “This new program brings an Ivy League J-School education directly to students across the United States,” reads one post from the Columbia Journalism School on X. “With guidance from CJS’s faculty of working journalists, you can develop your reporting skills while continuing to live and work in your community.” Roughly half of enrolled M.A. candidates at Columbia Journalism School are international students, Aditya Soni and Edmund Lee reported for Reuters. Uncertainty in immigration policies and visa challenges under the Trump administration caused “a sharp drop” in international applications to Columbia, according to Reuters, and contributed to the program’s pause. Here’s the initial note from Cobb: Dear CJS M.A. Alumni, I am writing to share an update about the Master of Arts program at Columbia Journalism School. As part of our ongoing commitment to keeping our graduate education timely and innovative, the administration is initiating a critical evaluation of the M.A. curriculum. To give this review the focus it deserves, we are temporarily pausing admissions for the upcoming admissions cycle. We want to reassure you directly: this evaluation phase reflects our commitment to continuous excellence. It does not alter the standing, prestige, or lasting value of your CJS M.A. degree. The M.A. degree is grounded in deep domain expertise, rigorous analytical reporting, and subject-matter authority—qualities media organizations and independent journalists need now more than ever. The groundbreaking work produced by our alumni network across global newsrooms continues to define the high standards of this program and reinforce the strength of your credential. Periodic curricular review is a standard practice at Columbia to ensure our specialized tracks advance alongside the media landscape. Current M.A. students are completing their nine-month curriculum without interruption, receiving the full scope of concentration coursework, thesis advisement, and faculty mentorship. We remain immensely proud of your achievements and the impact of your reporting worldwide. If you have questions, please contact Dr. George Miller, associate dean for academic affairs. Sincerely, Jelani Cobb Dean & Henry R. Luce Professor of Journalism This story was updated. Photo of Columbia University used under a Creative Commons license. Every 140 minutes.) “Disparaging journalism is a far more central part of Fox News programming than it is of either MSNBC or CNN programming.” By Philip M. Napoli , Adam Meskouri , Anjini Mani , Grant Socol and Harrison Walley Oct. 8, 2026, 2:38 p.m. In 2025, trust in journalism reached a record low . According to Gallup, only 8% of Republicans expressed trust in the news media, compared with 51% of Democrats. New data show an uptick among Republicans, but overall trust remains near this record low, and the gap between Republicans and Democrats remains substantial. One of the key drivers of this lopsided decline in trust in journalism may be the extent to which news outlets spend time bashing other news outlets, or bashing the news media in general — a phenomenon we call inter-journalism disparagement . Our research team at Duke University’s DeWitt Wallace Center for Media & Democracy recently completed a study of the prominence of this phenomenon on each of the “big three” cable news networks (CNN, Fox News, MSNBC/MS NOW); whether it has increased or decreased over time; and whether there are significant differences in the rate of disparagement across networks. The results were stark. Fox News far exceeds the other networks, with inter-journalism disparagement taking place once every 14.5 minutes. In contrast, CNN engages in inter-journalism disparagement roughly every 140 minutes, and MSNBC every 61 minutes. To conduct this analysis, we gathered 15 years of cable news transcripts (2011-2025) for each network. We gathered a random sample of one week’s worth of programming for each year. 1 With this approach, we ended up with 3,543 transcripts and almost 19 million words across the three networks, which equates to roughly 62,000 pages of text. Given the volume of text to be analyzed, we trained OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 to identify attacks against the news media. We developed a 20-page instruction document to help the model code instances of disparagement. GPT-5.5 consistently achieved 99.5% accuracy at identifying inter-journalism disparagement and 100% accuracy for avoiding false negatives, compared to human-coded samples. (You can read more details about the entire training and analytical process here .) We defined inter-journalism disparagement as negative statements about the conduct or content of an explicitly identified journalism target (such as a specific news organization, or the news media in general). Our definition, which is described in greater depth in the full paper, needed to be quite detailed in order for ChatGPT to produce accurate results. Examples of inter-journalism disparagement include: CNN’s Dan Pfeiffer describing “political journalism writ large” as “bad,” “problematic” and “failing massively.” MSNBC’s Rachel Maddow describing The Washington Post’s editorial page as “rabid” and “foaming,” and “super right-wing,” noting: “I can’t believe this is in this real newspaper.” Fox News’ Mark Levin telling viewers that “MSNBC and CNN…have been lying and lying and lying to you for years.” What we found when comparing the three networks tells us a lot about the dynamics of contemporary cable news and partisan journalism. First, Figure 1 shows the rate of journalism disparagement across each of the big three networks. Because the volume of text that we analyzed varies across each network, our primary metric was the rate of disparagement per 1,000 words of transcript text. In this figure, we show not only the rate per 1,000 words, but we also convert that rate into a time-based frequency, using the industry standard of 1,000 words equaling approximately six minutes of air time. In Figure 2, we graph the frequency of inter-journalism disparagement over time. Here, we see that the massive difference between Fox News and CNN/MSNBC persists over the 15-year time period. Still, we do see some dips in the volume of disparagement on Fox News in the two-year periods leading up to the 2016 and 2024 elections, with journalism disparagement levels on Fox News rebounding to near-peak levels in 2025. We haven’t figured out yet what to make of this pattern. CNN and MSNBC seem to converge in their disparagement activity starting around 2017, with MSNBC’s disparagement rate decreasing somewhat, and CNN’s disparagement rate increasing somewhat. This pattern aligns with recent research that has shown, in other contexts, that CNN and MSNBC programming are converging in ways that suggest diminished differences between the more “centrist” CNN and the more left-leaning MSNBC. A key takeaway here is that we should not think about Fox News and MSNBC as flip sides of the same partisan journalism coin. At least in relation to inter-journalism disparagement, these left- and right-leaning cable networks behave very differently. Disparaging journalism is a far more central part of Fox News programming than it is of either MSNBC or CNN programming. In order to get a deeper understanding of these differences, we also identified the targets of the disparagement. These results are presented in Figures 3 through 5. Figure 3 presents a breakdown of the most common targets of disparagement on Fox News. By far the most frequent target of disparagement on Fox News is “the media.” Following in a distant second is CNN, with the “mainstream media” rounding out the top three targets. Other relatively frequent targets include The New York Times, MSNBC, and The Washington Post. As should be clear, Fox News devotes far more attention to disparaging journalism as an institution than it does to attacking individual news sources. This stands in stark contrast to what we see when we look at the results for CNN and MSNBC. Looking first at CNN, Figure 4 shows that the network’s most frequent target is Fox News (though with a frequency that wouldn’t crack the top three of the Fox News list). Similarly, as Figure 5 shows, Fox News is also the number one target on MSNBC. Both CNN and MSNBC have the same top three, with Fox News followed by “the media” and the “right-wing media.” These instances of institutional disparagement happen far less frequently on CNN or MSNBC than they do on Fox News. Finally, we were also able to identify which hosts or anchors were the most frequent disparagers of their fellow journalists. Those results can be seen in Figure 6. Given the lopsided amount of inter-journalism disparagement on Fox News, it is not surprising that this graph is dominated by Fox News personalities, with Sean Hannity taking the top spot, followed by Greg Gutfeld and Tucker Carlson (note: our graph for Howard Kurtz reflects his move from CNN to Fox in 2013). This study didn’t distinguish further in terms of the nature of the disparagement across the three networks (for example, in terms of severity or legitimacy). This is something we are exploring in the next stage of this work. Nor did we examine whether viewer exposure to inter-journalism disparagement reduces trust in specific outlets or the institution of journalism. That certainly seems like a reasonable assumption, given the dramatically lower levels of trust in journalism among Republicans that we noted at the outset. We plan to investigate this relationship directly in future research. But what we do see in this research is that disparagement of the institution of journalism, and of particular news outlets, is a much more prominent component of Fox News programming than it is of either CNN or MSNBC. Some researchers have proposed that this kind of high-volume disparagement of news sources that don’t tow the same partisan line takes us beyond traditional notions of partisan journalism and into the realm of “anti-media media.” The goal of anti-media media is to “weaponize the facade of journalism against the roles assigned to journalism” in a democracy. Based on our findings, Fox News fits this characterization. Philip M. Napoli is the James R. Shepley Professor of Public Policy, director of the DeWitt Wallace Center for Media & Democracy, and director of undergraduate studies for the journalism and media minor in the Sanford School of Public Policy at Duke University. Adam Meskouri is a politics researcher at Harvard and Duke. Anjini Mani is an undergraduate at Duke. Grant Socol is a graduate research assistant at Duke. Harrison Walley is an undergraduate at Duke. Rather than analyze the entirety of the networks’ output over this time, we created a “constructed week” for each year, which is a common practice in this kind of content analysis. This involves selecting a random Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, etc. within each year, so that the sample of programming was reasonably representative of the year as a whole. We included all programming across all dayparts in our constructed weeks. Note: MSNBC was only available through 2023; the network became MS NOW in late 2025. Subscribe another address A study of nonprofit newsrooms reveals some cracks in the model’s foundation (Adobe Stock) Plus: Audiences aren’t too keen on AI news anchors, journalists say government funding doesn’t compromise their independence, and disillusionment in the profession is prevalent. By Seth C. Lewis and Nick Mathews Oct. 6, 2026, 2 p.m. Editor’s note: Mark Coddington , Seth Lewis , Tamar Wilner , and Nick Mathews write a regular newsletter on recent academic research around journalism. We’re happy to bring each issue to you here at Nieman Lab. Over the past decade, nonprofit news has been seen as one of the bright spots in U.S. journalism — an emblem of hope for the future amid a landscape littered with failures and financial struggles. RELATED ARTICLE Nonprofit news is growing strong — especially local nonprofit news, a new report shows Hanaa' Tameez October 8, 2025 With an average of 10 local newspapers closing each month , joining the thousands that have met that fate already, conditions out there are grim. Largely in response, more than 6,000 nonprofit foundations have made major investments in local news initiatives, totaling some half a billion dollars or more in direct funding for journalism. As a result, the number of U.S. nonprofit news organizations has been growing by double-digit percentages year-over-year. It’s fair to question whether this is sustainable. But in the meantime, at least, what’s not to like about this arrangement — this major push to subsidize local journalism at a time when the for-profit model for it is rapidly vanishing? Behind the scenes, it seems, there are cracks in the foundation, ones that appear to call for greater scrutiny to understand how sustainable and effective this model truly is moving forward. As described in an ethnographic study published recently in Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly, Jocelyn McKinnon-Crowley of the University of Memphis spent four months in late 2023 and early 2024 embedded in a four-person nonprofit newsroom in a midsized Rust Belt city, and also interviewed news workers at seven other nonprofit outlets. She focused on the question of labor: What is the impact of this type of journalism on the work and the workers involved? Her main finding is blunt: “The emphasis on funding, on money, and on organizational concerns has become the top priority for individuals working for nonprofit news entities.” And, as journalists “busy themselves” with these administrative chores and organizational imperatives — to keep grant money coming in, to keep funders happy, etc. — it not only comes at the expense of the journalism product but also extracts a heavy toll of unpaid labor from the news workers involved. The situation, McKinnon-Crowley writes, “leads to a double worker exploitation where journalists feel morally obligated to do good work as journalists and to do good work for a morally just (nonprofit) organization.” This exploitation, she says, is perpetuated by the nature of nonprofit reliance, as foundations often “take decision-making power away from journalists and the institution of journalism.” A clear example of this, she says, is the grant-making process, which can require an undue level of administrative burden and can force journalists to put the priorities and interests of funders ahead of those of the community. The result, she contends, is a pernicious cycle: Rather than allowing space for journalists to center the needs of their community, the voices and opinions of the funders are prioritized into perpetuity as nonprofits continually need external funding. This reproduces social inequality, as journalists are incentivized to favor those who can distribute wealth, mirroring similar global trends where the news contributes to making the “information rich get information richer.” Part of the challenge is that, unlike the wall that typically exists between editorial and advertising at for-profit news organizations, there are few clear lines of separation. Funders tend to sit on boards overseeing the news outlets. They shape application forms and set renewal cycles. Journalists interviewed described the “mental formulas they are constantly calculating to keep producing the news.” While such concerns have always been present to some degree — and for-profit news managers, no doubt, are often plenty stressed about their own funding arrangements — McKinnon-Crowley suggests these problems are particularly tough for nonprofit newsrooms given how small and precarious they tend to be, and given how quickly funding provided through one grant cycle can disappear entirely in the next. Even more, the researcher found a distressing level of unpaid work that seemed to be the rule, not the exception, in small-outlet nonprofit journalism. In one example, there was a journalist who officially held titles as executive director and managing editor, though he was not necessarily compensated for such higher-level work. Moreover, that was only the start of his duties required to keep the organization humming. McKinnon-Crowley writes: From what I observed, here is a list of some of his unofficial job duties: fundraiser, party planner, grant writer, mentor, teacher, board member, publisher, figurehead, reporter, editor, tech support, building maintainer, sounding board, community-liaison, coffee-buyer, freelance coordinator, radio personality, podcast scripter, scheduler, photographer, and social media manager. The upshot: Much of the actual work that this person wanted to do as a journalist was, by his own admission, “slipping through the cracks.” McKinnon-Crowley summed it up this way: “As I observed in the newsroom, if you have to return cheese trays from banquets and create fundraising emails, the split priorities lead to gaps in what the organization is able to do.” So, what should be done? McKinnon-Crowley recommends that funders give recurring money without restrictions, fund positions on a longer-term basis (5 to 10 years minimum), help pay for administrative overhead, require less paperwork burden in reporting back, and stop dictating coverage decisions. For nonprofit newsrooms, she says it’s time to start having more conversations about these issues — about what counts as unacceptable interference on the part of funders as well as what the risks are of asking journalists to do too much for too little compensation. In a service-oriented occupation like journalism, working within a “doing good” ethos of a nonprofit only accentuates the likelihood that reporters will treat their jobs like callings, get exploited in the process, and end up burned out and disillusioned (see more on that theme in the roundup below). RELATED ARTICLE A new book looks at how AI is rewiring the newsroom, for better and worse Seth C. Lewis August 6, 2026 “Human versus AI news anchors: A survey study on audience satisfaction and the emotional connection.” By Yuan Ji, in Journalism. China has been one of the world’s leading laboratories for AI news anchors. The experiment began in earnest in 2018, when the Xinhua News Agency introduced a virtual news presenter capable of delivering news around the clock. The pitch was simple: AI could provide a tireless, endlessly replicable alternative to a human anchor. Nearly a decade into that experiment, however, audiences don’t seem ready to trade in the humans. That’s the finding that stands out from a new study of 343 Chinese news consumers by researcher Yuan Ji. The study examined how audiences perceive AI anchors, including their engagement, emotional connection, and satisfaction compared with human anchors. The numbers tell a fairly clear story. Only 4.96% of respondents said they found AI anchors very engaging. Another 25.07% said they were somewhat engaging. So nearly three-quarters of respondents did not describe AI anchors as engaging in either of those ways. The satisfaction gap is even more pronounced. Just 5.25% said they were more satisfied with AI anchors than with human anchors. Another 24.78% said they were equally satisfied. That means roughly seven in 10 respondents did not report being equally or more satisfied with AI anchors. For news organizations, the finding raises an important question: What happens when technology solves a problem that audiences don’t necessarily think needs solving? AI anchors offer obvious efficiencies. They can work continuously, be reproduced across broadcasts and locations, and potentially reduce the costs associated with producing and presenting routine news. But those advantages matter less if audiences don’t find the result engaging or satisfying. That’s an important consideration for journalists as AI moves deeper into news production . The technology is getting better at mimicking the mechanics of journalism. But journalism is more than mechanics. As Yuan Ji found, audiences also respond to the people delivering the news — and to the sense of connection, credibility, and human presence those people provide. The finding doesn’t mean AI won’t change journalism. It does suggest that news organizations should think beyond what AI can do and consider what audiences actually value . Efficiency may be one reason to use an AI anchor, but efficiency alone doesn’t guarantee engagement or satisfaction. For now, the numbers offer some good news for human journalists in television. AI may be ready for the news desk, but audiences, at least for now, still seem to want a person sitting behind it. RELATED ARTICLE In Canada, a government program to support local news tries to determine who’s most deserving Sarah Scire May 8, 2020 “Government-funded watchdog journalism? Analyzing Canadian media workers’ self-perceptions of independence under the local journalism initiative.” By Chris Arsenault, in Journalism Practice. Government funding might seem like an obvious threat to journalistic independence. But Canadian journalists who receive public money say it hasn’t interfered with their work. Instead, many still point to advertisers as the bigger threat. This new study explores the journalists working under Canada’s Local Journalism Initiative , a federal program that has provided more than $128 million since 2019 to support hundreds of reporting positions at news organizations across the country. Researcher Chris Arsenault interviewed 22 journalists whose positions are supported by the program. What they said complicates the familiar concern in journalism, that accepting government money inevitably makes it harder for reporters to hold power to account. The journalists certainly recognized the optics. Many worried that government funding could make audiences question their independence or create the appearance of a conflict. But none said the funding had actually changed what they could report. None could point to a story they had avoided or softened because of the government support. And none could identify a source who had treated them differently because their salary was publicly funded. When journalists described actual threats to their independence, they were more likely to talk about advertisers. Several reporters recalled situations in which advertisers had made it more difficult to scrutinize local businesses, organizations or other powerful figures. For these journalists, commercial pressure wasn’t an abstract concern about appearances — it was something they had experienced in their newsrooms. That distinction is worth considering in an industry where the traditional business model has collapsed in many local communities. Journalists may understandably worry about accepting money from the government. But if the alternative is a newsroom with fewer reporters, fewer resources, and greater dependence on advertisers, public funding may sometimes give journalists more room to do independent reporting, not less. The journalists weren’t convinced the funding program could fix the larger financial problems facing local news, however. Many saw it as temporary help rather than a long-term solution. The findings suggest journalists may need to think differently about where threats to independence actually come from — whether from a dependence on government or advertising or some other source. Public funding may not eliminate the challenges facing local journalism, but it seems positioned to give reporters the resources and freedom to do work that commercial pressures have sometimes made harder. “‘This is how journalism has always been done’: White neutrality, newsroom norms, and an AI intervention in source diversification.” By Gavin Adamson, Asmaa Malik, Shari Okeke, and Jisele Bailey-Hay, in Journalism. Adding AI to the newsroom does not necessarily help journalists find better sources in the moment. In a new study of Canadian journalists, the technology was more useful as a mirror, helping reporters look back at their coverage and see whose voices they routinely include — and whose they don’t. Researchers interviewed 12 journalists at a mid-sized Canadian daily and demonstrated an AI tool designed to track the types of sources appearing in news stories. The tool categorizes sources into groups such as politicians, authorities, experts, organizations, and people speaking from personal experience. The journalists generally supported more inclusive sourcing. They saw it as important to accurate, fair and accountable journalism. But they also described why it can be difficult to put that ideal into practice. Time pressure, unsurprisingly, was a major obstacle. Reporters working on deadline often turn to sources they know they can reach quickly, including government officials, police, academic experts, and other institutional voices. Finding people outside those established networks takes time, particularly in newsrooms that have fewer reporters and less time for relationship-building. The result can be a heavy reliance on white and official sources, with the same voices and institutions appearing repeatedly in the news even when journalists recognize that their coverage would benefit from a broader range of perspectives. In this study, the AI tool was found to do little to change that during the reporting process. The journalists did not envision using it to tell them whom to call for a story or to help them find a source before deadline. Instead, they saw value in using it afterward, reviewing individual stories or larger collections of coverage to identify patterns in their sourcing. That makes the technology less of a reporting assistant and more of a feedback mechanism. It could help a reporter or editor notice, for example, how often official sources appear in their coverage or how rarely people with direct experience of an issue are quoted. That kind of reflection could matter if newsrooms use it as part of their regular editorial conversations. The technology can make patterns visible that are otherwise easy to overlook amid the daily rush of producing the news. But seeing a problem is not the same as fixing it. An AI system can identify who appeared in a story. It cannot build relationships with communities, earn the trust of unfamiliar sources, or give reporters more time to do the work. Overall, AI can help newsrooms see their sourcing habits more clearly, but it cannot, at present, create the conditions necessary to change them. If source diversity is going to become a sustained part of journalism, it will require newsroom expectations and resources to support it, not simply another piece of technology. “Stuck between democracy and a layoff: Connecting journalists’ personal disillusionment to overall normative press evaluations.” By Alexis Haskell, in Journalism Practice. Many journalists enter the profession believing they can make a difference. They expect to inform the public, explain complicated issues, give people a voice, and contribute to democracy. This new study suggests that when those expectations collide with the realities of working in journalism, journalists can become disillusioned with more than their own jobs. Alexis Haskell surveyed 695 U.S. journalists and found that disillusionment is a measurable experience among American journalists. The concept is different from burnout, the researcher argues. Burnout describes exhaustion and being overwhelmed by work. Disillusionment describes a deeper break between what journalists expected their careers to be and what they actually experienced. On average, the journalists surveyed were more disillusioned than not. Haskell measured the concept through their feelings about their work, their expectations for the profession and their sense of purpose. That disillusionment was also reflected in how journalists viewed journalism as a whole. Those who were more disillusioned were more likely to give the press lower marks for five of six democratic roles examined by the study. They were less positive about journalism’s ability to inform, analyze, provide a forum for public discussion, foster social empathy, and mobilize audiences. The strongest relationships were found in analysis and the public forum. More disillusioned journalists were particularly likely to believe the press was failing to help people understand complicated issues or provide space for public conversation. There was one exception: Disillusionment was not related to journalists’ evaluations of investigative journalism. Haskell suggests that investigative work may occupy a different place in journalism’s professional culture. It is highly prestigious, frequently celebrated through major awards and often associated with individual achievement. The other roles are more directly tied to journalism’s service to audiences and communities. That difference gets at what makes disillusionment important. Journalists who are disillusioned aren’t necessarily saying they can no longer do good journalism. They may instead be questioning whether journalism, as a profession, is accomplishing what they believed it was supposed to accomplish. The finding connects the personal experience of working in journalism with a broader assessment of the field. When journalists encounter low wages, layoffs, shrinking staffs, and other pressures, the consequences may extend beyond their own careers. They may begin to lose faith not just in the job, but in journalism’s ability to fulfill the public purpose that drew them to it in the first place. A previous version of this piece stated that 550 nonprofit newsrooms operate in the U.S. This is inaccurate and it is difficult to estimate the number of nonprofit newsrooms in the country. results.evidenceText: Rex Ryan Arrested For Allegedly Hitting 2 Pedestrians, Running Over Their Feet Former NBA Star Baron Davis Gives Cold Response to Sister's Lawsuit Over Home Ex-NFL Coach Rex Ryan's Alleged Hit-And-Run Victims Speak Out Ex-NFL Star Shawne Merriman: Read Texts With Friend From Day Playboy Model Died Matthew Stafford's Wife Kelly Fires Back at Facelift Comment Aaron Rodgers Poses With Brother Jordan After Years-Long Family Feud Metropolitan Nashville Police News Rex Ryan turned himself in to authorities Wednesday morning ... after the former NFL head coach allegedly ran over the feet of two pedestrians while driving his pickup truck in Nashville. It's a shocking allegation against a guy who LOVES feet. According to Nashville PD, the 63-year-old former Jets coach was driving his truck just before midnight last Thursday when he made a right turn, running over the feet of two people who were crossing the street. Getty The alleged victims told police Ryan kept driving, but they managed to catch up to him at a red light ... where a heated argument kicked off, with Rex even getting out of his vehicle. After exchanging words, the pedestrians told cops Ryan bolted without exchanging information ... but they were able to snap a photo of his license plate. The pedestrians went to the authorities, and a warrant was issued for Rex's arrest. The charges ... two counts of leaving the scene of an accident, two counts of failing to give information/render aid, and two counts of failing to obey traffic signals. Getty His bond has been set at $6K. The whole incident is ironic, if nothing else. Back in 2010, Deadspin published videos of Ryan rubbing a woman's feet, and the jokes always been, the dude loves feet. results.evidenceText: Dianna Russini's comeback over before it started as livestream plagued by tech issues Skip to content Credit: The Russini Report By Drew Lerner on 11/11/2026 11/11/2026 Less AI and more AA in your search results. Believe it or not, the offshore sportsbook nobody had heard of until it announced a weekly show starring Dianna Russini earlier this week wasn’t ready for its big moment. The aforementioned sportsbook, BetUS, was unable to get its livestream of The Russini Report off the ground at noon ET on Wednesday, when the show was set to make its debut. The page on its website featured an embedded video with elevator music and rotating pictures of Russini with a caption reading “show starts soon” for more than 30 minutes past 12 p.m. ET. And funnily enough, that video wasn’t even an embedded livestream, but just a 90-second clip that would play on repeat. Those who looked for The Russini Report on other platforms also struck out. The X page for the show posted a link that said “WATCH HERE” that was completely broken and didn’t even lead to a webpage. The Russini Report YouTube channel did not feature any sort of livestream. And the BetUS Vimeo account, which embedded the 90-second clip on its website, was set to private. 🚨🔴THE MOMENT IS HERE. WE ARE LIVE! 🔥 🎥WATCH HERE: https://t.co/6M35HOJrG6 🎙️🏈 THE RUSSINI REPORT with @DMRussini officially kicks off! 🔥 Breaking NFL news, insider scoops & unfiltered takes! 🏆 Bill Parcells 🎙️ @DamonAmendo 🔥 @SpikeEskin 📺 WATCH LIVE ON BETUS TV! https://t.co/pLfXt1I4x4 — The Russini Report (@RussiniReport) November 11, 2026 If there was a worst-case scenario that Russini and BetUS imagined for the show’s debut, this probably exceeded those expectations in the worst way. At 12:24 p.m. ET, nearly a half-hour after the show was scheduled to start, the show’s X handle claimed it was the overwhelming number of people trying to watch the stream that “broke it.” Well… you broke it. 😅 The premiere of The Russini Report drew a record-breaking audience today! We’re adding more seats so everyone gets in. Stay with us! We’ll be back shortly. 🙏 — The Russini Report (@RussiniReport) November 11, 2026 “The premiere of The Russini Report drew a record-breaking audience today!” the post embarrassingly went on to claim. “We’re adding more seats so everyone gets in.” How can a show that never even happened draw a “record-breaking audience,” you may ask? We’re still trying to figure that out ourselves. And for starters, blaming the people tuning in for the show for the technical difficulties, and not whoever is producing it, won’t exactly put Russini and BetUS in the good graces of the fans she’s looking to win back. It’s impossible to take this venture seriously . The X handle doesn’t even have a profile picture. This is amateur hour all around. And as this post goes live around 12:40 p.m. ET on Wednesday, there is still no show to speak of. If there’s a definition of Dead On Arrival, this could very well be it. UPDATE [12:53 p.m. ET]: The first episode of The Russini Report was posted on Vimeo about 50 minutes after it was scheduled to debut. The show appears to be prerecorded, though the original post advertising the show at noon ET seemed to suggest it’d be live. Russini also opens the show by letting viewers know she will keep an eye on emails being sent in, with the implication she’d address them live on the air. It’s unclear if the original plan was to do the show live or prerecord it. Either way, there was some mixed messaging. Russini largely stuck to football throughout the episode, though at the very end she thanks her “new family at BetUS” before thanking her “own family.” About Drew Lerner Drew Lerner is a staff writer for Awful Announcing and an aspiring cable subscriber. results.evidenceText: Hundreds of ‘pink slime’ local news outlets are distributing algorithmic stories and conservative talking points - Columbia Journalism Review Editor’s Note: This is the first of our four pieces on this network. In August 2020, we found that the size of the network had nearly tripled to over 1200 sites. In October 2021, we found that the network had received funding from multiple dark money groups as well as collaborated with advocacy groups on topics to […] " /> Editor’s Note: This is the first of our four pieces on this network. In August 2020, we found that the size of the network had nearly tripled to over 1200 sites. In October 2021, we found that the network had received funding from multiple dark money groups as well as collaborated with advocacy groups on topics to […] "> Editor’s Note: This is the first of our four pieces on this network. In August 2020, we found that the size of the network had nearly tripled to over 1200 sites. In October 2021, we found that the network had received funding from multiple dark money groups as well as collaborated with advocacy groups on topics to […] "> b Tow Report   b Editor’s Note: This is the first of our four pieces on this network. In August 2020, we found that the size of the network had nearly tripled to over 1200 sites . In October 2021, we found that the network had received funding from multiple dark money groups as well as collaborated with advocacy groups on topics to cover prior to the 2020 Election.   A n increasingly popular tactic challenges conventional wisdom on the spread of electoral disinformation: the creation of partisan outlets masquerading as local news organizations. An investigation by the Tow Center for Digital Journalism at Columbia Journalism School has discovered at least 450 websites in a network of local and business news organizations, each distributing thousands of algorithmically generated articles and a smaller number of reported stories. Of the 450 sites we discovered, at least 189 were set up as local news networks across ten states within the last twelve months by an organization called Metric Media. Titles like the East Michigan News , Hickory Sun, and Grand Canyon Times have appeared on the web ahead of the 2020 election. These networks of sites can be used in a variety of ways: as ‘stage setting’ for events, focusing attention on issues such as voter fraud and energy pricing, providing the appearance of neutrality for partisan issues, or to gather data from users that can then be used for political targeting. On October 20, the Lansing State Journal first broke the story of the network’s existence. About three dozen local news sites, owned by Metric Media , had appeared in Michigan. Further reporting by the Michigan Daily , the Guardian and the New York Times identified yet more sites. Ultimately, previous reporting has identified around 200 of these sites. Our analysis suggests that there are at least twice that number of publications across a number of related networks, of which Metric Media is just one component. Over a two-week period starting November 26, we tapped into the RSS feeds of these 189 Metric Media sites, all of which were created this year, and found over fifteen thousand unique stories had been published (over fifty thousand when aggregated across the sites), but only about a hundred titles had the bylines of human reporters. The rest cited automated services or press releases. Sign up for CJR’s daily email Many of the stories attributed to automated services (Metric Media News Service, Local Labs News Service, etc.) relied on data releases from federal programs like the Department of Education and Department of Health and Human Services, Congressional Research Service, the Federal Election Commission, and the Census Bureau. Another frequently used data sources in Metric Media’s automated stories is GasBuddy, a Boston-based startup that monitors gas station prices in North America and Australia. Some of the pieces attributed to human writers also rely on public data, from a Tax Foundation study that established the cents per gallon each state collected in wine taxes, in one instance, or a builders association study that rated structural deficiencies in bridges in another. Interspersed between stories about real estate prices and the best place to purchase premium gas based on zip code, newsier pieces appear, sometimes to quote a state senator about how the federal government should not play a role in education . Others quoted various exclusively Republican officials like US senators, chairpeople, or communications staff of the state GOP, about the impeachment process being a witch hunt or abuse of power . The networks can be traced back to conservative businessman Brian Timpone. In 2012, Timpone’s company Journatic, an outlet known for its low-cost automated story generation (which became known as ‘ pink slime journalism ’), attracted national attention and outrage for faking bylines and quotes, and for plagiarism. Journatic rebranded as Locality Labs in 2013; Locality Labs is behind many of the publications we discovered that mimic the appearance and output of traditional news organizations. These sites do not bear much information about their political use or funding, but some of them have been funded by political candidates and lobbying campaigns. Metric Media , Locality Labs (or LocalLabs), Franklin Archer , the Record Inc. , and Local Government Information Services (LGIS) are the main organizations involved in operating these networks of publications, and Timpone is associated in one way or another with each of them. Michigan Daily has detailed the convoluted relationship between these organizations. Some of these mysterious, partisan local news sites publish physical newspapers and many have minimal social media presence. At first, they do not appear to be owned by the same network or organization, but a number of clues suggest that they are intimately linked. Our analysis demonstrates the links between the networks by identifying shared markers, such as unique analytics tokens, server IP addresses, and even shared design templates and bylines on articles. Further, the Privacy Policy and Terms of Service for many of these websites—but not all—suggest they are part of Locality Labs, LLC. Websites and networks can aid campaigns to manipulate public opinion by exploiting faith in local media. The demise of local journalism in many areas creates an information vacuum, and raises the chance of success for these influence campaigns. The strategy is further made possible by the low cost of automating news stories, repurposing press releases (including obituaries from funeral homes), and replicating design templates, as well as the relative ease with which political or single-issue campaigns can obscure their funding and provenance. One in five newspapers has closed in the past decade , and many other outlets have significantly cut staff and reporting. This bleak landscape for local news creates space for this cottage industry of outlets that claim to produce journalism—typically during election cycles—and create and amplify material to support political outcomes, sometimes even physically mailing advertising materials that masquerade as newspapers but are not labeled political advertising. These publications cover certain candidates and topics, including limited government, tort reform, and labour unions, with a conservative bias. It is not clear how effective the sites are, but their architecture and strategy is useful to understand the way they co-opt the language, design and structure of news organizations. Automation has been touted as a way to create stories where there are few reporting resources, and it can be used to build credibility. It can also make a news organization look far more prolific than it is. Potentially adding to the credibility of these sites is their Google search ranking: in the case of some of the websites set up in 2015-2016, we observed that once sites had gained ample authority, they appeared on the first page of Google Search results just below the official government and social media pages. The Lansing State Journal ’s story highlights Metric Media’s intent to launch hundreds of such sites to “fill the void in local communities.” And, while Metric Media hasn’t been embroiled in controversies like its sibling organizations, the Journal’s story quotes Matt Grossmann, director of Michigan State University’s Institute for Public Policy and Social Research, who said, “many [articles] on [Metric Media site The] Lansing Sun appeared to be right-leaning.” Using multiple network analysis tools, we found at least 450 websites including the ones identified by previous reporting. There are dedicated networks with anywhere between five and forty sites per state in eleven states. Additionally, every state in the US (and Washington DC) has a dedicated “business daily” (e.g. Michigan Business Daily , Utah Business Daily ), and there are several international “business daily” websites (e.g. Toronto Business Daily, Mexico Business Daily, Manila Business Daily) as well . These are augmented by several single-subject sites (e.g. American Security News , Tobacco Newswire , Farm Insurance News ), and community sites that aggregate events, news, and business services information (e.g. Metro East Today , Wilton Review , Palmerton Guide ).   450 sites, 12 state networks, 5 corporate entities The 450 websites span twenty-one different networks operated by five distinct corporate entities. Below, we provide further detail about each of these organizations and how they’re linked. Figure 1: Breakdown of sites across networks, including the sites for multiple corporate entities or parent organizations (“Organizations”) such as LGIS, Franklin Archer, Metro Business Network, or Dan Proft’s PAC Liberty Principles. The overall distribution of sites across the networks is shown in Figure 1, with Franklin Archer’s Local News Network the single largest network with almost 130 sites. In the case of Franklin Archer, we conflated nine standalone sites that bear all the heuristics of their local news sites, even though these sites were not explicitly listed on the organization’s website. These include Surprise Journal , El Paso Review , and Lansing Reporter . With the Local News Network sites added to the 51 sites in the Metro Business network, the overall number under the Franklin Archer banner stands at 179, a close second to Metric Media, which has 189 publications across ten states. Metric Media’s North Carolina operation alone has 46 sites, making it the third biggest individual network in our dataset. For clarity, we have also conflated 25 standalone sites—sixteen topical sites, and nine international sites—under “LocalLabs: International” and “LocalLabs: Topical” in Figure 1 . These sites have a Locality Labs , LLC privacy policy or shared analytics identifier, but no other associations. In some cases, the privacy policy is not even linked on the homepage. The Mexico Business Daily , for example, doesn’t mention any affiliation in its “About Us” or “Contact” pages, and there is no privacy policy on its homepage. This link suggests it is a Locality Labs property. CISTRAN Finance follows the exact same pattern. In other cases, like the Toronto Business Daily or the Balkan News Wire , the privacy policy is linked to from the homepage, but no other affiliations are mentioned. In our analysis so far, websites on the Metric Media state-centric networks only link to other sites from the same state, including stories from Franklin Archer’s Metro Business network. There are, however, few indicators that the sites are operated by the same organization. On sites in both networks, the privacy policies and terms of service suggest they are operated by Locality Labs, LLC. Stories covering vastly different topics across the network share bylines, as well as similar—often identical—templates. These anecdotal pieces of evidence can only be gleaned after identifying the scale of the operation. To measure the scale of the operation, we relied on website metadata and network forensics: the sites shared IP addresses and various analytics identifiers. Within the same network—and even the same organization—that is expected behavior. It is highly unusual for sites to share IP addresses and analytics identifiers if they are not connected, but that’s exactly what we found in these networks, as can be seen below.   Shared IP addresses Each domain maps to an IP address, which identifies the server where the site is hosted. Across this greater network of networks, including the domains for the organizations, we found about twenty-five unique IP addresses. Some of these networks, including the biggest—Franklin Archer: Local News Network—don’t share an IP address or server with any other network as can be seen in Figure 2. Some only share IP addresses with other sites that belong to the same parent organization. For example, some state-level Metric Media properties—the publications in New Mexico, Arizona and Montana—share a server. But, Metric Media’s Maryland properties (which includes North Baltimore Journal , Harford News , Montgomery News ) also sit on the same server as the LGIS sites, which is more unusual. Similarly, it is improbable for sites within Franklin Archer’s Business Network to share an IP address with LocalLabs’ international or topical sites, unless the two organizations share resources. Some of the parent organization’s websites live on the same server as some of the LocalLabs’ topical properties, too. To wit: The Record (therecordinc.com), Franklin Archer (franklinarcher.com) and Dan Proft’s super PAC Liberty Principles (libertyprinciples.com) are on the same server as Tobacco Newswire , FDA Reporter , and FDA Health News . Figure 2: Network graph of shared IP addresses; each different edge colour represents a different IP address   Shared Google Analytics IDs Even though there were over twenty Google Analytics IDs, only five were used on more than one network. Of these, three identifiers were shared within Metric Media sites only, while another three were shared among Franklin Archer, LGIS, and the LocalLabs sites ( Figure 3 ). It is highly unlikely for independent, supposedly unrelated organizations like LGIS and Franklin Archer to share analytics identifiers. Figure 3: Network graph of shared Google Analytics IDs; each different edge colour represents a different Google Analytics ID At the time of writing, the Franklin Archer organizational website (franklinarcher.com), publications belonging to LGIS, and topical websites like American Security News , Power Newswire, and Higher Education Tribune shared the same Google Analytics ID. International sites like Gulf News Journal and a handful of business dailies also had that same identifier.   A Single Shared NewRelic ID and Quantcast ID Perhaps no other identifier illustrates the convoluted nature of these networks as well as the NewRelic ID ( Figure 4 ) and the Quantcast ID ( Figure 5 ). Most of Metric Media’s properties didn’t have a corresponding NewRelic ID, nor did the Florida network’s. ther networks, though, shared the same identifier, including Metric Media’s Maryland sites. Also, for the first time, we see the publications within the Record network, the first site of which was established in 2004, sharing an identifier with the greater network. Figure 4: Network graph of the single shared NewRelic ID Similarly, a single Quantcast identifier was used across LGIS, Record, and Metric Media sites. ( Figure 5 ). Much like the NewRelic ID, this too shows the connected nature of the networks. Figure 5: Networks connected by a single unique Quantcast ID. The Franklin Archer publications don’t seem to be relying on Quantcast identifiers at all, but Metric Media does, as do the Record network and LGIS. When we discovered the high volume of sites intricately linked across a convoluted network, we set about trying to identify the people behind these organizations, and their backgrounds. In reporting from the Lansing State Journal , Michigan Daily , and the Guardian , as well as our own analysis, one name appeared time and again: Brian Timpone. The sites in our dataset go back to 2004 with the inception of the first publication—the Madison-St. Clair Record— which is now part of the Record network. In the next section, we’ll trace through the emergence of various publications, networks, and their impact.   The Record Network The Record Network is a system of eleven publications, the first of which—the Madison-St. Clair Record —went live in 2004. The network’s publications cover the legal system in eight states; one of the outlets, Legal Newsline, is not bound to a single state. Even before Journatic was set up in 2006, Timpone was the founding publisher of sites in the Record network, which have come under scrutiny for being run by advocacy groups disguised as media organizations. Timpone is currently listed as founding publisher of the Madison-St. Clair Record and the Louisiana Record identifies him as the publisher. According to the “About Us” page on a subset of Record network sites (including Legal Newsline, Madison-St. Clair Record and Florida Record ), they are owned by the US Chamber Institute for Legal Reform , an affiliate of the US Chamber of Commerce—an organization, according to OpenSecrets , that since 2008 has been one of the biggest “dark money” spenders in US elections. Fifteen years later, these sites are still very much active.   LocalLabs/Locality Labs LocalLabs, another Timpone company, was a rebranding of Journatic in the aftermath of a 2012 scandal over plagiarism, falsified quotes , and fake bylines . For the last twenty months or so, the website for LocalLabs has simply said “We’re improving our site. Stay tuned for a new and improved LocalLabs.com.” Previously, the website detailed the services the organization provided, declaring that “LocalLabs offers community news production, advertising and advertorial content, print special sections and web and mobile application management.” We found over forty websites with the disclaimer “a product of LocalLabs” or a privacy policy/terms of service page suggesting the sites are operated by Locality Labs, LLC. Fifteen of these sites, all registered in 2018 , belong to a single network in a single state: Florida. At the time of writing, we had not found a Metric Media operation in Florida. results.pageDescription: The race in the special election for Ohio’s open senate seat is its final stages.
results.evidenceText: Husted addresses HB6 ties, rising prices in Ohio Senate push Skip to content Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google COLUMBUS, Ohio (WOIO) - The race in the special election for Ohio’s open senate seat is its final stages. Current Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, was selected by Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine to serve the final two years of former Sen. JD Vance’s term after Vance was elected vice president. Husted is trying to stay in Washington but is being challenged by former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, who lost two years ago to Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno. The polls have indicated this is a very close race. Some polls indicate Brown has a slight lead, others say it’s Husted. Today, I was given 15 minutes with Husted while on the campaign trail in Columbus. In our one-on-one interview, I asked about the closeness of the race and what he will try to do to win in the closing weeks. I also asked about the two areas Brown and the Democrats are using to attack Husted. First, his connection to House Bill 6 while he was lieutenant governor in Ohio, which ended up being the largest corruption scandal in state history. Husted had to testify in the trail against two former FirstEnergy executives accused of bribing lawmakers to get HB6 passed. The second area Husted is being attached to is the issues of data centers. While lieutenant governor, a number of data centers opened in the state. Husted was quick to point out that whenever a new data center would open, then-Sen. Brown was quick to celebrate the opening and send out media releases. In the above interview, Husted addresses both issues and topics on the economy and rising prices for families. results.pageDescription: As Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy came under fire for releasing an attack ad featuring his Democratic competitor Amy Acton's estranged mother, a mysterious news site was running a Facebook ad boosting the controversial video.
results.evidenceText: California conservative group linked to Ohio news site promoting Ramaswamy Acton ad - Los Angeles Times Advertisement California Mystery Ohio news site boosting Ramaswamy’s Amy Acton ad tied to conservative California nonprofit President Trump listens as gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy speaks Oct. 12 at a campaign rally at the Covelli Centre in Youngstown, Ohio. (Jacquelyn Martin / Associated Press) By  Clara Harter Staff Writer Follow Oct. 25, 2026 8:08 AM PT 87 10 min Click here to listen to this article Share via Close extra sharing options Email Facebook X LinkedIn Threads Reddit WhatsApp Copy Link URL Copied! Print 0:00 0:00 1x This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here . See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> As Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy came under fire for releasing an attack ad featuring his Democratic competitor’s estranged mother, a mysterious news site was running a Facebook ad boosting the controversial video. The Buckeye Bulletin, which bills itself as an Ohio-based news platform committed to “reliable journalism” and “strong editorial standards,” popped up suddenly this spring and began pumping out a steady stream of pro-Ramaswamy content. The publication’s articles have no bylines. There is no list of staff. The website does not feature digital advertisements, nor does it prompt readers to subscribe, but there is also no disclosure of who is funding it. Advertisement A closer look at the Buckeye Bulletin’s Meta advertising data shows that its Facebook and Instagram accounts are managed by the Lincoln Media Foundation, a nonprofit organization affiliated with the Orange County-based Lincoln Club — the oldest and largest conservative donor organization in California. IRS documents show that the club and foundation are associated organizations and share at least two key executives. Meta’s advertising data show that the Lincoln Media Foundation manages the Instagram and Facebook accounts for the Buckeye Bulletin. (Meta) The Buckeye Bulletin, Lincoln Club and Lincoln Media Foundation did not respond to requests for comment. Advertisement The Bulletin appears to be a partisan site posing as a local news outlet ahead of the midterm elections, a strategy political scientists refer to as “pink-slime” journalism. This is not the first time a pink-slime outlet has been linked to the Lincoln Media Foundation. In 2024 Max Read, director of civic innovation for the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, identified seven such alleged outlets . With the exception of one Los Angeles-focused site, those outlets all targeted critical states for the 2024 presidential election such as Georgia, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Read reported that the media group had spent more than $63,000 on Facebook and Instagram ads, resulting in up to 18 million impressions during the last election cycle. “[The sites were] very clearly designed to try to influence the information environment ahead of the presidential election,” Read told The Times. “They had all been started early in the year and used advertising on Meta platforms to juice their engagement numbers.” When asked by The Times to take a look at the Buckeye Bulletin, Read said it appeared to be “pretty much copy and paste the same tactic that they used in 2024, even down to the aesthetics of the Facebook page and Instagram account.” “It seems like they realized this worked at some level in 2024 and is worth doing again this year,” he said. Advertisement Earlier this year, CalMatters identified another outlet tied to the Lincoln Media Foundation called the California Courier, which had been circulating Facebook advertisements criticizing Gov. Gavin Newsom and the statewide redistricting ballot measure Proposition 50. California Could this mysterious news site influence California’s 2026 election? The Courier is part of a growing ecosystem of news publications that publish biased articles in an attempt to surreptitiously influence elections. Jan. 11, 2026 Since the Buckeye Bulletin’s Facebook and Instagram pages launched in March, the outlet has shared posts touting endorsements of Ramaswamy — a biotech billionaire and former presidential candidate — as well as his platform for addressing Ohio’s healthcare crisis and his stance on religious freedom in schools. Simultaneously, the outlet’s social media posts have highlighted the refusal of his opponent — Amy Acton, Ohio’s former public health director — to debate, comments on how she “shut down” the state’s economy during the COVID-19 pandemic and a video with a watermark from right-wing political activist Laura Loomer. Last week, the outlet turned attention to Ramaswamy’s controversial campaign ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur. In the ad, Arthur calls her daughter a liar and urges voters not to support her. However, the ad did not acknowledge that Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather, Arthur’s husband, was indicted for raping Acton when she was a child — an omission that drew fierce condemnation from Democrats and some Republicans, including Ohio’s Republican Gov. Mike DeWine. Others, including President Trump and Vice President JD Vance, an Ohioan, have defended the ad. Arthur and her husband fled after his 1978 indictment to Pennsylvania, where he died in 2004 without having been brought back to Ohio to face the charge. Advertisement Peppered between political content on the Bulletin’s social media feeds is a smattering of reels related to nonpolitical news, often featuring videos lifted directly from local TV stations. These other posts are used to create a “veneer of genuine local journalism,” Read said. The language on the Bulletin’s About Us page displays markers of artificial intelligence such as generic mission statements, polished but repetitive phrasing, and vague claims about journalistic standards with no details about the publication’s staff. Of the last 30 posts shared on the Bulletin’s Facebook as of 5 p.m. Friday, 21 were about state or national politics and 10 were about the gubernatorial race. Engagement on the posts dealing with Ramaswamy and Acton is consistently strong for a page with around 5,600 followers. For example, a Wednesday post on Ohio State Medical Assn.’s PAC endorsing Ramaswamy received more than 770 likes, 260 comments and 150 shares. Another video posted Wednesday with the label “Amy Acton refuses to debate, says mother is lying about her” received more than 4,800 likes, 1,500 comments and 500 shares. Meanwhile, a nonpolitical Wednesday post on a chemical explosion in Toledo received two likes, no comments and no shares. The unassuming social media scroller or person who clicked onto the website would have no clue of the Buckeye Bulletin’s apparent connection to a group of wealthy Southern California Republications. Advertisement The Lincoln Media Foundation was started by leaders of the historic Lincoln Club , which was founded in 1962 and once counted John Wayne and former President Nixon as members. Today, the club describes itself as home to “the most prominent business and thought leaders” in California and says it offers members the opportunity to meet world leaders and “experience their hobbies come to life through a combination of extravagance and leisure.” The foundation notes that it uses a digital approach to reach communities left out of the national conversation, but its website does not disclose providing funding to any news outlets. IRS records show that the nonprofit’s financial activities kicked up dramatically in 2024, the latest year for which data are available. The Lincoln Media Foundation reported $3.88 million in revenue in 2024, compared with $738,000 in 2023, $453,000 in 2022 and $415,000 in 2021. The Buckeye Bulletin’s Facebook and Instagram accounts have spent just over $10,000 boosting posts this year, according to Meta’s ad library . That’s barely a drop in the bucket in Ohio, where hotly contested races for governor and U.S. Senate have drawn hundreds of millions in spending. But presenting a slanted political view under the guise of local news tends to offer more bang for your buck than traditional advertisements, said Georgia Kernell, an associate professor in the departments of communications and political science at UCLA. Advertisement “Voters are so sick of ads; they’re getting tons of clear paid advertisements on the radio, on the television and on their social media feeds now,” she said. “Anything that can kind of look different is going to be more likely to keep their attention.” Presenting as a traditional news source also increases the likelihood of viewers believing that the information presented is well-researched, she said. Nik Usher, associate professor of communications at the University of San Diego, said it’s unclear how much influence pink-slime journalism is having on voting behavior, but political strategists are willing to try any new approach to possibly make a difference in tight races. “This is one strategic effort to throw more spaghetti at the wall, hoping it’ll stick,” Usher said. Creators of these partisan sites further stand to benefit from the fact that artificial intelligence tools are constantly scraping content from news websites without paywalls. Researchers at NewsGuard recently found that leading AI chatbots are citing pink-slime websites nearly half the time when users ask questions about candidates and issues in the midterm elections. Advertisement Democrats and Republicans have increasingly leveraged pink-slime journalism to influence voters in the past few election cycles. In 2020, the New York Times identified a network of 1,300 news sites that paid freelance writers to produce biased content for Republican groups and corporate public relations firms. In 2024, the left-leaning Star Spangled Media group used a site called the Morning Mirror to promote down-ballot Democratic candidates, according to research from Columbia Journalism School’s Tow Center for Digital Journalism. More recently, the evolution of AI has increased the ease with which these websites can be populated with content, eliminating the need to pay writers and automating the production of social media posts. Usher described pink-slime websites as “explosive bombs for public trust” that take advantage of the gap created by the loss of independent local papers and further diminish expectations for news to be fairly reported. “Once these sorts of sites are pointed out to the public it further undermines distrust in political institutions, political parties, the news media,” Usher said, “especially when AI is associated with this kind of stuff.” More to Read As local news deserts grow, nonprofit invests nearly $600 million in journalism Nov. 10, 2026 Voices Chabria: What decent people get wrong about the Amy Acton ad Oct. 25, 2026 Who is Vivek Ramaswamy and why did so many of his GOP presidential rivals attack him?
