(Photo: Governor Mike DeWine / YouTube) Gov. Mike DeWine says he won't campaign with Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican he endorsed for governor, and declined to call him one of the GOP ticket's 'really good people.' The rebuke follows DeWine's condemnation of Ramaswamy's advertisement attacking Democrat Amy Acton through her estranged mother, Donna Arthur. DeWine says his endorsement stands. Key points DeWine's direct defense of Acton's honesty against the ad's accusations Cledith Arthur's criminal charges for sexually abusing Acton as a child Trump and Vance's defense of Ramaswamy's ad against Republican criticism By Jen Ziegler Gov. Mike DeWine is refusing to campaign with Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican he endorsed to succeed him, and declined to include Ramaswamy among the “really good people” on the GOP ticket when a reporter pressed him to clarify his praise. The rebuke came Friday, one day after DeWine publicly condemned a Ramaswamy campaign advertisement attacking Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton through her estranged mother, despite the family’s documented history of childhood sexual abuse. DeWine has demanded that Ramaswamy withdraw the advertisement, defended Acton’s honesty against its accusations and now ruled out campaigning alongside his own party’s nominee for governor. Yet he refuses to withdraw his endorsement, citing his earlier commitment to support the Republican ticket. “We have some really good people on that ticket,” DeWine told WEWS reporter Morgan Trau, according to the station’s October 23 report . Asked whether Ramaswamy was one of them, the governor paused before explaining whom he meant. “Well, I was really talking about people I’ve worked with … for years and years. I’ve served with them in public office in Ohio.” Ramaswamy, a businessman and former presidential candidate, has never held elected office. DeWine’s answer left little ambiguity about whom he was praising. Given an opportunity to include his endorsed successor among the Republicans he considers “really good people,” the governor instead described longtime public officials with whom he had served — a group that does not include Ramaswamy. With the November 3 election approaching, Ohio’s sitting Republican governor is keeping his endorsement of Ramaswamy while refusing to stand beside him on the campaign trail. DeWine defends Acton’s honesty, contradicting Ramaswamy’s attack The governor’s refusal to campaign with Ramaswamy follows an even more direct disagreement over the Republican nominee’s treatment of Acton, who served as DeWine’s health director during the COVID-19 pandemic. Ramaswamy’s advertisement features Donna Arthur, Acton’s estranged biological mother, accusing her daughter of lying about her childhood. The attack centers on a family history involving abuse, neglect and criminal charges against Acton’s stepfather. Court records obtained by WEWS show that Acton’s stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested and charged with sexually abusing her when she was a child. He fled before trial and later died. Acton’s mother lost custody of Acton and her brother, and Acton has said she has had no contact with her mother since she was 12. Ramaswamy nevertheless put Arthur in a campaign advertisement attacking Acton’s credibility. He subsequently acknowledged that the advertisement came from his campaign and announced plans to spend $4 million promoting it on television and digital platforms. DeWine called reporters to the Ohio Statehouse on Thursday to condemn the advertisement and demand its removal. “It’s deeply, deeply, deeply troubling,” DeWine said. “It needs to come down; it’s just wrong to continue to run it.” DeWine did more than object to the campaign’s decision to involve Acton’s estranged mother. He directly defended Acton’s truthfulness, rejecting the accusation at the center of Ramaswamy’s advertisement based on his own experience working with her. “In regard to telling the truth, my experience with her and working closely with her every single day was that she certainly told the truth; that’s my experience,” DeWine said. DeWine’s assessment directly contradicts the advertisement’s portrayal of Acton as a liar. The governor worked closely with her during one of the most consequential periods of his administration, while Ramaswamy’s campaign has relied on accusations from a mother who lost custody of Acton decades ago. Ramaswamy has defended the advertisement rather than withdrawing it. His campaign has maintained that Arthur’s accusations concern Acton’s credibility, not the sexual abuse she experienced as a child. DeWine has rejected that separation, arguing that the family’s documented history makes the advertisement especially wrong. DeWine keeps his endorsement but refuses to campaign Despite condemning the advertisement and refusing to campaign with Ramaswamy, DeWine has insisted that his endorsement will remain in place. “I’m not changing the endorsement. I endorse the whole ticket,” DeWine told reporters Thursday. He explained that he had committed to supporting Ohio’s Republican candidates, many of whom are longtime colleagues. But his comments Friday drew a distinction between those Republicans and the gubernatorial nominee whose advertisement he had just condemned. The governor’s position leaves Ramaswamy with an endorsement from Ohio’s highest-ranking Republican state official but without his willingness to campaign alongside him. DeWine has also previously praised Ohio Senate President Rob McColley, Ramaswamy’s running mate and a Republican from Napoleon in northwest Ohio. McColley has worked with the governor as a legislative leader, unlike Ramaswamy, who entered the gubernatorial race without prior elected-office experience. The distinction matters for the Republican ticket. DeWine’s refusal to campaign with Ramaswamy does not extend, at least publicly, to McColley or other statewide Republican candidates. The governor has not announced whether he intends to make separate appearances with them before Election Day. Nor has DeWine publicly identified any previously scheduled appearances with Ramaswamy that were canceled. What he has established is that he will not campaign with the Republican seeking to replace him. Trump and Vance defend the ad as Ohio Republicans split The dispute has divided prominent Republicans in the final weeks of the governor’s race, with President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance defending Ramaswamy while DeWine and other Republican figures have criticized the advertisement. Trump defended the attack and encouraged Ramaswamy to continue airing it. Vance, appearing in Ohio on Wednesday, criticized Republicans objecting to the advertisement and praised Ramaswamy for confronting Acton. Other Republicans have publicly rejected the campaign’s tactics. U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, DeWine’s former lieutenant governor, said he would not have run the advertisement. Secretary of State Frank LaRose made a similar statement, while former U.S. Rep. Jim Renacci urged Ramaswamy to move away from the controversy. Those criticisms have not amounted to a coordinated withdrawal of Republican support for Ramaswamy. DeWine’s position, however, goes further than disapproving of an advertisement: He has now ruled out campaigning with the nominee himself. That refusal comes as the Republican ticket seeks to hold the governor’s office following DeWine’s two terms. Ramaswamy and McColley face Acton and her running mate, David Pepper, in the November 3 election. DeWine has made clear that he will not withdraw his endorsement. He has also made clear that he will not campaign with Ramaswamy, and when asked whether the nominee belonged among the “really good people” he praised on the Republican ticket, he declined to include him. With Election Day approaching, Ramaswamy retains the governor’s endorsement — but not his willingness to share a campaign stage. See more of our trusted coverage in your search results. results.pageTitle: ‘Pink Slime’: Partisan journalism and the future of local news
results.pageDescription: As we hurtle towards 2024 elections, interest in pink slime journalism and the continued growth of partisan local outlets with deep, often opaque, ties to dark money, advocacy groups and other special interests has only grown.
results.evidenceText: ‘Pink Slime’: Partisan journalism and the future of local news - Columbia Journalism Review b Image: What is Black and green and pink all over, Hana Joy b Sign up for the daily CJR newsletter . Download full report here. It is now four years since the Tow Center’s landmark investigation exposed the scale of an opaque “pink slime” news operation using the veneer of local journalism to push partisan talking points in the run-up to a presidential election. That study , by Priyanjana Bengani, marked the beginning of a program of Tow Center research that has already extended beyond the duration of a presidential term. As we hurtle toward a likely rematch in November, interest in pink slime journalism and the continued growth of partisan local outlets with deep, often opaque ties to dark money, advocacy groups, and other special interests have only continued. That is why we have compiled our research and reporting into a collection, edited by Andrea Wenzel, associate professor at Temple University and Tow Center research fellow. Sandwiched between an introductory chapter tracing the recent history of pink slime journalism and a discussion of perspectives on the phenomenon from journalism scholars and practitioners interviewed for this report, we bring together Bengani’s series of digital forensic investigations into the emergence, expansion, funding, and function of Metric Media; case studies exploring the production, distribution, and content of partisan local news during the 2022 midterm elections; and Sara Rafsky’s in-depth audience study. As well as centralizing the Center’s extensive body of work, this provides an opportunity to consider the broader questions about dark money and opaque partisan news in the local news ecosystem. These include questions about journalistic norms , and the extent to which they might be revised to fit partisan news outlets. Questions about transparency, funding, and objectivity. What it means to be a journalist, to do journalism, to be a news organization. The short- and long-term implications of a localized information war between rival outlets funded with varying degrees of transparency by deep-pocketed partisan donors. What role, if any, these outlets (or variations on them) will play in the reconfigured local news ecosystem. Are they the future of local journalism? What responsibilities do technology companies have, and what could or should they do? How should these operations be factored in to efforts to secure local journalism’s future? Questions such as these have grown louder over the past four years and will reach fever pitch as the days tick down to what is guaranteed to be another fraught election campaign. ‘Flooding the local zone’ Pink slime journalism floods and dilutes the local news ecosystem with low-quality information. In this regard, its presence and volume create a challenge that forces us to look beyond its (lack of) audience engagement and is far more complicated to track. By “muddying the waters so that consensus isn’t achievable,” a flooded zone is said to increase cynicism toward, among others, truth and institutions, creating an environment ripe for political polarization and culture wars. As well as undermining trustworthy, transparent journalism, pink slime plays an important role in stoking local information wars by attracting like-minded players to enter the fray or encouraging “opponents” to fight fire with fire. The intensification of this battle between competing narratives has the ingredients to create confusion, increase cynicism, and feed perceptions of partisanship—factors that may accelerate the rate at which citizens turn away from trustworthy local news more generally. As such, the threat of pink slime journalism extends beyond any one producer, network, outlet, or narrative. The gradual drip of its pollution, and its role in stoking information wars in a local news environment already in a state of disarray, has the potential to be far more insidious. The bulk of our research has centered on the Metric Media network (later Pipeline Media). Networks often cited as part of the same conversation —about blurring the lines between journalism and advocacy due to things like transparency about their connections to partisan funders or dark-money groups, adopting the look and feel of local news outlets while disguising their partisanship, and heavy use of microtargeted digital advertising to reach persuadable voters with partisan messaging during election cycles—include the Star News Network of so-called “Baby Breitbarts,” Main Street Sentinel, Courier Newsroom, Texas Scorecard, Local Report Inc., and American Independent Media. The mere mention of some of these networks is enough to spark debate. Should some be welcomed for having a “ view from somewhere ,” or are they “ empty partisan hackery “? How should we distinguish between the two? Is it “ false equivalency ” to discuss these networks as part of the same conversation? In July 2020, the editor in chief of Courier Newsroom, which was then owned by progressive dark-money PAC ACRONYM, said : Courier Newsroom and its affiliated sites are independent from ACRONYM.… Painting all partisan-leaning outlets with the same brush is dangerous and too often creates false equivalency between very different types of newsrooms. All outlets in the Courier Newsroom network operate with integrity and adhere to traditional journalistic standards.… Courier aims to combat the misinformation spread by such right-wing sites pretending to be “local news” by providing readers with transparently progressive local reporting. After the 2022 midterms, Tara McGowan, founder of both ACRONYM and Courier, told Fortune that the network should be distinguished from outlets included in a NewsGuard study of digital ad spending: Courier is “using every tool available to us to better inform passive news consumers who are being inundated with disinformation online,” she said in a statement. “Because of this, old guard media elites have decided to paint us with the same broad brush they use for actual so-called pink-slime operations like the ones mentioned by NewsGuard’s report.” The extent to which any of these networks meets any particular definition of “pink slime” is arguably beside the point. What is important is that pink slime has played—and continues to play—an active role in the proliferation of these operations, each new entrant edging the local information ecosystem closer to an undesirable reconfiguration as a battlefield for partisan information wars. As recently as November 5, 2023 , Courier Newsroom’s homepage was replete with rhetoric positioning its local newsrooms as soldiers in a partisan information war. Visitors to its website were immediately greeted by a statement detailing the company’s plan to “WIN THE INFO WAR” being waged by “Right-wing media and political figures.” Courier, it said, was “fighting back with newsrooms and journalists all across the country.” Until at least June 1, 2023 , this language of partisan warfare was continued on a page titled “Take Action” that sought to recruit an “army” of “Good Info Messengers” with the pitch: America is engaged in an info war—and we cannot let right-wing pundits and politicians win that war. We’re building an army to counter the likes of Steve Bannon, Tucker Carlson, and Donald Trump. References to information warfare have since been scrubbed from Courier’s homepage. (So, too, has a statement, on its “About Courier” page—present until at least August 27, 2023 —that it is “building the largest left-leaning local news network in the country.” By September 20 , that language had been revised to replace “left-leaning” with “pro-Democracy.”) Will nonpartisan, independent local journalism be a victim of the cross fire in a localized partisan information war? Reports of local journalism’s relative trust advantage over the national news media are often accompanied by warnings about the fragility of that advantage. John Sands, of the Knight Foundation, warned in 2019: [L]ocal news outlets don’t exist in a vacuum.… The same forces that have eroded trust in the national media are now beginning to filter down to the local level. While more Americans trust their local news outlets more than national, that trust is more fragile than previously understood—and vulnerable to the same perceptions of partisan bias that threaten confidence in the national media. Trust as it relates to journalism is, of course, a slippery and hotly contested question. But if we take the nationally representative Gallup/Knight Foundation poll American Views 2022: Part 2. Trust, Media, and Democracy , published in January 2023, some of the main drivers of that erosion of trust in national media were: an overwhelming array of news providers competing for attention; perceptions of political partisanship and bias; perceptions that the press intends to mislead, misinform, or persuade; difficulty discerning facts and feeling informed; and perceptions that journalists and news organizations are unreliable, detached from their audiences, and indifferent about the impact of their reporting. Most of these factors have arguably been less applicable to the local news media. But the rapid rise of sprawling pink slime networks and the adjacent onset of partisan information war based on contesting narratives from opposite sides of the political divide can change that. This may have ramifications for trust in information from the local news media more broadly , leaving open the possibility that the short-term relief of swinging tight elections may come at the longer-term cost of making life even more challenging for local news providers. What part will opaque, partisan outlets play in the reconfigured local news ecosystem of the future? Discussing the Star News network of state-specific “ Baby Breitbarts ” in May 2018, Eric Levitz opined in Intelligencer : [A] democracy in which both parties fund biased, but aggressive and factually accurate, local political reporting would be far better than one in which little-to-no such reporting exists. Thus, left-leaning billionaires and interest groups should probably start preparing to enter the local media fray themselves. The economics of local news might no longer sustain “fair” political reporting—but “balanced” is still within reach. Opinion will be divided on this. But the large sums being spent on partisan local news have arguably edged us closer to what Levitz envisioned. Most of the outlets that have emerged from the recent expansion of local news networks with red and blue affiliations might reasonably be described as aggressive. The extent to which their output would be described as factually accurate varies, while debates over the ethics of which facts are prioritized or included rage on. More recently, in a NiemanLab prediction for 2024 titled “We’ll see partisan media more clearly,” Anthony Nadler, one of the experts interviewed for our report, wrote: I think we’re near a breaking point where media critics, journalists, foundation funders, policymakers, and scholars can no longer assume partisan journalism occupies a marginal part of the news sphere. In this environment, Nadler argues, “as partisan media becomes more central to politics, we will need to think about it with more nuance, seeing it as more than a menacing rival to professional journalism.” In the case of the networks discussed here, it is not just their partisanship that raises questions, but their transparency around their backers, motives, and ties to dark money. The local news crisis, in part caused by a collapse of the industry’s business model, has created a scramble to find viable ways to revive and sustain local journalism. Outlets funded by dark money have no such concerns; dark money is the business model. As such, we should be prepared for it to form part of the local information ecosystem for as long as the special interests funding it believe it is serving their needs. The disparity between those with vast sums of (dark) money at their disposal and those without also creates questions for platform companies. A tactic used by many of these networks involves heavy spending on advertising on technology platforms to microtarget specific (persuadable) segments of the electorate. NewsGuard tallied $3.94 million of Meta ads by four networks during the 2022 midterm cycle. One of them, the Main Street Sentinel, disappeared after less than a year, having spent around $1.4 million on Facebook ads (many of them targeting citizens in Michigan with stories supportive of Democrats involved in midterm races) between February 25, 2022 (eight days after its domain was registered and less then three weeks after the creation of its Facebook page) and November 18, 2022, ten days after Election Day. The Wayback Machine’s latest snapshot is dated February 8, 2023. This led NewsGuard to criticize platforms for allowing advertisers to create and manage their own disclosures. On Facebook and Instagram, Meta’s “lax advertising policies…allow them to mask their partisan funders and ties.” Consequently, “partisan networks can, and often do, identify their funders as seemingly apolitical entities, about which little is known.” In the aftermath of the 2020 election, McGowan described how the news media’s failings had contributed to Courier’s creation: [I]f mainstream media outlets at the national or state level were savvier about marketing their news content to audiences who live in these narrative deserts and are being inundated with disinformation, they would be more effectively countering it, and we wouldn’t need to build our own full infrastructure to do that. And [doing that is] insanely expensive. I mean, since starting the organization, we’ve raised close to $100 million and spent nearly every dollar of it. That’s not sustainable. Multiple experts interviewed for our report argued that local journalism is the best antidote to pink slime and its ilk. But it is fair to assume that few local news outlets with a more conventional business model would be able—or willing—to compete in terms of the purchase of eyeballs. Without redress, new or existing outlets will surely face an uphill struggle for attention in a local news environment that can be dominated by outlets able to use funds from deep-pocketed partisan donors to put their output in front of strategically microtargeted audiences. That leaves questions about what could or should be done to level this particular playing field. In the meantime, the work continues trying to bring that field into focus. Download the report here. results.pageDescription: Gravação foi feita em outubro e mostra fluxo de veículo antes do feriado de Nossa Senhora Aparecida
results.evidenceText: Vídeo não mostra congestionamento causado por fuga de brasileiros do Paraguai | Aos Fatos 12 de novembro de 2026 , 18:01 Vídeo não mostra congestionamento causado por fuga de brasileiros do Paraguai Por Luiz Fernando Menezes Boataria política Checagem Compartilhe Adicione o Aos Fatos às suas fontes do Google fonte preferencial Posts compartilham vídeo de congestionamento como se tivesse sido gravado após crise do Ueno Bank; Registro foi feito em 10 de outubro, antes do feriado de Nossa Senhora Aparecida; Caso do Ueno Bank aconteceu cerca de um mês depois. Um vídeo que mostra uma fila de carros deixando o Paraguai em direção ao Brasil não foi gravado após a crise do Ueno Bank como afirmam postagens nas redes sociais. As peças desinformativas usam um registro feito um mês antes da crise, quando a região vivenciou um grande fluxo de automóveis por causa do feriado de Nossa Senhora de Aparecida, no dia 12 de outubro. Postagens com o conteúdo enganoso reuniam ao menos 32 mil interações nas redes sociais da Meta até a tarde desta quinta-feira (12). Siga o canal do Aos Fatos no WhatsApp e receba nossas checagens e reportagens URGENTE, fila de BOLSONARISTA deixando o Paraguai Rumo ao BRASIL 07/11/2026 É falso que tenha sido gravado em 7 de novembro um vídeo que mostra um congestionamento na fronteira entre Brasil e Paraguai. As peças desinformativas sugerem uma fuga de brasileiros após a crise do Ueno Bank e o impeachment do presidente Santiago Peña. A gravação, no entanto, é anterior ao fechamento do banco. Por meio de busca reversa, Aos Fatos identificou que o mesmo vídeo foi publicado nas redes no dia 10 de outubro de 2026 , antes do caso paraguaio e do resultado do segundo turno das eleições brasileiras. Ver esse post no Instagram Um post compartilhado por Bruno Queiroz | Compras no Paraguai 🇵🇾 (@brunodequeiiroz) O autor da gravação original, um influenciador brasileiro que vive no Paraguai, desmentiu as peças de desinformação e confirmou que a gravação foi feita no dia 10 daquele mês próximo à Ponte da Amizade, que liga Foz do Iguaçu e Ciudad del Este. Indícios presentes na gravação também comprovam que as imagens foram registradas próximo à fronteira. Em determinado momento do vídeo, é possível ver um outdoor com a palavra “Monalisa”, referente a uma loja que fica próxima à ponte. Boataria política Explicador Como a queda do banco Ueno no Paraguai acabou com o governo de Santiago Peña A crise desencadeada pelo Ueno Bank começou no dia 3 de novembro, quando o BCP (Banco Central do Paraguai) anunciou o fechamento da instituição. O banco foi acusado de manipular normas legais e políticas para acelerar seu crescimento de forma artificial. Peña, que era vinculado ao banco, renunciou dois dias depois, mas o Congresso paraguaio continuou o processo de impeachment. No dia 6, o Senado aprovou o afastamento e Peña foi preso . O Ueno Bank possuía 1,7 milhão de clientes e, segundo as autoridades paraguaias, cerca de US$ 2,8 bilhões em depósitos. Até a última segunda-feira (9) , cerca de US$ 335 milhões haviam sido devolvidos (cerca de 11% do total estimado). Esta peça de desinformação também foi checada pela APF Checamos . O caminho da apuração Aos Fatos fez uma busca reversa por prints do vídeo compartilhado e encontrou a gravação original no Instagram. A reportagem também procurou informações que confirmassem a localização e a data da gravação. Por fim, Aos Fatos consultou reportagens sobre a crise do Ueno Bank para construir um contexto resumido sobre o caso. results.pageDescription: Ministro decidiu manter o calendário previsto desde a aprovação da PEC, que extingue a escala a partir de 16 de dezembro deste ano
results.evidenceText: Flávio Dino não adiou fim da escala 6x1 para o final de 2027 | Aos Fatos 12 de novembro de 2026 , 15:45 Flávio Dino não adiou fim da escala 6x1 para o final de 2027 Por Luiz Fernando Menezes Políticas públicas Checagem STF Flávio Dino Compartilhe Adicione o Aos Fatos às suas fontes do Google fonte preferencial Posts alegam que o ministro Flávio Dino teria adiado o fim da escala 6x1 para dezembro do ano que vem; Não houve alteração no calendário desde a aprovação do novo regime; Os dois dias de descanso passam a ser obrigatórios a partir de 16 de dezembro de 2026. Não é verdade que o ministro do STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal) Flávio Dino adiou o fim da escala 6x1 para dezembro de 2027, como afirmam publicações nas redes sociais. Apesar de entidades terem solicitado a extensão do prazo, Dino decidiu manter o calendário original, que torna os dois dias de descanso obrigatórios a partir de 16 de dezembro de 2026. Postagens com o conteúdo enganoso reuniam ao menos 10 mil interações nas redes da Meta até a tarde desta quinta-feira (12). Siga o canal do Aos Fatos no WhatsApp e receba nossas checagens e reportagens AGORA: Flávio Dino adiou a proposta do fim da escala 6x1 para dezembro de 2027; será que Erika Hilton vai questionar? São enganosas as publicações que afirmam que o ministro do STF Flávio Dino adiou o fim da escala 6x1 para dezembro de 2027. Os posts que trazem esse conteúdo misturam e distorcem pontos da EC (Emenda Constitucional), que continua em vigor, com o calendário previsto desde a aprovação. Sancionada em 16 de outubro, a EC nº 141/2026 , que reduz a escala de trabalho, estipulou os seguintes prazos de transição : Até 16 de dezembro de 2026: a jornada de trabalho deve ser reduzida para 42 horas e os dois dias de repouso semanal passam a ser obrigatórios; Até 16 de dezembro de 2027: a jornada deve ser reduzida para 40 horas. Boataria política Checagem É falso que Lula recuou sobre fim da escala 6x1 A CNI (Confederação Nacional da Indústria) e a CNC (Confederação Nacional do Comércio de Bens, Serviços e Turismo), no entanto, entraram com ações no STF para tentar aumentar os prazos para a adoção da nova jornada. As organizações argumentam que o prazo de 60 dias é insuficiente para reorganizar atividades e turnos, renegociar convenções coletivas e realizar novas contratações. As duas ações foram sorteadas para Dino, que decidiu, nesta quinta-feira (12), não acatar a extensão do prazo para a transição. O ministro, no entanto, abriu uma nova janela de 90 dias, contados a partir de 16 de dezembro de 2026, para que os sindicatos e empregadores revisem acordos coletivos. "Em hipótese alguma, será afastada a incidência da norma constitucional que assegura, após 16 de dezembro de 2026, o direito a 42 horas semanais e dois repousos semanais remunerados", decidiu. A íntegra das decisões pode ser conferida aqui e aqui . A liminar ainda deve ser analisada pelo plenário do Supremo. O caminho da apuração Aos Fatos checou o calendário aprovado pelo Congresso Nacional para explicar quais os prazos previstos para cada uma das alterações na jornada de trabalho. A reportagem também analisou as duas decisões liminares de Dino sobre o assunto publicadas nesta quinta-feira (12). results.evidenceText: Vídeo não mostra Lula sendo afastado de outros presidentes na COP31 | Aos Fatos 12 de novembro de 2026 , 13:45 Vídeo não mostra Lula sendo afastado de outros presidentes na COP31 Por Luiz Fernando Menezes Boataria política Checagem Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva Compartilhe Adicione o Aos Fatos às suas fontes do Google fonte preferencial Posts sugerem que vídeo mostraria Lula sendo afastado dos demais líderes que participaram da COP31; Gravação registra momento que presidente foi realocado para seu local oficial, mas continuou ao lado de representantes; Lula apareceu na foto oficial na primeira fileira de líderes. Não é verdade que um vídeo mostra o presidente Lula (PT) sendo afastado dos demais líderes da COP31 (Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima), como sugerem publicações nas redes sociais. A gravação mostra o momento em que ele é realocado para a foto oficial. Lula não só participou do registro, como apareceu na primeira fileira. Postagens com o conteúdo enganoso reuniam ao menos 2.000 curtidas no Instagram e também circulavam no WhatsApp, onde não é possível estimar o alcance com precisão. Siga o canal do Aos Fatos no WhatsApp e receba nossas checagens e reportagens VERGONHA. LULA É AFASTADO DOS DEMAIS LÍDERES NA COP 31 Posts enganam ao sugerir que Lula teria sido afastado dos demais líderes durante a foto oficial da COP31, que acontece na Turquia até o dia 20. A gravação, na verdade, mostra o momento em que o petista é levado ao seu local oficial para o registro. Na gravação divulgada pela imprensa , é possível observar que Lula estava ao lado do presidente turco, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, quando uma assessora o orientou a caminhar até a posição correta. Apesar de ter sido reposicionado, Lula permaneceu na foto e apareceu na primeira fileira de chefes de Estado (veja abaixo). Lula ficou posicionado na primeira fileira de líderes da COP31 (Ricardo Stuckert/PR) Lula viajou para a Turquia na última segunda-feira (9) para participar da COP31. O presidente discursou na abertura do evento e realizou reuniões bilaterais com outros líderes, como a presidente interina da Venezuela, Delcy Rodríguez, o primeiro-ministro da Noruega, Jonas Gahr Støre, e o próprio Erdoğan. Segundo a agenda oficial, o presidente seguirá na sexta-feira (13) para as Filipinas, onde participará da 49ª Cúpula da Asean (Associação de Nações do Sudeste Asiático). Conteúdos desinformativos que sugerem que Lula teria um mau relacionamento com outros líderes internacionais costumam circular durante viagens oficiais do presidente. O Aos Fatos já desmentiu alegações semelhantes sobre a reunião do G7 em 2024 e a Cúpula da Asean em 2025 . O caminho da apuração Aos Fatos localizou a gravação que circula nas redes sociais e checou o contexto com base em reportagens da imprensa e nos registros oficiais do evento. results.pageDescription: Ministro Marco Aurélio Bellizze multou plataforma em R$ 7,5 milhões e aponta atraso e pouca transparência na moderação
results.evidenceText: Investigação sobre fazendas de IA de Aos Fatos e Democracia em Xeque subsidia decisão do TSE sobre Meta | Aos Fatos Méuri Elle/Aos Fatos 12 de novembro de 2026 , 12:37 Investigação sobre fazendas de IA de Aos Fatos e Democracia em Xeque subsidia decisão do TSE sobre Meta Por Luiz Fernando Menezes Eleições 2026 Nota TSE inteligência artificial Meta Compartilhe Adicione o Aos Fatos às suas fontes do Google fonte preferencial TSE penalizou Meta por atrasos e cumprimento incompleto de ordens judiciais; Decisão envolve levantamento publicado pelo Aos Fatos sobre rede de perfis durante a eleição de 2026; Relator criticou a falta de transparência e afirmou que a capacidade de influência das plataformas exige controle. O TSE (Tribunal Superior Eleitoral) multou em R$ 7,5 milhões a Meta, empresa responsável pelo Instagram e Facebook, por descumprimento de prazos e ordens judiciais voltadas a frear uma rede de desinformação de extrema direita e assegurar a isonomia nas eleições. A decisão é unânime. O processo cita os dados de um levantamento do Instituto Democracia em Xeque publicado pelo Aos Fatos , que revelou a atuação de uma "fazenda de conteúdo" formada por 255 perfis que, com o auxílio da IA, promoveram pautas da extrema direita, atacaram o STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal) e espalharam desinformação eleitoral. Juntas, as publicações produzidas pela fazenda acumularam 58 milhões de visualizações e 5 milhões de curtidas e comentários em um período de um mês. Eleições 2026 Reportagem Fazendas de IA inflam pauta da extrema direita com 255 perfis e mais de mil posts Em seu voto, o relator e ministro do TSE Marco Aurélio Bellizze apontou três problemas centrais na conduta da plataforma: atraso sistemático na resposta às ordens, cumprimento incompleto das medidas e falta de transparência. Segundo o ministro, a empresa forneceu relatórios com dados genéricos ou agregados e até documentos em inglês, dificultando a fiscalização judicial. No despacho, o ministro considerou o valor de R$ 7,5 milhões “adequado à relevância de controvérsia envolvendo a integridade do processo eleitoral e que não é desproporcional à capacidade econômica da representada”. Exemplos de posts da rede inautêntica que estavam disponíveis na época da reportagem (Reprodução/Instagram) A decisão aponta ainda a falha da Meta em sinalizar conteúdos gerados por IA. O TSE exigiu que a plataforma corrigisse seus mecanismos de rotulagem e tornasse indisponíveis novos posts irregulares. Segundo o tribunal, a empresa cumpriu essa determinação apenas de forma parcial. Ao argumentar pela condenação, Bellizze criticou o "poder informacional" das big techs. O ministro ressaltou que a distribuição da informação e as decisões de moderação afetam diretamente a igualdade de oportunidades entre as candidaturas e a formação autônoma da vontade do eleitor. "A transformação digital não pode criar uma zona de imunidade regulatória justamente no ambiente em que parcela significativa da vontade política contemporânea é formada", concluiu Bellizze. O relator afirmou, no entanto, que não é possível apontar que a empresa atuou de forma deliberada para interferir no resultado das eleições. Essa acusação carece de provas robustas “cuja comprovação não foi possível constatar nesta via célere e limitada”. A representação foi ajuizada pela coligação do presidente Lula (PT). A campanha acusou a Meta de praticar “seletividade algorítmica” ao restringir o alcance orgânico de conteúdos de esquerda ao mesmo tempo que permitia a circulação de publicações irregulares favoráveis ao adversário. No entendimento da campanha, a empresa silenciou “vozes relevantes do campo progressista, sem qualquer transparência ou explicação quanto a seus critérios”. Na ação, a Meta disse que “não interfere nas eleições e que a paridade de armas (igualdade de oportunidades) exigida é de tratamento, e não de resultado”, conforme trecho da decisão. A empresa declarou ainda ter cumprido parte das determinações e que as demais estariam sendo atendidas. Em nota enviada ao Aos Fatos , a Meta disse que “cumpre a legislação eleitoral brasileira e aplica as mesmas regras a todos os candidatos e partidos”. A empresa observou ainda que vai continuar apresentando os fatos e se “defender de alegações falsas nos processos em curso”. O que revelou o levantamento Publicado pelo Aos Fatos antes do primeiro turno das eleições, o levantamento do Instituto Democracia em Xeque revelou uma rede de fazendas de conteúdo formada por 255 perfis que publicaram 1.204 posts entre 15 de agosto e 15 de setembro. O conteúdo era distribuído por meio de diferentes perfis que publicavam juntos e compartilhavam suas audiências por meio do recurso de collabs do Instagram. Situação semelhante apareceu em outro levantamento do Aos Fatos específico sobre publicações que simulavam apoio ao ministro do STF André Mendonça. Entre as publicações, havia ataques contra políticos de esquerda, além de violência de gênero e transfobia. Várias publicações, inclusive, foram geradas por IA (veja abaixo). Janja é representada em imagens hiperssexualizadas e comparada a animais em publicações da fazenda (Reprodução/Instagram) Mesmo que grande parte do conteúdo fosse sintético, a grande maioria não estava identificado como tal. Apenas 155 dos 1.204 posts (12,9%) apresentavam alguma identificação de uso de inteligência artificial. Em 134 casos, o próprio autor declarou ter usado a tecnologia; nos demais, a identificação veio de metadados incorporados aos arquivos. results.pageDescription: For Olivia Reingold, one of the most prominent and prolific contributors to The Free Press, defending Israel takes priority over the facts.
results.evidenceText:
Bari Weiss’s Most Loyal Soldier Advertisement Advertisement Return to Homepage Top Stories: Online outages at major banks Clancy to face retrial Trump heads to China Huang weighs Nvidia comeback FAA ground stop aftermath Trump's trip to Asia Lutnick-Nvidia scrutiny FAA ground stop in photos Uncalled midterm races Trump's Mideast stance Olivia Reingold calls herself an anti-cancel-culture journalist. Her work at The Free Press looks like public relations work for Israel. ( The Free Press / Youtube) On September 8, 2025, a video shot in Columbia University's bookstore went viral on X. Over the elegant sounds of Antonio Vivaldi's "Spring," it cut between shots of available titles, all of them presumably assigned to students: Frantz Fanon's ; a children's book about the late Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg; Richard Rothstein's ; Robert A. Dahl's ?; and, among others, the Quran. The caption reads: Went to the Columbia University bookstore — these are some of the books students are reading this semester. A bookstore employee told me the Qur'an is required reading for all freshman [ sic ]. The content creator behind the video was the staff writer Olivia Reingold, one of the publication's most prolific contributors. In her influencer-style Instagram reels , she's made a career of defending Israel and the GOP while attacking New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, others on the Left, and anyone else who may dissent from Israel's policy objectives. Reingold is part of a new wave of young pro-Israel influencers and content creators who see social media as another front in the Zionist struggle. After October 7, with Israel's massacre in Gaza and the US public's ensuing backlash against Israel, new content creation opportunities emerged for those seeking to do hasbara. A Hebrew word that translates to "explanation," hasbara refers to pro-Israel public relations, often with a less than complete regard for the truth. In this respect, Reingold has joined a new right-of-center cohort of American pro-Israel influencers. On her website , she refers to herself as a "truth teller" and writes that "there is nothing more valuable than integrity." Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Unlike other pro-Israel influencers, however, Reingold claims to be not a mere influencer or content creator but a journalist. But it is hard to tell where the hasbara ends and the reporting begins. Reingold's Journalism Start with Reingold's bookstore post. In the video, the Quran is the final supposedly inflammatory title we see after Fanon's and the rest. At Columbia, the Quran is assigned to second-year students, not all freshmen, in the required Contemporary Civilization course. Here, however, the suggestion is that it's unacceptable even as an object of study. This ignores the Quran's place in a secular, scholarly course as one text among many major works of world literature. I took Contemporary Civilization this past academic year and found no instructor urging students to adopt radical Islam. Excerpts from the Old and New Testaments are likewise assigned across Columbia's Core Curriculum. In fact, in the video, you can clearly see a giant stack of just below the Quran, though Reingold zooms in only on the latter. Her implication that Fanon, Rothstein, and Dahl are anathema to a proper university education is just as absurd. These are serious, influential writers — whatever one may think of them — whose work clearly belongs in a university curriculum. But for Reingold, the problematic nature of these texts is self-evident and further proof that Columbia is a hellscape of radicalism. It is a mirror image of the Right's favorite (and sometimes true) "ultrawoke" caricature — the perpetually offended young person — but produced by a publication that markets itself as anti-identitarian and pro–free speech. The month before the bookstore post, Reingold cowrote an exposé alleging that the photos of twelve Palestinian children featured in as evidence of Israeli-induced starvation "lacked important context" because the children had underlying medical conditions. To pro-Israel partisans, she had debunked a story — in the , no less. But of course, underlying conditions do not refute the fact of starvation; children already ill are more likely to die first in a famine. Reingold provided no counterevidence to prove that the children were not starving or that the Gaza Strip was not in a humanitarian crisis. For her exposé, she reached out to Yannay Spitzer, then an economist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, whose comment she paraphrased as "Hunger in Gaza is largely declining since Israel resumed aid deliveries in late May after its nearly 80-day blockade." And yet, to say hunger declined after Israel lifted the blockade is to concede that Gaza had been experiencing mass hunger because of it. Advertisement Advertisement In an Instagram reel , Reingold treats the fact that the same children, ill "not just with malnutrition," appeared in photographs by different people as evidence of "coordination" — the implication being that they were being paraded around by pro-Palestinian forces as part of a propaganda drive. She claims that she did "something so simple, it's shocking no other journalist bothered to do it": translating their names into Arabic and finding local reports, which she says discuss underlying conditions more than anglophone sources do. Some of those conditions, she concedes, had in fact reported. Still, her work, by her own estimation, produced "a more nuanced story." And yet the reel's conclusion was anything but nuanced: that Israel was not responsible for famine and that "the average Gazan does not look like that." None other than Benjamin Netanyahu reposted it with the caption "Facts matter." For Reingold, the defense of Israel's war is paramount. Her defense turns the suffering of starving children — images that would disgust any normal person — into a question of public relations. The pushback against her defense of Israel, she claims on her website, was "a global cancelation campaign." Reingold's Religion Reingold's partisanship appears as something like a religion. But that religion is not Judaism or merely a belief in the Jewish national project; it is deference to the unflagging righteousness of a modern nation-state with a sophisticated military, nuclear weapons, a powerful American lobby, near-total control over the occupied territories, and a foreign policy that repeatedly massacres civilians. Advertisement Advertisement That may be why Reingold, again using the language of wokeness, calls images of starving children across mainstream media "problematic": they make her uncomfortable and call into question her unflinching loyalty to the Israeli state. Interestingly, Reingold was not always this way. She writes of becoming an "October 8th Jew" (she is part Jewish, on her father's side), saying she came to "the Arab-Israeli conflict as a nearly blank slate," open to the claim that Israel is an apartheid state guilty of genocide. She describes the later realization that this "wasn't a civil rights movement. . . . This was about Jews" that moved her in the opposite direction. Now, rather than treat widespread outcry over Israel's atrocities as a legitimate political response to a state's actions, she recasts it as evidence of antisemitism. For instance, earlier this summer, Reingold insinuated that a Jewish Voice for Peace activist she interviewed was not really Jewish on the grounds that the person had not grown up Jewish. By this questionable standard, it seems Reingold herself would not qualify as Jewish either. But what she is saying is clear: a real Jew must be an avid supporter of Israel. This is an ideological loyalty test in defense of a state's conduct, not a description of Judaism or even of Zionism. I have no reason to doubt Reingold's account of how she arrived here. Her earlier work — at Georgia Public Broadcasting , Yellowstone Public Radio , , and Matthew Yglesias's , which a LinkedIn post says she conceived and helped launch — contains no hint of the "October 8th" partisan she would become. Advertisement Advertisement This is where it's hard not to feel a bit sorry for her. She appears to believe that Mamdani's election, declining support for Israel, and sympathy for Palestinians signal a new antisemitism. In her words , "Anti-Zionism is antisemitism." At a time when many American Jews saw the horrors unleashed upon Gaza and began to question their support for Israel's current regime, to the extent that a recent survey shows that Mamdani is more popular among US Jews than Netanyahu is, Reingold went in exactly the opposite direction. A report she coauthored on the Democratic Socialists of America's 2026 New York primary victories in June ran under the scary subtitle "On Tuesday, radical House candidates won big in the city. 'It doesn't feel safe to be Jewish anymore.'" Her earlier piece , "How to 'Make Your Campus Palestinian,'" framed Jewish students' recruitment into pro-Palestinian activism as a cynical strategy to legitimize antisemitism. It is true that student protests did sometimes veer into territory broadly alienating to many Jewish students; in rare cases, some individuals adopted downright violent rhetoric (there will always be cranks). But ultimately, the American outcry was and is directed at a foreign government's violence, financed by the United States — not "the Jews." In explicitly tying the protection of Jews to support for Israel, Reingold is insisting on the actions of Israel as the will of all Jews, a mirror of what antisemites often do. Bari Weiss's Heir Other examples abound. In April, a Reingold piece about Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed ran at under the headline "Michigan Gets Its Own Mamdani." In it, she asks El-Sayed "whether he believes in Israel's right to exist as a Jewish state." Reingold describes him, when he asks what she means by "Jewish state," "narrowing his eyes" in response. In another piece about Jewish parents with Mamdani-voting children, she sides with parents horrified by their children's choices; one hoped to supervise a daughter's absentee ballot to make sure she would not vote for Mamdani. Meanwhile, a May " investigation " by Reingold into Mamdani's wife, Rama Duwaji, chastises her for the contents of a Spotify playlist and for " liking " a Tucker Carlson clip on Instagram about AIPAC and its failure to register as a foreign lobby. Ironically, for a publication founded on opposition to cancel culture, here was the perfect example of it — scrutinizing minute social media activity in order to depict someone in the worst possible light. It is easy to criticize Reingold as an internet personality with less than savory politics. But she has found a niche doing clear hasbara at . With founder Bari Weiss increasingly occupied by her controversial role at CBS News, Reingold has arguably become the outlet's most visible persona. In Reingold, we have a younger version of Weiss, tweeting and Instagramming in defense of a constantly war-making and increasingly unpopular state, but without Weiss's more composed and occasionally believable journalistic posture. results.pageDescription: From whiteboard explainers to pop culture references, journalists are using personality to connect with skeptical audiences and make news accessible
results.evidenceText: What journalist-creators know about trust that newsrooms don't - Poynter What journalist-creators know about trust that newsrooms don't - Poynter DONATE What do you want to search? Submit Sign In | Membership News Training Ethics Fact-Checking Media Literacy AI Events Future of Public Media Newmark Ethics Center IFCN MediaWise PolitiFact Donate About Us Press Freedom Watch The Poynter 50 Podcasts Artificial Intelligence Business & Work Reporting & Editing Fact-Checking Ethics & Trust Local News Journalism, Media & Communication Training Poynter Membership Categories Consulting & Coaching For ACES Members For Local News Funders All Categories Broadcast & Visual Journalism Business & Work Ethics Fact-Checking & Media Literacy Leadership Reporting & Editing Writing Poynter ACES Introductory Certificate in Editing Poynter ACES Intermediate Certificate in Editing Poynter ACES Advanced Certificate in Editing Workshops and Coaching Tools for Funders Ethics Ethics Training Ethics Articles AI Ethics Public Editor Project Get Ethics Advice Fact-Checking Articles IFCN IFCN Grants International Fact-Checking Day Teen Creator Network PolitiFact MediaWise Media Literacy Resources AI Literacy Ambassadors Teen Creator Network Research & News International en Español MediaWise Training All Events The 2026 Poynter Journalism Prizes Ethics & Trust Reporting & Editing (Screenshots/biancanobilo) By: Gabrielle Lazor November 11, 2026 For 19-year-old Shelby Moore, the news doesn’t usually come from a headline. It’s most often packaged within the 9:16 aspect ratio of a TikTok or Instagram Reel, where journalists like Eva Pound, an associate booking producer for Punchbowl News, break down politics — sometimes with a pop culture twist. In one series, Pound explained the 2026 midterm elections in the style of reality TV, calling it “Keeping Up With the Kampaigns.” Why the parody? “Because I can promise you that U.S. politics has more money, higher stakes and more drama than any reality TV show. Period,” Pound said in an Instagram Reel that amassed more than 103,000 likes.   View this post on Instagram   A post shared by Eva Pound (@evainthenews) Framing political drama like a reality TV plot “makes it fun and enjoyable but also easy to understand … because lots of people these days don’t look at the news — we’re just all consuming TikTok,” Moore said. The College of William and Mary student is hardly alone. According to the Pew Research Center , 38% of adults ages 18 to 29 regularly get news from news influencers — people with large social media followings who often post about news, politics or social issues. That’s more than four times the share of adults 65 and older (8%). A growing number of journalists are meeting young audiences where they scroll. In doing so, they are discarding legacy media’s traditional stoicism in favor of personality-driven storytelling and pop culture fluency. Above all, they’re leveraging social media algorithms to make news accessible and digestible. Meeting audiences where they scroll “History Uncensored” host and former CNN anchor Bianca Nobilo needs only a couple of minutes and a whiteboard to break down geopolitics for her 269,000 Instagram followers and 112,000 TikTok followers. The whiteboard, a hallmark of Nobilo’s content , emerged organically after several of her friends complained that news stories lacked historical context.   View this post on Instagram   A post shared by Bianca Nobilo (@biancanobilo) “My belief has always been since I’ve been doing this … is that everyone is busy in their own lives,” Nobilo said. “It’s my job to metabolize all the information.” “You can’t expect people to participate properly in democracy if they don’t have the necessary knowledge, but life doesn’t provide time for that knowledge a lot of the time,” she said. Camille McCallum, 32, admits that her screen time is “embarrassingly high.” Social media accounts for roughly 75% of her news diet. With so much news behind paywalls, she finds it easier to follow individual creators. “As I’ve followed news creators, the news comes more directly to me through the algorithm,” McCallum said. McCallum, an influencer and founder of the lifestyle brand Black Woman on a Mission, recently delivered a presentation to political creators on effective get-out-the-vote content. Her biggest takeaways: Young audiences want creators who fill specific knowledge gaps accurately, and they want it in a winning format. She pointed to Pound’s “Kampaign” series as an example. Naturally, surfacing above the algorithmic abyss requires content that is both helpful and entertaining. “Effectiveness comes down to being accurate,” McCallum said. “We’re in an age of mis- and disinformation, so I’m constantly looking for creators I can trust, who cite sources, link articles, and are not just giving their opinions.” The independent trade-off Producing news outside the institutional aegis of legacy media can be a double-edged sword. Independent creators may trade away the safety net and industrial fact-checking power of big newsrooms, but working outside the reputation of an institutional brand can also help them reach audiences who distrust traditional outlets. “I’m frequently interested in how people who are vehemently one side or the other will share my content as proof of their argument,” Nobilo said. (Just check out any one of her comment sections.) Americans’ trust in mass media remains dismal . In a 2025 Gallup poll , seven in 10 Americans said they had “not very much” confidence (36%) or “none at all” (34%) in the news. Among Republicans, trust stood at just 8%. For many viewers, a traditional outlet’s name can be a scarlet letter. “I think, naturally, if you’re an independent personality, that does make you more flexible to move through these groups,” Nobilo said. Without a masthead attached, viewers across party lines can consider a journalist’s reporting without triggering preconceived notions. (Nobilo noted that being a blonde woman covering geopolitics in a predominantly male field brings its own biases.) The converse holds as well. “When you’re part of an institution, you experience the halo effect of that institution to their target audience,” Nobilo said. “You don’t need to earn the trust of somebody who is a CNN viewer … they naturally trust that if CNN has hired you, you meet their standards.” Still, Moore agreed that she’s more inclined to trust an individual journalist than a legacy news organization. Pulling back the curtain The distinctions between terms like “journalist-creator,” “news influencer” and “multimedia reporter” can be blurry. Pew Research defines news influencers as individuals with large followings who regularly post about news, political or social issues. Those personalities can be wholly independent or tied to established newsrooms. But among trained journalists, “influencer” has become sort of a “dirty word,” said Mimi Yates, an investigative reporter for the Daily Mail’s Underground UK team, because “influencing” goes against journalistic principles of integrity. “‘Creator’ is more palatable,” she said. Yates regularly uses Instagram carousels to give the “story behind the story,” showing her reporting process and making her work more transparent. There’s credibility in clarity. Even though Axios senior AI reporter Madison Mills covers a beat that lends itself to jargon, she uses the same language in her videos as she does in her reporting. She said that consistency builds trust with her audience because she doesn’t dumb down stories for social media. Jackie Davalos, a former journalist turned bakery owner, pointed to Mills “as one of the first that I saw really showing her personality — doing her makeup while explaining, like, Disney earnings.” “Even though I hear about these things at work, I was still super engaged,” Davalos said, recalling her time at Bloomberg with Mills. “Not even because she was a friend or a colleague, but because it was very easy to understand and it was accurate.” For Davalos, personality-driven reporting does something legacy media organizations often neglect: it peels back the curtain on the reporting process. “There’s a lot of trust issues, as everyone knows, when it comes to the journalism industry,” Davalos said. “Showing that you’re human, and that there are real barriers at every turn when you’re doing this work — the internal battles, the reporting challenges — kind of helps take the righteousness out of journalism.” “Sometimes it can feel like journalists are talking at you, not necessarily bringing you into the conversation. I don’t think it does us any favors to make this work seem really mysterious.” This kind of journalism doesn’t fund itself. results.title: Laurels and Darts
results.pageDescription: An Atlantic reporter says far-right influencers such as Nick Fuentes offer clues to where US politics is going.
results.evidenceText: Ali Breland on Why It’s Important to Cover the Online Far Right - Columbia Journalism Review b The Interview Photo courtesy of The Atlantic b Sign up for the daily CJR newsletter . Donald Trump’s second term has been defined by a symbiotic relationship with right-wing influencers, podcasters, and self-labeled journalists. Joe Rogan helped his reelection campaign reach young male voters. A week after Trump returned to office, Karoline Leavitt , the White House press secretary, designated seats for “new media” in the press briefing room. Less than a year later, the corridors of Pete Hegseth’s Pentagon belong to right-wing reporters and podcasters, following the exodus of legacy media . A MAGA influencer’s video triggered an immigration crackdown in Minneapolis. Trump and his creator crew have risen together. And as the president’s policies have grown more outlandish, so have those who purport to cover them. In January, clips of several right-wing influencers dancing to Ye’s “Heil Hitler” in a Miami nightclub suddenly went viral. The cast of characters that night included Andrew and Tristan Tate, right-wing internet stars and self-described misogynists; Nick Fuentes, a white-nationalist online streamer; and Braden Peters, a twenty-year-old online streamer who goes by the name Clavicular. In the weeks since, Clavicular has become ubiquitous. He walked the runway at Fashion Week, appeared as a guest on The Adam Friedland Show , and was profiled by the New York Times . I reached out to Ali Breland, a staff writer for The Atlantic who has been covering the far-right corners of the internet for almost a decade, to discuss this increasingly influential digital bubble. He told me that he sees this level of interconnectedness between the fringes and the mainstream as a recent but “concerning” trend. The administration is not just emboldening the far right, he said; the far right is inspiring Trump’s politics. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity. ILN: A few weeks ago, I couldn’t escape a video of the Tate brothers, Nick Fuentes, and other influencers I was unfamiliar with dancing to Ye’s “ Heil Hitler” song , which made me really confused about the current state of the far right. What were your thoughts seeing that video? AB: I was a little bit surprised, because these characters don’t often link up. But it made sense—these kinds of worlds have been melding for a while. They’re influential for people who are young and disposed to like various levels of being right-wing. Everyone, on some level, is political. You have someone like Andrew Tate, who is more in the “manosphere”—he’s been engaging with the Trump administration, but his primary function is not to change electoral politics. Whereas Nick Fuentes’s explicit goal is to influence the political right, and he’s stated that several times.  What about Clavicular, who has since become an internet star in his own right? Like many of these guys, he’s a symptom of something that already exists. In incel communities, “looksmaxxing” [the ambition to maximize masculine beauty] has been around for almost a decade. The Cut had a whole story about it in 2022. Clavicular is the end point of these things, and while he’s worth examining, I think he’s more like a flash in the pan. Nick Fuentes is also a symptom, but I think he has much more agency than Clavicular. So how does he fit into this picture of the far right? The logical reason is that incels are typically part of the right-wing ecosystem. It could also be that Clavicular, who personally said that he wasn’t all that political, is being operationalized by these right wing figures for their own political agenda. You say that Clavicular is not a crucial character, yet he’s received a lot of mainstream media attention. What did you think about his coverage? My armchair media critic perspective is that if any weird phenomenon goes viral enough, it can become a story. Clavicular seems to be an example of that. I do think that the profiles of him were useful, but I would definitely cover him as part of a shift that is going on amongst younger men. I’ve seen looksmaxxing creep into other corners of life: I personally know younger people who are chewing tough gums to strengthen their cheekbones. He is symptomatic of the nihilistic stream of slop that is going viral now. How do you weed out which of these characters are actually worth looking into?  I try to figure out who has a hard resonance beyond simply having a lot of online engagement. I think the most important thing is to figure out who is making inroads with people in power. Fuentes is someone I’ve been following for a long time because I’ve heard rumblings that young staffers in the administration are paying attention to him. Much of the language that was once reserved for the far right has now been internalized by the government. We’ve seen official accounts posting weird penguin memes and responding to individual tweets with personal insults . How do you see the interplay between the far-right internet bubble and the Trump administration? If it were just a couple memes that seem to be pulled from this world, you could call it coincidental, but the things that keep recurring are a lot like far-right imagery . When I see that over and over again, it makes me think that there are people within the administration who spend a lot of time in these spaces and try to speak to the same audience. You’ve covered the far-right corners of the internet all throughout the Trump era. What has changed the most in terms of the work you do, the figures and communities you write about? When I started doing this, around 2017, there used to be a dichotomy. There was a radical fringe that was influencing the mainstream, but it was distinct; and then there was the mainstream establishment that excited various fringe, online groups because they saw the potential for their ideas to be carried out. These things are no longer distinct. The white-supremacist groups are no longer excited about the potential; they’re excited about their ideas actually being carried out. Another example of this is Charlie Kirk. As long as I’ve been covering this beat, Charlie Kirk was prominent to varying degrees. He was mostly a libertarian, he was okay with gay people, and he only talked about white identity politics in a negative manner. Fast-forward to 2022, and Charlie Kirk was engaging with fringe figures and having race scientists on his podcast. He was giving them cover. The far right used to rely heavily on demonstrations of physical power like the Unite the Right march in Charlottesville, Virginia. How did it turn into an online phenomenon? There are two ways to answer this. One is that the online sphere just matters tremendously: Nick Fuentes has directly cited the adjustment of X’s policies to allow people like him back on and to speak in a manner that previously would have been considered hate speech. That enabled both his personal stock and the stock of his ideas to grow. But these groups don’t need to show up in the street anymore, because the administration is showing up for them. I was talking to a former leader of the Proud Boys recently , and he said, to paraphrase, “The administration is sending ICE out to do the kinds of things that are beyond anything we are able to.” In the first administration, there was a line that law enforcement couldn’t cross, so the Proud Boys did it—they went out and antagonized anti-fascist protesters, for example. That doesn’t need to be done anymore, because there are no such lines for ICE. Are these the same people who have always been on the far right? It’s hard to say with absolute precision, but you can see that these ideas are becoming more salient with younger people. Polling shows that there is a large number of young people who are very open to anti-Semitic ideas. Nick Fuentes is able to consistently generate six-digit viewership on his streams, which indicates that the audience is shifting younger. Previously, you had people mostly in their late twenties and thirties on the far right. Now we see a group of people who are closer to eighteen. You started writing about Fuentes before he was broadly popular. How do you see his rise, and why did he become so successful? Why him? The reason I always kept an eye on him is that he’s talented. He is very good at speaking into a camera in an entertaining way. He has good comedic timing. He has charisma. He also understood the weak or, as he puts it, “compromised” spots of right-wing ideology. He was able to point out what he saw as contradictory. He’s not beholden to major corporate donors, so he doesn’t have to hold his tongue or navigate multiple interests. He just accepts his position and takes it all the way. He was also one of the first people to speak of the immiserated conditions of young people in this modern version of the American economy. That’s a really key part of his message that I think a lot of people miss. You absolutely cannot ignore the racism and the anti-Semitism, but the savvy thing he did was to speak to people who were not doing well in a way that large swaths of the political class didn’t. He was talking about how people cannot afford houses before Trump or even Charlie Kirk did. Figures like Fuentes love attention, and they’ve recently received a lot of it from the mainstream press. It can be argued that, by reporting on them, you are actually enabling them. How do you navigate that? I spend a lot of time thinking about who specifically matters and why. Like, what is already occurring that we don’t know about? The reason I ended up covering Nick Fuentes is that he was already getting a lot of views. His streams get more views than any single article I write about him. Maybe there’s some sort of extra impact of the article coming out, but it’s about something that’s already pretty influential and shaping people’s lives. But occasionally, you’ll see mistakes. A pretty big one was Dark MAGA a few years ago. If you looked at it, all of the tweets about Dark MAGA had, like, twelve likes on them. It was not a real thing. The single most important moment in the development of the idea were the articles that came out on it. What do you think is the most valuable thing to come out of this coverage? I think that it gives people an understanding of the movements and ideologies that they might not have a clear framework for. Nick and others have made it part of their project to be pro-America without referencing white supremacy or Nazism. So what people like myself do is go back and note these connections and parallels. Another thing that’s useful is giving a sense of the memes and seeing how these ideas make their way into the mainstream. How influential do you think the far-right media bubble could get? I think it’s already here. Like, the disdain and hatred for Somali immigrants existed way before Trump went into Minneapolis. I don’t know if the administration made a decision based on that, but the online and the physical worlds are fundamentally connected. It’s probably going to become even more of a thing as younger people who have been more deeply steeped in the internet get older. So it is here, and it will be here for a long time. Has America ever needed a media defender more than now? Help us by joining CJR today . Ivan L. Nagy is a CJR Fellow. More from CJR Is It Crazy to Go to Journalism School?
