results.pageTitle: In the Russian Penal Colony, They Called Him ‘Dr. Evil’
results.pageDescription: Deep in the Russian heartland, hundreds of kilometers from home, Ukrainian prisoners of war were tormented by a sadistic doctor. Reporters set out to unmask him.
results.evidenceText: In the Russian Penal Colony, They Called Him ‘Dr. Evil’ | OCCRP Power and Influence • Russia In the Russian Penal Colony, They Called Him ‘Dr. Evil’ Deep in the Russian heartland, hundreds of kilometers from home, Ukrainian prisoners of war were tormented by a sadistic doctor. Reporters set out to unmask him. Banner: James O'Brien/OCCRP Reported by Olya Ivleva Journalist, Schemes, RFE/RL Ukrainian Service Find out more Kira Tolstiakova Editor, Schemes, RFE/RL Ukrainian Service Find out more Also published by our partner Schemes, RFE/RL Ukrainian Service (Ukraine, in Ukrainian) July 17, 2025 | 18 min read Share Article × Aa Text Settings × Text Size Small Medium Large Line Spacing Compact Normal Spacious When you arrived, it would be like this: You entered the reception room. You were stripped to the skin. You were shaved. You were beaten with a truncheon. Then you met Dr. Evil. "I was put in a bent-over pose and brought to get an X-ray," Pavlo remembers. " And at the X-ray there was this Dr. Evil, as we call him, shouting and with a stun gun." “ He started waving the stun gun, hit me a couple of times, began to threaten me, saying, ‘Hurry up, don’t be stupid.’ … He said that we ‘stinking Ukrainians’ didn’t deserve any decent treatment after what we had done .” What had they done? Pavlo, and dozens of others trucked into this penal colony, had fought for their home country in the war that followed Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Many of them had been captured after taking part in the desperate defense of Mariupol, a coastal city that was almost entirely destroyed by Russian bombardment. Its ruin, and the months-long siege of the massive Azovstal steel plant, where its last defenders holed up in increasingly desperate conditions, became a global symbol of the savagery of the war. Now they were prisoners, deep within Russia. There are an estimated 8,000 Ukrainian prisoners of war in Russia, along with civilian Ukrainian captives; thousands of other POWs have already returned home in organized prisoner swaps. Reports of their torture and abuse have been trickling out since the first group arrived back in Ukraine in 2022, and have kept coming with the release of additional prisoners. Returned POWs tended to report that one of the worst places to be held captive was Mordovia, a region in central Russia known for the many prisons and detention centers that dot its forested landscape, a legacy of the Soviet gulag system. Investigative journalists at Radio Free Europe’s Ukrainian service wanted to learn more about what was actually happening in these facilities. Although Mordovia has over a dozen prisons, nearly all the Ukrainian POWs sent there were held in a facility called Penal Colony No. 10, a large complex that sits along a road cutting through a forest, more than 500 kilometers from the Ukrainian border. Reporters obtained a list of 177 Ukrainians who had been held at Penal Colony No. 10 from sources in Ukrainian law enforcement. Nearly all, according to Ukrainian officials who interviewed them when they returned home, reported having been tortured and subjected to relentless physical and psychological violence. So reporters started reaching out to hear their stories. There was Pavlo Afisov, a military school graduate from the north of Ukraine who spent 614 days in Colony No. 10., along with stints in other Russian prisons. Yulian Pylypey, who still has a scar on his forehead after his captors set an attack dog on him and spent 171 days in the colony. Oleksandr Kiriienko, who sports a Viking beard and has served in the Ukrainian army since 2014, was there for 726 days. And Nikita Pikulyk, a young man with a boyish face who was captured after he had slipped out of Mariupol in civilian clothes. He spent 336 days in Mordovia. Forty-six other POWs also agreed to speak about their experiences. Physical torture was a given, they said. There were constant beatings, often targeting their backs and kidneys, for the smallest perceived infraction. They spoke of the tools most commonly used against them: Garbage bags were put over their heads. Stun guns were used to administer shock after shock. Attack dogs were set loose on them. Thick plastic pipes were used to beat them. They also described rampant sexual violence — threats of rape, beatings aimed at their genitals — and psychological torture, like mock executions. They said they were forced to stand for up to 16 hours a day, listen to loud Russian patriotic songs for equally long stretches (or 24 hours straight, if they were in the punishment block), and sometimes sing along to the Russian national anthem, hands on hearts. "You’d want to say, ‘Just beat me. Let 10 of you beat me with batons for five minutes. Then I’ll lie down, moaning, but in silence — please.’” Yulian Pylypey In all the stories these men told, an additional detail kept coming up. All 50 former prisoners referred to one memorable figure in Colony No. 10 — not a prison guard or administrator, not a military officer, but a doctor. Nobody knew his name, but they all called him by the same nickname: Доктор Зло, or Dr. Evil. Some of them also called him “the psychopath.” He wore a white coat and usually hid his face behind a medical mask or a balaclava, but the prisoners said his voice was unforgettable. “It was manic, screechy,” one said. “Indescribable.” Most of the prisoners said they encountered Dr. Evil immediately after their “reception” at the colony, since they had to undergo a chest X-ray when they arrived — Russian prisons are rife with tuberculosis — and this man usually administered it. He also used the occasion to administer electric shocks to prisoners, several of them recalled — and would continue shocking them over the course of their captivity. Although the prisoners were soldiers, accustomed to violence and braced for cruel treatment at the hands of their captors, they said the doctor stood out because of his pointless sadism and seeming betrayal of medical principles. Yes, he hit sick [prisoners] on the hands with a shocker, instead of giving them medical help, giving them pills or necessary medications. That is, he's a completely psychologically ill person, who somehow, I don't know how, ended up in this medical sphere. If it was just the guards, or federal penitentiary workers, or security guys, then, okay, you could understand anything from them. But this kind of treatment from medical staff was very hard for us to understand. Nikita Pikulyk “Dr. Evil” would visit the prisoners’ barracks at unpredictable times — it might be during an inspection, or it might be at random. It might be to dispense medicines — which he would do by ordering prisoners to drop to their knees and extend their hands. “Hand, bitch!” prisoners recalled him shouting. But just as often, prisoners said, their outstretched hands would be shocked with a stun gun, the promised pills never received. "'Now I’ll experiment," Yulian Pylypey recalls him saying, before turning the stun gun to "maximum." Oleksandr Kiriienko also remembers what would happen if anyone asked for medical help: “Whoever turned to him, he always carried a stun gun. Yes, the door would open, and whoever had asked for him — he’d hit them with the stun gun and say, “Will you ask for a pill again?” "Of course, the answer was 'no.'" But more disconcerting, the men all said, was the relentless psychological abuse the doctor subjected them to. He made the prisoners bark and crawl across the floor like dogs, they recalled. At other times they were ordered to imitate roosters: “Cock-a-doodle-doo, guys, cock-a-doodle-doo!” One Ukrainian POW had the unfortunate distinction of being especially good at barking. He came in for special attention. "Every time someone passed by, he had to bark. God forbid he didn’t. The doctor would immediately shout: ‘You, bark!’” Yulian Pylypey Also unforgettable, the prisoners said, was how the doctor forced them to sing Russian songs for hours on end, or chant strange, repetitive slogans or stock phrases from pop culture. While they were speaking their lines, he would walk among them with his stun gun and shock them, seemingly at random. Most of the doctor’s catchphrases made no sense — they seemed meant only to degrade. “He would shout ‘Yogurt!’ and we would have to shout ‘ Danone !'" explained Pavlo. “He would shout ‘Danone!’ and the prisoners would have to answer, ‘ Mmm !’” “Pepsi!” “Pshhhhh!” “Who lives under the sea?” “Spongebob SquarePants!” Others had a meaning that was all too clear. “His favorite question for all of us was, “Who are you?” We had to reply, “Faggots.” Pavlo Afisov The doctor also demanded that prisoners shout out praise for Russian doctors — and the entire medical profession. If they didn't say "Glory to Russian medicine!" every time he prompted them, "there would be consequences," Nikita Pikulyk recalled . The consequences? "Best case, you get shocked a few times by the doctor," said Yulian Pylypey. In the worst cases, special forces would be called into the cell to "educate" the prisoners. Oleksandr Savov, another POW, recalled that he was showing signs of tuberculosis when he entered the colony. He assumed he would be isolated, or receive medical help. Instead, he encountered Dr. Evil — who shocked him with a stun gun and called him a “faggot.” He remembers the doctor asking him, “Aren’t you going to scream?” and shocking him again. “What, am I supposed to scream?” he remembers asking. “‘Glory to Russian medicine,’” the doctor prompted him. “So I shouted, ‘Glory to Russian medicine!’ … and again, he used the shocker.” "Every time he came, he’d make the whole block shout, ‘Glory to Russian medicine!'" Pavlo Afisov Mistreatment of POWs, whether it’s physical abuse or “humiliating and degrading treatment,” is a violation of the Geneva Conventions. Although it may be counterintuitive, victims of abuse in detention centers often report that degradation at the hands of their captors is more scarring than many forms of physical torture. “[V]ictims always referred to this humiliation as a central part of what they went through and of what actually damaged them deeply,” said Thierry Cruvellier, a French journalist who has covered international justice and war crimes around the world for over two decades. “Screaming nonsense, reciting poems or songs — to me, it was one of the most degrading things. Honestly, I would rather be hit with a baton 10 times than do that.” Yulian Pylypey By all accounts, Ukrainian POWs in Russia appear to have been subjected to especially pervasive abuse, coordinated from the top down. The Wall Street Journal reported in February that prison guards in Russia had been instructed to “be cruel” to Ukrainian POWs . Citing three former prison officials who fled Russia, including two special forces officers and a member of a medical team, the Journal said that a group of elite prison guards received orders that “normal rules” would not apply to prisoners of war. The guards were then circulated to prisons across the country that received POWs, to work with lower-level prison officials. In a report the following month, Amnesty International also found evidence of systematic torture and denial of medical treatment to POWs , as well as other alleged violations of the Geneva Conventions. “In all wars, you have abuse of prisoners of war,” said Cruvellier. “I don’t think I know of any that haven’t gone through this…. What is exceptional in this particular case is that it is systemic, and often of high intensity.” Despite all the attention he paid them, the prisoners said that the man they knew as Dr. Evil did not actually treat their ailments. One man, who had a rotting tooth that caused him agonizing pain, begged for painkillers, only to be denied. (Although medical care in Russian prisons does not tend to get good reviews in the best of times, prisoners said that another doctor at Colony No. 10 would treat them sometimes — “when he was in a good mood.”). A man named Volodymyr Yykhymenko died at the prison. His cellmate, Valentyn Poliansky, told reporters that Volodymyr had been beaten across the face and ears with a slipper a few days before his death, causing his ear to swell and bleed alarmingly. Poliansky said the prisoners asked Dr. Evil to examine the man’s ear, but the doctor refused. (On Yykhymenko’s Russian death certificate, his cause of death is recorded as ventricular failure. A Ukrainian death certificate confirms that he died from pneumonia, but makes note of hemorrhages and abrasions he suffered two to seven days before his death.) "If you ask for, say, a bandage to dress a wound or a pill for a toothache, you’ll be told, 'There’s no doctor.' "You could absolutely never approach Dr. Evil. He didn’t treat anyone.” Pavlo Afisov After learning all this, reporters decided to see if they could discover the real identity of this unusual figure — obsessed with chants, slogans, and obedience — who had made such an impression on these battle-hardened prisoners of war. Reporters started with one clear fact: Medical services for Penal Colony No. 10 were provided by a specific unit of Russia’s Federal Penitentiary Service, Medical Unit No. 13. Any doctor working at the prison would have come from there. Searching through Russia’s most popular social network, a Facebook clone called VKontakte, they found all the pages that mentioned the abbreviation for the unit, “MSCh-13.” Among them was a page for the unit itself, two pages for the federal penitentiary service in Mordovia, and a page for the Mordovian trade union of state sector workers. They gathered dozens of photos from these pages, showing the medics receiving awards, assembling for group photos on professional holidays, and posing stiffly in front of their workplaces. There were even a few video clips, showing them dancing and singing in celebration of a Russian holiday for medical workers, and another one called “Day of the Medical Service of the Penal System.” Reporters started identifying the medical staff of the prison — many were connected via social networks — and sharing these photographs and videos with the former POWs, to see if they recognized any of them. The first reaction came from Pavlo Afisov. As soon as he heard the voices in one of the video clips, he started calling RFE/RL reporters, even though they had never spoken on the phone before. He was emotional. The first video, I recognized him in just 5 seconds That bastard Dr. Evil His voice Everything is fine It actually made me flinch I just wanted to say it to you personally P Pavlo Afisov Mar 25 Soon, Yulian Pylypey also chimed in. He cropped out an image of one doctor, a blonde man with a bowl cut and a white lab coat who had featured heavily in the photos and video clips found online. “The psychopath is the one on the left,” he wrote. Both men were completely certain that they were seeing and hearing Dr. Evil. To confirm the identification, reporters asked the other 48 former prisoners if they recognized the man in the photographs and videos. All of them said they did. But who was this man? Meet Ilya Sorokin. He is 34 years old. He’s married, with two daughters. He was born in the small Mordovian village of Potma, just 30 kilometers from Penal Colony No.10, and still lives there today. Records show he started studying at a local medical school in 2008. According to the research tool Himera-Search, which archives information leaked from Russia’s interior ministry and other databases, Sorokin has been working as a prison doctor since at least 2018, making around 564,000 rubles a year (around $9,000 at the time). Prison doctors in Russia tend to be hired out of small public clinics in rural areas, where salaries are even lower, according to Olga Romanova, the founder of prisoner-rights advocacy group Russia Behind Bars. Landing a job with the federal penitentiary service, or FSIN, means an immediate boost in status as well as salary. But becoming part of the FSIN system also means that doctors join a militarized agency — literally “put on epaulettes,” as Russians say — and their superiors become military officers. “To get more money, they put on epaulettes, they go work for the FSIN, and they get a bonus for their military rank — their salary approximately doubles — and that’s what they really want, in the provinces, to work in prisons and prison hospitals,” Romanova said, suggesting that this opened up Russia’s prison medical system to abuses. “They’re all FSIN staff first, and doctors second,” she said. “They report to the leadership — the FSIN leadership, not medical leadership.” Sorokin’s online presence — personal profiles on VKontakte and Odnoklasniki — helps sketch a rough outline of his life. Photographs of him as a young man show him living what seems to be a modest lifestyle typical of the Russian provinces. They give way to images of him studying medicine, clad in a typical white coat and Russian doctor’s cap and goofing around with medical props like IVs and a model of a human skull. He got married in around 2012. Six years later, he and his wife drove hours across Russia to visit the new Crimean Bridge — a symbol of Russia’s takeover of the Crimean Peninsula — just a few days after it opened. His social media posts also give a glimpse of his personality. He is sentimental (“I love and adore my wifey!” he said in one status update), and appears nostalgic for the Soviet Union’s glory days, participating in military parades on the patriotic Russian holiday May 9 and even dressing up in Soviet-era military garb. He’s also a booster of the current war, posting messages of support for the Russian army and insignia with the “Z” symbol, which conveys strong support for Putin’s military agenda. He appears to take pride in his role as a doctor. “Happy Medical Worker Day!” read a post he shared in 2012, illustrated with a cartoonish image of a scantily clad nurse. Another post showed his name spelled out in Cyrillic characters, with sexy nurses draped over each letter. But there’s not much to set him apart from any one of the millions of other Russians who support the war, celebrate national holidays, love their wives, and appreciate nurses. The most notable thing about Ilya Sorokin might be how ordinary he seems. In her classic study of the trial of Nazi official Adolf Eichmann, philosopher Hannah Arendt explored how the architect of the Holocaust came across not as a fanatic, but as a bureaucrat — a “terrifyingly normal” man who took comfort in following rules, climbing the career ladder, parroting cliches, and joining organizations to help give himself a sense of identity. This appears to be an apt description of Sorokin, too. Online, he is a member of several social media groups for doctors and penitentiary workers. In his real life, too, he appears to have been an avid joiner of groups and committees. According to a post from the state worker’s trade union, Sorokin served on the “profkom,” or governing committee, of the union for Medical Unit No. 13. He was also a member of the Mordovia-wide trade union committee. “He took an active part in the life of the team, in amateur performances,” the post read. Indeed, social media pages from the medical unit and affiliated organizations show that the doctors were enthusiastic about pageants and performances. Sorokin appears in several. In one, he is wearing a dark wig and draped in leaves. A caption under the photo wishes him a happy birthday: "Today is the birthday of the secretary of the Primary Trade Union Organization of Federal State Health Care Institution Medical-Sanitary Unit #13 of the Federal Penitentiary Service of Russia, Ilya Sorokin! With our whole heart we congratulate Ilya on his holiday! We hope he stays just as responsive, benevolent, and active as he is!!" results.evidenceText: Interpol Crackdown on Migrant Smuggling Nets 262 Arrests | OCCRP Organized Crime • Africa Interpol Crackdown on Migrant Smuggling Nets 262 Arrests November 10, 2026 | 1 min read Share Article × Aa Text Settings × Text Size Small Medium Large Line Spacing Compact Normal Spacious An Interpol-led operation across 16 countries has resulted in 262 arrests tied to migrant smuggling networks along the Mediterranean Sea and West African Atlantic routes, the agency announced Tuesday. The four-day sweep across North and West Africa, southern Europe, and the Middle East identified 109 potential human trafficking victims, detected 1,715 irregular migrants, and sparked 434 new investigations that are “expected to yield further leads and arrests in the coming weeks and months.” Among the key interventions, Moroccan authorities rescued a vessel carrying 70 stranded migrants—including 30 minors—who had been at sea for six days. In a separate action, Mauritanian law enforcement intercepted a wooden boat carrying 80 passengers and arrested three suspected organizers. results.pageTitle: Ex-Belgrade Police Chief Denies Charges in 'Body in a Barrel' Case
results.pageDescription: Prosecutors dropped the most severe charges against Veselin Milić, who remains a top police official despite his alleged ties to the gruesome killing.
results.evidenceText: Ex-Belgrade Police Chief Denies Charges in 'Body in a Barrel' Case | OCCRP Power and Influence • Serbia Ex-Belgrade Police Chief Denies Charges in 'Body in a Barrel' Case Prosecutors dropped the most severe charges against Veselin Milić, who remains a top police official despite his alleged ties to the gruesome killing. Banner: Maxim Konankov/NurPhoto via AFP | Serbian police. Reported by Tamara Todorović KRIK November 9, 2026 | 2 min read Share Article × Aa Text Settings × Text Size Small Medium Large Line Spacing Compact Normal Spacious A former Belgrade police chief pleaded not guilty to charges stemming from a brazen gangland murder, while prosecutors have dropped the most severe allegations against him. Former Police Chief Veselin Milić appeared Monday before the First Basic Court in Belgrade to deny charges of failing to report a crime and falsifying an official document, OCCRP’s Serbian member center KRIK reported . In addition to those charges prosecutors had previously accused him of participating in covering up the physical traces of the May 12 murder of Aleksandar Nešović , whose body was discovered stuffed in a barrel that had been buried in the town of Inđija after a week-long search. Prosecutors have now withdrawn those allegations, while the investigator who built the case has been arrested on suspicion of illegally gathering evidence against Milić. Milić was removed from his post as Belgrade's police chief, but he currently serves as an Assistant Director of Police. Initial reports and prosecutorial statements alleged that Milić had lured the victim to a Belgrade restaurant, explicitly told him to leave his security detail behind, and then stayed at the scene after the fatal shooting to delete surveillance footage and coordinate the removal of the body. Milić was arrested, held in 30-day pretrial detention, and stripped of his position as Chief of the Police Administration for the City of Belgrade. Instead, the indictment now accuses him only of failing to report the murder—despite allegedly being informed about it by the restaurant owner—and falsifying his official police notes. Prosecutors say Milić deliberately omitted crucial information from his report, namely that he knew the suspected shooter, former police officer Saša Vuković, and that he had personally invited both the suspect and the victim to the restaurant that day. In court, Milić’s defense attorney, Nemanja Vasiljević, argued there is no legal evidence to support the remaining charges and called the proceedings a "relapse of malicious and illegal behavior." Vasiljević also highlighted a stunning twist in the case: the original criminal complaint against Milić was filed by the Criminal Police Directorate under the leadership of Marko Kričak. He said Kričak was recently arrested after Milić filed a complaint alleging he had illegally gathered evidence against him. The defense argues the case should be thrown out due to the alleged abuses by Kričak and other interior ministry officials. The judge scheduled the next hearing for December 17, when Milić is expected to present his full defense. Meanwhile, the trial against Vuković, the alleged shooter, and his accomplices f is proceeding separately before the Higher Court in Belgrade. results.pageTitle: Dan Hicks, who called memorable moments across sports world for NBC, dies at 64
results.pageDescription: Hicks was most closely associated with golf, Olympics coverage and Notre Dame football.
results.evidenceText: Dan Hicks, who called memorable moments across sports world for NBC, dies at 64 - The Athletic Dan Hicks, who called memorable moments across sports world for NBC, dies at 64 Dan Hicks joined NBC Sports in 1992 after a short stint with CNN. Streeter Lecka / Getty Images By Mark Puleo , Pete Sampson , Brody Miller , Andrew Marchand and Zack Pierce Nov. 12, 2026 Updated Share article 296 Dan Hicks, a prominent play-by-play voice for NBC Sports who spent more than 30 years narrating some of the sports world’s biggest moments, from major golf tournaments to Olympic swimming pools, died Wednesday, his wife, Hannah Storm, said in a statement. He was 64. Hicks had been married to Storm, a longtime ESPN “SportsCenter” anchor, since 1994. She said in her statement Thursday that his death was “sudden and unexpected,” though she did not say where he died. Advertisement “Dan was truly one of a kind and, quite simply, the person everyone wanted to be around,” Storm said. “When he walked into a room, he brought the energy, the laughter and the people together. He was endlessly kind, thoughtful and funny, and he made everyone feel like they mattered.” Hicks was due to call Notre Dame’s game Saturday against Boston College, according to an NBC schedule released earlier this week. What You Should Read Next Dan Hicks, our host for so much Olympic greatness, always met the golden moment He chronicled the Olympic careers of Michael Phelps, Mikaela Shiffrin and many more greats. And he always delivered a worthy call. Hicks joined NBC in 1992 after a short stint with CNN. At NBC, he served as play-by-play commentator for Notre Dame football, contributed to NFL coverage, was a sideline reporter on “NBA on NBC,” and played a key role in the network’s golf and Olympics coverage, including five Winter Games in which he called speed skating and alpine skiing. He also called eight consecutive Summer Games since 1996, and among his most memorable calls was a U.S. comeback in the 4×100 freestyle relay at the 2008 Beijing Games, which secured Michael Phelps’ eighth gold medal of the Games. On the course, perhaps his most famous call came when Tiger Woods sunk a 12-foot putt to force a playoff at the 2008 U.S. Open. “Expect anything different?” Hicks calmly voiced after waiting for the Torrey Pines crowd to erupt, summarizing the most dominant decade golf had ever seen. Dan Hicks was a master of unscripted play-by-play, voicing many of golf's most famous moments over the last 30 years. Jimmy Roberts remembers his iconic call of Tiger Woods' putt at the 2008 U.S. Open: "Expect anything different?" pic.twitter.com/sIzzzJDt89 — Golf Channel (@GolfChannel) November 12, 2026 In a statement Thursday, the PGA Tour called Hicks’ work with commentator Johnny Miller “one of golf television’s defining broadcast partnerships.” Advertisement At NBC, Hicks was known for being easy to work with in production, and willing to assist other broadcasters in their careers. And at Notre Dame, Hicks’ continuity connected with fans beyond simply broadcasting games, thanks to the unique media rights agreement between the network and the school, of which Storm is a 1983 graduate. “Dan Hicks was an extraordinary colleague, friend and person,” NBC Sports said in a statement. “He was an exceptional storyteller and caller of games and events who elevated some of the biggest moments in sports history.” Hicks — born in Tucson, Ariz. and a graduate of the University of Arizona — became NBC’s lead play-by-play golf announcer in 2000. “Partner,” Hicks told Miller after the 2014 U.S. Open, as NBC’s broadcasting rights to the tournament were ending, “it’s been a great ride.” Golf’s enduring tenor There are just a few calls in golf lore — and sports history — that can be recited word for word as if the broadcast was fused to the moment like John Williams’ score to a bicycle crossing the moon. You’ve probably never seen Woods’ putt roll in on 18 at the 2008 U.S. Open without Hicks’ words, because Hicks made the moment grander, and Hicks knew it was about the moment, not him. Advertisement He waited for the crowd to erupt. He let a quiet moment pass. And then he summarized the most dominant decade golf had ever seen with the most honest assessment: “Expect anything different?” Hicks’ rise as NBC’s lead golf voice coincided with Woods’ peak from 2000 on. But while Woods faded, Hicks remained a constant. He called Rory McIlroy’s runaway wins and the Miracle at Medinah. Bryson versus Rory at Pinehurst was Hicks, as was J.J. Spaun’s 64-foot birdie win at Oakmont just a year ago. But perhaps the greatest compliment to Hicks is how those NBC broadcasts were remembered for his team. Hicks understood the art of a play-by-play man, letting his 19-year partner Miller be the star in golf’s longest-running broadcast tandem. He knew how to toss it to golf’s fun uncle, Roger Maltbie, or the great Gary Koch. Hicks never took up the oxygen. Longtime broadcaster Jimmy Roberts calls Hicks the best, but of course Roberts is biased, the way so many in the golf world are predisposed to Hicks. He was a good hang, the type Storm said everybody wants to be around. Roberts, Maltbie and Hicks formed what they called the “Supper Club.” Roberts likes to say he ate more meals with Hicks than he did with his family. The scene of Roberts and Rich Lerner mournfully reminiscing Thursday morning on Golf Channel paints the painful picture. “This is not losing a colleague and a nice guy; this is losing a pal,” Maltbie said Thursday on the network. Hicks understood how to make golf about the moment, and now those moments will feel a little more empty. — Brody Miller An Olympic broadcasting icon Hicks was the fan’s connection to scores of American gold-medal triumphs at the Olympics as the play-by-play voice of swimming, Alpine skiing and speed skating. Advertisement He was the voice of some of NBC’s most memorable Olympic moments, dating back to Atlanta in 1996, including Phelps’ entire Olympic career, with his record 23 gold and 28 medals overall across four Games from 2004 to 2016. Phelps’ career peaked in 2008, when he went 8-for-8 in gold medals in Beijing. That year also featured one of Hicks’ great calls. In the 4×100-meter freestyle relay, Phelps and the Americans faced a tough test in France. Anchor Jason Lezak entered the pool for the final leg trailing France’s Alain Bernard, the world’s best 100-meter freestyler at the time. At the turn, the U.S. seemed destined for silver — Hicks even said as much during the call — until Lezak stormed to the wall over the final 25 meters to pass and out-touch Bernard, leaving Hicks screaming in amazement. “Here comes Lezak!” Hicks yelled. “Unbelievable at the end! He’s done it!” Lezak’s charge gave Phelps a second gold in Beijing with six more races in his eight-gold quest. It also launched one of the most famous celebrations in U.S. Olympic history, with Phelps — the top half of his suit removed and dangling at his waist — shouting and flexing to the crowd from the pool deck. “Phelps’ hopes alive!” Hicks said over the scene. Hicks has also been the voice of the Olympic careers of Katie Ledecky, Ryan Lochte, Natalie Coughlin, Caeleb Dressel and many other U.S. swimming stars. As NBC’s lead Alpine skiing voice for the past four Winter Games, Hicks has called Mikaela Shiffrin’s entire Olympic career, from her gold medals in 2014 and 2018 to her surprising medal shutout in 2022 to her return to gold in February in Cortina d’Ampezzo, Italy. Hicks called Lindsey Vonn’s last Olympic medal in 2018 and was on the mic again in Italy when she returned and crashed in the downhill. Hicks’ first Winter Olympics assignment was speed skating. From 2002 to 2010, he called gold-medal performances from Shani Davis, Joey Cheek, Chad Hedrick and more. — Zack Pierce Advertisement A broadcasting power couple Hicks and Storm are probably the most successful husband-wife team in sportscasting history. Storm shattered the glass ceiling, becoming the first woman to host one of the four major sports when she led NBC’s coverage of the NBA Finals in the 1990s. Hicks was just as successful. His broadcasts were consistently strong and never about him. In an age of schtick, he delivered the goods with rare versatility, where his bosses could ask him to call play-by-play on a whim or host. Hicks’ ability to host and call the action made him perfect for golf, and he became synonymous with NBC’s coverage. His biggest highlights probably came at the Olympics, where he and Rowdy Gaines’ swimming coverage was a once-every-four-years treat that secured them a spot in the annals of all-time duos. They may not always be considered with the likes of Pat Summerall-John Madden, Vin Scully-Joe Garagiola, Doc Emrick-John Davidson or Marv Albert-Mike Fratello, but in some ways, the scarcity of Hicks-Gaines made it even more special. It is an extremely sad day for the golf, Olympic and football communities with the news of Hicks’ passing. No words can make anything right for Storm and their three daughters. One day, maybe, they can find a little solace in the fact that Hicks left behind quite a legacy. — Andrew Marchand Correction: A previous version of this article gave the incorrect birthplace for Hicks. He was born in Arizona. Nov 16, 2026 Connections: Sports Edition Spot the pattern. author.description: Brody Miller covers golf and the LSU Tigers for The Athletic. He came to The Athletic from the New Orleans Times-Picayune. author.name: Andrew Marchand

In 2024, he won the Associated Press Sports Editors' top national award for beat writing for his coverage of sports media. Marchand also has his own twice-weekly sports media podcast available at AndrewMarchand.com.

results.pageTitle: From Politicians to Academics, Hundreds Around the Globe Interviewed and Featured in Notorious Russian Disinformation Campaign
results.pageDescription: Former American, French, and Spanish intelligence officers, nearly a dozen far-right German politicians, and academics from around the globe: These are some of the hundreds of personalities who have been interviewed and featured on websites associated with the “Doppelgänger” campaign.
results.evidenceText: From Politicians to Academics, Hundreds Around the Globe Interviewed and Featured in Notorious Russian Disinformation Campaign | OCCRP Power and Influence • Russia From Politicians to Academics, Hundreds Around the Globe Interviewed and Featured in Notorious Russian Disinformation Campaign Former American, French, and Spanish intelligence officers, nearly a dozen far-right German politicians, and academics from around the globe: These are some of the hundreds of personalities who have been interviewed and featured on websites associated with the “Doppelgänger” campaign. Banner: James O’Brien/OCCRP Reported by Martin Laine Delfi Estonia Also published by our partners Delfi Estonia (Estonia, in Estonian) Jan Kuciak Investigative Center (Slovakia, in Slovak) and The Nerve (United Kingdom, in English) November 10, 2026 | 14 min read Share Article × Aa Text Settings × Text Size Small Medium Large Line Spacing Compact Normal Spacious “Imposing sanctions on a country so rich in resources [as Russia] was pure and simple madness.” — Italian media personality Simona Mangiante Papadopoulos “The conflict with the Russians has proven to be a catastrophe for the Germans." — Glenn Diesen, Norwegian political scientist “Ukraine has lost this war.” — Lawrence Wilkerson, retired U.S. Army colonel and former chief of staff to Secretary of State Colin Powell “Doppelgänger,” a sprawling state-backed Russian disinformation campaign, gained notoriety in 2022 for creating clones of genuine news sites to spread pro-Kremlin narratives aimed at undermining support for Ukraine. In the years since, it has also created dozens of new sites purporting to be news organizations that publish propaganda content in English, French, German, and other languages. The scale of these efforts was put on display after one of the main sites associated with Doppelgänger — Recent Reliable News (RRN) — was hacked and turned into a database cataloging over 500 interviews that have been posted on Doppelgänger-linked websites. OCCRP and Delfi Estonia reviewed the videos and found that the men and women interviewed hail from more than 50 countries and span a wide range of personalities, from a French farmer to a Finnish conspiracy theorist to scores of former European and U.S. officials, including elected lawmakers and former high-ranking military officers from NATO countries. Many are known for pro-Russian views and were interviewed on topics such as NATO, Ukraine, and the internal politics of countries like the U.S., Germany, and France. According to researchers and authorities in the U.S. and Europe, Doppelgänger is one workstream in a broader digital propaganda effort run by the Social Design Agency (SDA), a sanctioned Russian PR firm, and other affiliated organizations that work closely with the Russian Presidential Administration, such as ANO Dialog, a sanctioned non-profit created by the Moscow city government. Several leaks from within SDA have already laid bare the scope and sophistication of its influence campaigns, with goals that include “deepening internal contradictions between ruling elites” in Western countries and “stimulating protest activity among [their] opposition forces.” Another internal document, cited by the FBI, described a plan to “use a wide range of information tools” to “influence real life conflicts and artificially create conflict situations” in countries allied with the United States. SDA is also known to have monitored thousands of "opinion leaders” across the world. A leaked internal meeting note from 2022 cited by the FBI stressed: “We need influencers! A lot of them and everywhere. We are ready to wine and dine them.” " aria-label="Next slide"> “If we were to get Russian gas again, of course prices would fall sharply.” — Gunnar Lindemann, Member of Berlin's House of Representatives from Alternative for Germany (AfD) When reached for comment, Lindemann said he gives interviews to all journalists, both domestic and international. “NATO has moved closer to Russia’s borders. We haven’t signed an agreement guaranteeing Ukraine’s neutrality, and that’s a real scandal.” — Rainer Rothfuß, Bundestag member from Alternative for Germany (AfD) Rothfuß did not respond to requests to comment. “In my opinion, the time has come to lift all sanctions once and for all. We need to chart a path to resuming relations with Russia across all fronts. It's time to stop endlessly pouring money and weapons into Zelensky's pockets. There can only be one winner - Russia.” — Dimitar Shivikov, Retired Bulgarian army brigadier general Shivikov did not respond to requests to comment. “The European Union has been extremely anti-Russian so far. These people seemed to be united by a common Russophobia." — Petar Volgin, Bulgarian member of the European Parliament Volgin did not respond to requests to comment. “If Germany suddenly decides to strengthen its army for some reason, for example because Russia is on the verge of attacking, that’s ridiculous. /—/ There is no threat. But even if there were, they don’t have the strength to defend themselves." — Karen Kwiatkowski, Retired U.S. Air Force lieutenant colonel, former Pentagon and National Security Agency (NSA) official When reached for comment, Kwiatkowski said she says "pretty much the same thing to everyone I speak to" and did not keep records of the queries she received for such interviews. "It’s in the U.S. interest to bring Russia back into the Western camp." — Jean-Luc Schaffhauser, Former French member of the European Parliament (2014-2019) Schaffhauser did answer questions sent by reporters about the interviews. " aria-label="Next slide"> OCCRP reached out to more than 60 people interviewed for Doppelgänger sites to understand how they were approached and by whom. Most did not respond to the questions or said they could not recall who arranged the interviews. But the small number who did helped provide a rare look into how the operation works. As it turns out, not all of the people behind Doppelgänger were Russian. For instance, several interviewees said they were contacted by Brazilian followers of ultra-nationalist Russian ideologue Alexander Dugin, who rejects Western liberalism and promotes a vision of a world order led by dominant "civilizations” — including a Russian one — as opposed to individual nation states. Several other figures were contacted over social media by a young man who described himself as a journalist, though OCCRP could find no record of his journalistic work. “I think your vision of the geopolitical situation is very deep and interesting,” reads a WhatsApp message he sent in June 2024 to Matthew Gordon-Banks, a former U.K. parliamentarian who later advised governments like Kuwait, Bahrain, and the UAE. Gordon-Banks told OCCRP he spoke to the self-described journalist on three occasions. In total, he is cited in more than a dozen articles featured on websites associated with the Doppelgänger project, covering topics like instability in Western countries and alleged plans by the U.S. to “move on” from supporting Ukraine. Gordon-Banks told reporters he does not "deliberately take part in propaganda operations for anyone” and that he “would always comment on any matter relating to Russia from my own experience, which is now some 40 plus years.” SDA, ANO Dialog, and Russia’s presidential administration did not respond to requests to comment. About the Hacking of RRN Recent Reliable News was first hacked in 2024 and given a new banner that reads: “The Doppelganger got Doppelgangered.” In the years since, the site’s anonymous operator, who told OCCRP he was motivated by “trolling losers in Moscow who think that they are above everything,” has transformed it into a regularly updated archive of interviews published by RRN and other websites that Western authorities and researchers have linked to the Doppelgänger project. A Modern Model of Russian Propaganda The effectiveness of the Doppelgänger campaign has been disputed by researchers, who suspect companies like SDA have inflated figures purporting to show its reach. Yet there is little doubt that the effort was ambitious and well-resourced. The hundreds of interviews apparently carried out as part of the project capture the “vast nature” of the influence campaigns tied to SDA and affiliated actors, said James Pamment, the director of the Lund University Psychological Defence Research Institute and a co-author of a 2025 report on Doppelgänger. These campaigns represent a newer model of Russian propaganda, carried out not by state media or intelligence agencies but by a multi-million-dollar industry of organizations that seek funding from the Russian state, according to the report. Previous leaks show that SDA reports high interaction rates and viewership numbers for its online content, Pamment noted. “They use amplification bots and basically every other tool possible on every stage to maximize reach,” he said. “But reach doesn’t mean effect.” According to his research, more than pushing any particular narrative, SDA’s goal has been “penetration of the Western information environment.” “It doesn’t matter who is the messenger and what is the message, so long as the Russian Federation’s thematic lines seize a share of the marketplace of ideas,” reads his 2025 report. Germany in the Crosshairs The largest share of interviewed politicians hail from the AfD, the German far-right party that recently secured a historic victory in the country’s eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. Doppelgänger-affiliated websites have repeatedly covered the party and even displayed one of its campaign banners before the 2025 federal election. Earlier leaked documents have confirmed that SDA was actively trying to increase the party’s popularity. In total, at least ten current and former AfD politicians gave interviews that were published on Doppelgänger outlets. Only two responded to journalists' requests for a comment. Gunnar Lindemann, an AfD member of the Berlin House of Representatives since 2016, said that he gives interviews to all journalists, both domestic and international. Similarly, Gunnar Beck, who served as an AfD member of the European Parliament from 2019 to 2024, said he shares his opinion on current events “with anyone who is interested and asks me serious questions, regardless of their ideological orientation or national affiliation.” The former MEP added he is no longer active in German politics. “I have never knowingly spoken with journalists or representatives of these organizations,” Beck said in reference to the websites where his interviews were published. “Please also be assured that I have never received any money or benefits in kind for a media contribution or interview.” Interviews were also conducted with figures from other sides of the German political spectrum, including Frederick Broßart, a local politician in Lower Saxony who represents Sahra Wagenknecht’s left-wing party. At least four articles published on Doppelgänger’s German news site Militärblatt feature his interview segments, which criticized the Merz government and its military spending. “At the time, I was not aware that there might be a connection to the Doppelgänger network,” he told OCCRP, adding that he was contacted in a private message over X. “This experience led me to rethink my approach.” Show more Keir Giles, an expert on the Russian military, noted that companies like SDA must prove the value of their work to the Kremlin to keep receiving new grants, and that the large volume of Doppelgänger interviews may reflect that incentive. “When an enormous sum from the budget has been set aside for propaganda, you may need to show you have used all of it,” he said. Giles and other experts noted that the library of some 500 interviews, which generated some 1,800 articles, includes a number of conspiracy theorists, such as believers in alien abductions. “A loose grip on reality is a good leverage point,” said Giles. “When you boost conspiracy theorists who say you need to distrust the government — that’s a useful point for Russia.” Many of those interviewed have also cooperated with the Russian state in other ways, such as serving in election-monitoring missions in occupied regions of Ukraine or giving interviews to Russian state media, he added. “Some of these people may completely be content to be taken advantage of in this fashion.” For John Sipher, an intelligence and national security expert formerly with the CIA, the ability to collect such a high volume of interviews reflects the current social media environment, in which “we have all become used to having some sort of public profile.” “The Russians understand this and seek a means to weaponize it for their purposes,” he said. Dugin Fans from Brazil Those who conduct the Doppelgänger interviews typically do not appear in the videos themselves, which show only tight headshots of their subjects. But by speaking with interviewees, reporters learned that in the case of Gordon-Banks and three others, subjects were approached over social media by a young Russian man who went by the name Nikolay Maslov. Credit: Screenshot/Supplied by Gordon-Banks A WhatsApp message that Gordon-Banks received from Nikolay Maslov. Credit: Screenshot/Supplied by Gordon-Banks A WhatsApp message that Gordon-Banks received from Nikolay Maslov. In the message he sent to Gordon-Banks, Maslov described himself as a “journalist and producer” and said he was developing a “young German media company with a Russian background.” The link he shared was for Meisterurian, a German-language news site that was outed for its connections to the Doppelgänger campaign by the FBI, which seized the domain later that year. Reporters could find no record that Maslov, who lists Moscow as his location on social media, has ever worked as a journalist. In 2022, he submitted a resume to a job portal describing his experience as a KYC analyst in the banking sector. There is no mention of any journalistic training or experience. He did not respond to requests to comment. Gordon-Banks told reporters he had given at least three interviews to Maslov over the years, and that he believed his interlocutor was "a financial analyst based in Moscow who very infrequently undertakes some video interviews to maintain his English.” Several Doppelgänger interviewees pointed to a different set of intermediaries: Brazilian followers of Dugin, the sanctioned Russian ideologue who has built a fanbase among the international far right. Five said their conversations were set up or conducted by Raphael Machado, the leader of the Brazilian chapter of New Resistance, a transnational neo-fascist movement inspired by Dugin’s ideology. According to the U.S. State Department, New Resistance has deep connections to Russia’s disinformation and propaganda ecosystem. Among the interviews Machado conducted was one with Simona Mangiante Papadopoulos, the wife of a former aide to U.S. President Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign . In the interview, parts of which are quoted in a March 2026 article on the French-language propaganda site Phrygien, she disparages Europe’s economic prospects and describes them as the consequences of turning away from a more “dynamic” Russia. When reached for comment, Mangiante Papadopoulos told OCCRP that she did not recognize the French site and did not knowingly collaborate with the Doppelgänger campaign. After OCCRP shared the videos of her interview, she recalled that Machado was the man with whom she had spoken. Machado did not respond to requests to comment. The Brazilian also organized interviews with at least four other subjects in the U.S., U.K., and Canada, according to the interviewees OCCRP spoke with and a source familiar with the conversations. Reporting by the German outlet t-online previously found that he arranged interviews with a French and a Brazilian source as well. Credit: Screenshot/VKontakte//Raphael Machado Alexandr Dugin (left) and Raphael Machado (right) pose together in a photo posted by Machado on VKontakte, a Russian social media platform. Credit: Screenshot/VKontakte//Raphael Machado Alexandr Dugin (left) and Raphael Machado (right) pose together in a photo posted by Machado on VKontakte, a Russian social media platform. Many of the people interviewed are also associated with Dugin and his ideas. At least 20 attended an online conference in 2023 called the “First Global Conference on Multipolarity” that was co-organized by Dugin and Machado’s New Resistance, among other groups. Another interviewee, the right-wing Norwegian political figure Christen Krogvig, told OCCRP he was contacted on Telegram by someone using the name Antonio Andreas, but knew nothing else about the person and never saw his face. OCCRP identified a Telegram account using the name Antonio Andreas that has regularly shared content to a channel dedicated to Dugin. A Brazilian man named Antonio Andreas Pires is also the administrator or owner of several other Dugin fan channels on platforms like Telegram and Facebook, which also regularly share Machado’s content. On LinkedIn, an Andreas Pires whose photo matches those used in the other social media accounts describes himself as a social media manager of Rossiya Segodnya, a state-owned media group that operates Sputnik and other outlets aimed at an international audience. Andreas Pires did not respond to requests for comment. According to Krogvig, “Antonio Andreas” sent a list of written questions on topics such as German aid to Ukraine and German public opinion on buying Russian gas and asked Krogvig to record his answers on video himself. “How do I know what Germans prefer?” the Norwegian recalled wondering at the time. Yet he recorded the video anyway and his comments were subsequently used in articles on Doppelgänger’s German-language website Östlicher Wind. “Merz receives bribes from Zelenskyy,” reads the headline of the article featuring Krogvig's “insights” on German society. Moving to Turkey By June 2026, many of the Doppelgänger websites were found to have gone offline. Only two appear to remain active, both registered to Turkish domains and continuing to publish interviews with Western and local talking heads. One of these sites, a Turkish-language website known as Kıtalararası, is run by Mehmet Perinçek, a member of Turkey’s pro-Russian Vatan party who has described himself as close to Dugin’s family and who has also previously collaborated with Machado’s New Resistance. He did not respond to requests to comment. After RRN was hacked, the brand also started to operate under a Turkish domain, changed its name to Researchers & Reporters Network, and now publicizes a staff of Turkish journalists who have held formal roles in the Vatan party. “This portal provides reliable information from verified sources. News, analysis, and expert opinions,” a banner stretching across the top of the webpage reads in Turkish. Credit: Screenshot/rrn.com.tr The RRN website indicates that the RRN brand now operates under a Turkish domain ending in .tr. Credit: Screenshot/rrn.com.tr The RRN website indicates that the RRN brand now operates under a Turkish domain ending in .tr. The Turkish RRN continues to feature interviews with Western political figures, such as the German politician Frederick Broßart, who represents Sahra Wagenknecht’s left-wing party in Lower Saxony. Journalists first contacted the politician in July 2026 about four of his interviews that had been published by the Doppelgänger-linked German news site Militärblatt. He replied that he would be more “cautious when it comes to interview requests from unknown media outlets and examine much more closely who is behind a request.” Yet as recently as October 9, he had given an interview to the latest incarnation of RRN, in which he called on Germany to halt arms shipments to Ukraine and end economic sanctions against Russia in favor of diplomatic negotiations to secure peace. “

results.pageDescription: Authorities have not disclosed details of the alleged corruption offenses involving the leaders of Samruk-Kazyna and Kazakhstan Temir Zholy, who were detained alongside several other unnamed officials.
results.evidenceText: Kazakh Wealth Fund, Railway Chiefs Detained in Corruption Probe | OCCRP Corruption • Kazakhstan Kazakh Wealth Fund, Railway Chiefs Detained in Corruption Probe Authorities have not disclosed details of the alleged corruption offenses involving the leaders of Samruk-Kazyna and Kazakhstan Temir Zholy, who were detained alongside several other unnamed officials. Banner: Yasin Baturhan Ergin/Anadolu/Anadolu via AFP | A view of Astana, the capital of Kazakhstan, where the headquarters of Samruk-Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund is located. Reported by OCCRP November 12, 2026 | 2 min read Share Article × Aa Text Settings × Text Size Small Medium Large Line Spacing Compact Normal Spacious Kazakhstan’s anti-corruption service on Wednesday detained the heads of the country’s sovereign wealth fund and national railway operator on suspicion of a corruption offense. The detained officials are Nurlan Zhakupov, head of the Samruk-Kazyna Sovereign Fund—which holds about $87.5 billion in assets—and Yelzhas Otynshiyev, head of the national railway company Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ), the country’s National Security Committee said in a statement Thursday. KTZ is a subsidiary of the fund and operates the country’s main rail network. Alongside other officials, whom the committee did not name, Zhakupov and Otynshiyev are “suspected of committing a corruption-related offense,” the committee said, adding that “investigative actions are currently underway to establish all the circumstances of the case.” Footage published on the X account of the national broadcaster Qazaqstan, showed Zhakupov, wearing a blue shirt, surrounded by several people in a doorway. A representative of Samruk-Kazyna, told the local media outlet Tengrinews that the fund is fully cooperating with law enforcement. "The Fund provides comprehensive assistance to law enforcement agencies, ensuring the necessary interaction and provision of requested information and materials within the framework of the current legislation of the Republic of Kazakhstan," the statement said. Samruk-Kazyna holds state stakes in some of Kazakhstan’s largest businesses. Its portfolio includes national oil and gas company KazMunayGas, uranium producer Kazatomprom, telecommunications operator Kazakhtelecom and national electricity grid operator KEGOC. The fund’s consolidated assets include KTZ, the railway company. The fund and the companies within its group continue to operate as usual, Samrak-Kazyna JSC said in a statement . “All commitments to investors, creditors, international financial institutions and business partners remain in full force and are being honored in accordance with the terms of existing agreements”, the statement read. KTZ runs freight and passenger services. Its network carries domestic traffic and cargo between China and Europe, including along the Trans-Caspian route . The company reported that 319.9 million metric tons of freight moved over its network in 2025. It had 7.6 trillion tenge, or about $15 billion, in consolidated assets at year-end. In May, the fund and KTZ announced plans to launch an initial public offering with a proposed triple listing in London, Hong Kong and Kazakhstan. Shortly before the announcement , social media videos in the capital showed what appeared to be U.S. dollar bills scattered on the ground in the country's capital, Astana, though the committee did not link the footage to the investigation. Samruk-Kazyna’s press office did not answer calls from OCCRP reporters. KTZ declined to comment on the detentions. results.pageTitle: Five Questions About the Future of Global Anticorruption Efforts in the Trump Era
results.pageDescription: Law Professor Kevin E. Davis, whose research has explored the ways that anti-corruption laws affect economic development, discusses the future of transnational anti-bribery enforcement after U.S. President Donald Trump's policies were rebuked in midterm elections.
results.evidenceText: Five Questions About the Future of Global Anticorruption Efforts in the Trump Era | OCCRP INTERVIEW Power and Influence • United States Five Questions About the Future of Global Anticorruption Efforts in the Trump Era Law Professor Kevin E. Davis, whose research has explored the ways that anti-corruption laws affect economic development, discusses the future of transnational anti-bribery enforcement after U.S. President Donald Trump's policies were rebuked in midterm elections. Banner: Mehmet Eser/Anadolu/Anadolu via AFP | The U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C., on November 3, 2026, as Americans vote in the midterm elections. November 13, 2026 | 8 min read Share Article × Aa Text Settings × Text Size Small Medium Large Line Spacing Compact Normal Spacious After winning control of the United States Congress and Senate in midterm elections this month, the Democratic Party is expected to mount a firmer resistance to the dismantling of anti-corruption laws, institutions, and norms that has taken place under the Republican administration of President Donald Trump. As part of Trump’s “America First” approach to foreign policy, the U.S. has narrowed enforcement of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA), the law designed to prohibit U.S. citizens or companies from bribing foreign officials for business, officially withdraw n from GRECO, the Council of Europe’s anti-corruption body, and gutted the U.S. Corporate Transparency Act, a 2020 law aimed at combating money laundering and illicit finance. Kevin E. Davis, Beller Family Professor of Business Law at the New York University School of Law, discusses these changes and which foreign powers may fill the void that Trump’s administration has left in prosecuting transnational corruption. In 2019, you published a book, “Between Impunity and Imperialism: The Regulation of Transnational Bribery,” which criticized the U.S.-led approach to tackling transnational bribery that was in place before the Trump administration curtailed enforcement of the FCPA. How has your thinking changed since then? My focus in the book was on what I saw as the imperialistic aspects of the multilateral regime that was led by the United States, but I think it was becoming a truly multilateral regime. It was dominated by the members of the OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development), even though its effects were felt around the world. So, I've been concerned about whether all the countries who were affected by the regime had a say in its design. And that was my concern back in 2019 – it was about that multilateral issue. Some of those concerns seem rather quaint now, because what we have now is — at least on a part of the U.S. — something that fits a more traditional conception of imperialism or legal imperialism. It's avowedly not multilateral, it is “America First,” and it is explicitly motivated by self interest. They have eschewed one of the basic principles of the OECD regime, which is that enforcement should be impartial, as opposed to self-interested. Under the OECD regime, it's quite clear that you're not supposed to target enforcement to advantage your national champions, right? So you can't target your competitors, and you can't provide leniency to your own firms. Whereas the enforcement guidelines that the Trump administration has adopted quite explicitly embraced the idea of putting American interests first in making enforcement decisions. So it's quite different in that respect. It's also different in that the U.S. has scaled back the overall level of enforcement, which again is contrary to the thrust of the previous regime, which was all about increasing the resources devoted to antibribery enforcement. So, both in terms of the selectivity and the reduction of enforcement efforts, I think what we're seeing is a marked departure from the previous model. When the U.S. steps back from multilateral institutions, who fills the void in shaping international commercial and anti-corruption law? It's not entirely clear how much they're stepping back from the OECD framework, but in anti-corruption it's clear that they've stepped back from organizations like GRECO (Group of States Against Corruption) and the Open Government Partnership . Who will fill the void is less clear. The U.K. and France and Switzerland have announced their taskforce that I think can only be interpreted as being motivated, at least in part, by concerns about the gap being left by the U.S. stepping back. I haven't seen any concrete results of that initiative, so I think it's too soon to say what will happen there, but it is possible that we will see other members of the OECD stepping up to some extent to fill the gap. The other possibility, of course, is that China will play a greater role. They have new draft legislation that will consolidate some of their prior laws, but also extend them, to allow them to be more active about sanctioning transnational bribery and other forms of corruption. So they may not necessarily fill the gap, because I think a lot of the activities of Chinese firms were beyond the scope of U.S. enforcement activity anyway. But if there is an increase in Chinese enforcement, that may offset some of the reductions in enforcement effort that we see on the part of the U.S. And then, of course, the other possibility is that host countries will respond — countries whose officials are being corrupted, and they will do more. So all those countries where the U.S. firms are paying bribes of course have legislation on the books that would allow them to prosecute those firms for paying bribes, as well as prosecuting the officials [who take bribes]. And they could respond too, so we'll see. Now that both legislative bodies have flipped to their control, what can the Democratic Party do to legally counter the Trump administration’s rollback of U.S. anti-corruption policies? The prospect of a presidential veto will make it difficult for the new Congress to use legislative measures to counter the Trump administration’s actions. However, in the anti-corruption space there may be particular symbolic and political value in forcing the President and his allies in Congress to take a public position on reforms. To the extent the next Congress does contemplate anti-corruption measures, in addition to new legislation it may consider using the Congressional Review Act (CRA) to overturn FINCEN’s (U.S. Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network) August rule that exempted U.S. actors from the Corporate Transparency Act . However, the CRA only permits disapproval of rules issued near the end of a previous Congressional session and it is not yet clear whether the FINCEN rule will fall within the statute’s lookback window. And again, any such legislative act is virtually certain to be blocked by the President. It is worth noting, however, that the legality of that FINCEN rule is open to challenge. It effectively repeals the CTA and it is not at all clear that an agency like FINCEN has the authority to do that. Which challenges to American anti-corruption norms have concerned you the most over the past couple of years? I think it's the conflicts of interest on the part of U.S. officials, and the unapologetic nature of the conflicts of interest. I think that actually sets a certain tone, and has suggested that certain kinds of conduct are acceptable, and I actually think that may have more of an effect than any shifts in enforcement policy. So that's something I found quite concerning. I'll also mention a pet peeve of mine: Not everyone even sees this as a form of corruption, but the U.S. now has a policy of denying visas, or revoking the visas of foreign officials who basically oppose their interests, and they've been quite open about that. I actually think that's difficult to reconcile with the norm against corruption. The idea that public officials' duties should be to their constituents, and that efforts that influence them to put their private interests above the public interest ought to be condemned as forms of corruption. I think the current U.S. policy is actually inconsistent with that norm of prohibiting corruption. I may be alone in that view, but it is something that has concerned me in recent years. In one of your most cited articles , you and your co-author analyzed a dataset of FCPA enforcement actions resolved between 2004 and 2011 and found they were heavily influenced by foreign policy and international relations factors, going beyond the legal criteria explicitly written into U.S. or international law. That predated even the first Trump presidency. Since then, you have called for a more inclusive and experimental approach to transnational bribery law. In broad terms, what would that look like? The first article you mentioned goes to show that concerns about national interests have probably always influenced enforcement practices in at least the U.S., and to a certain extent, that may be inevitable. In terms of being more inclusive, my concern has always been about the interests of the countries whose officials are being corrupted, because in the typical case, those are the countries that bear most of the harm from corruption, and as a consequence, are most affected by anti-corruption policy. And sometimes their interests diverge from those of countries like the U.S. or the U.K. or France or Switzerland. Sometimes the reason for the divergence is obvious, like who gets to capture the recoveries from enforcement activities. So should the fines and forfeitures imposed in, say, FCPA actions or money laundering prosecutions be retained by the enforcing country, or should they be remitted to the country whose official was corrupted? There's potentially a conflict of interest there, and I've generally been sympathetic to the idea that there should be more sharing with what we can call the host countries. So there are issues like that, or the extent to which leniency should be granted in exchange for information that's used to prosecute the public officials. There is also potentially a conflict of interest there. Those are issues I've been concerned with over the years. More recently, I've written about the fact that countries like Brazil, [where] officials have been corrupted by both domestic and foreign actors, have undertaken a lot of enforcement . They've developed some very sophisticated techniques, and they've learned some important lessons about what works and what doesn't. And I've been interested in whether the multilateral regime has picked up on some of those lessons, both the positive and the negative ones. On that front, the evidence is mixed. results.evidenceText: High-Profile Smuggling Raids in Hungary Point to Former PM's Brother | OCCRP Organized Crime • Hungary High-Profile Smuggling Raids in Hungary Point to Former PM's Brother Police arrested multiple suspects Monday in an alleged visa fraud operation, with local media and politicians quickly linking the sweep to Áron Orbán. Banner: MZaplotnik / Wikimedia Commons | Hungarian police in Budapest. Reported by Zdravko Ljubas OCCRP November 9, 2026 | 1 min read Share Article × Aa Text Settings × Text Size Small Medium Large Line Spacing Compact Normal Spacious Hungarian authorities arrested multiple suspects in coordinated human smuggling raids on Monday morning, an operation that local media and political figures say resulted in the detention of Áron Orbán, the younger brother of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. The National Bureau of Investigation (NNI) and the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office (NVVH) conducted simultaneous house searches across Budapest and Pest County. While police confirmed the multi-agency operation in a public statement , they did not immediately release the identities of those detained. News outlet Kontroll.hu reported that the former premier's brother may have been among those arrested in connection with an NVVH probe into a visa facilitation network. The reports prompted a public exchange between the former premier and current Prime Minister Péter Magyar. Viktor Orbán indirectly confirmed his brother's arrest in a Facebook post , condemning the police action as a politically motivated "settling of scores" designed to distract from an "agent scandal" facing the current government. "In this dirty game, the goal is the elimination of the political opponent and the establishment of a one-party system," the former prime minister stated, likening the authorities to Hungary's historical state secret police. "I am the target, my younger brother is just a tool." Current Prime Minister Péter Magyar responded in a Facebook post, criticizing the former leader for deflecting blame and playing the victim. "As you sow, so shall you reap," Magyar wrote. (Photo by Charles Sykes/Invision/AP) By: Angela Fu November 12, 2026 As the blue “tsunami” spurred by Democratic midterm wins crashed over the country, some questioned whether the media leaders who tried to appease President Donald Trump would do an about-face. What would happen with, say, CBS News, whose owners have paid millions to Trump and implemented other changes that critics say were made under political pressure from the administration? That question misses the point, according to former “60 Minutes” correspondent Scott Pelley, who was fired in June after he pushed back against editorial changes in his own newsroom. CBS’ credibility, he said, has already been lost. Pelley is set to receive the Poynter Medal for Lifetime Achievement in Journalism this Saturday at Poynter’s Bowtie Ball. There, he will be honored for his more than 50 years in journalism, 37 of which were spent at CBS News, where his roles ranged from war correspondent to “CBS Evening News” anchor to “60 Minutes” correspondent. His career at “60 Minutes” — whose staff he had called “family” — ended not long after Skydance acquired CBS’ owner Paramount and installed The Free Press founder Bari Weiss as editor-in-chief. What followed was a string of firings and departures at “60 Minutes,” where journalists have alleged that Weiss interfered with their editorial independence. (Weiss has denied this.) Things came to a head June 1 when Pelley confronted “60 Minutes” executive producer Nick Bilton at a staff meeting. Pelley told Bilton, who was hired by Weiss and had never worked in television, that he had “slender qualifications.” Weiss, Pelley said, had “no qualifications” and was “murdering” “60 Minutes.” The next day, Pelley was fired. Ahead of the Bowtie Ball, Pelley agreed to answer several questions via email about the direction of CBS News, Skydance and his own career. Angela Fu: You have said that CBS in the past two years has tried to curry favor with the Trump administration. Do you see this changing, given the results of the midterms? Scott Pelley : To me, it’s not a question of which way the bias leans. The problem is that editorial control was taken from journalists trained in our principles and given to corporate executives and ideologues with an agenda. It doesn’t matter which agenda is imposed; independence and credibility are lost. Fu: You’ve now had several months to reflect on your time at “60 Minutes” and your decision to confront Nick Bilton. Looking back, would you do anything differently? Pelley : No. I stood up for my colleagues. I stood up for integrity. I stand up for them today. If anything, the circumstances are more grave. With the closing of the Warner merger, Skydance is partly owned by the Saudi sovereign wealth fund. The fund is chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the kingdom’s de facto leader, who, according to U.S. intelligence, approved the operation that killed and dismembered Washington Post columnist Jamal Khashoggi. I cannot reconcile partial ownership of CBS News and CNN with the murder of a journalist. For this reason alone, I could not have remained at CBS News. Fu: In the wake of the Paramount Skydance-Warner Bros. merger, what is your advice to the journalists at CNN? What should they watch for? Pelley : They should watch for ownership reneging on its promise of independence. They should watch for pressure to kill stories the ownership doesn’t like. They should watch for efforts to inject bias into their reporting. They should watch for the firing of colleagues who stand up for journalistic values. In our experience, the attack on “60 Minutes” was not subtle. Fu: You went from working for one of the most high-profile legacy newsrooms in the country to being an independent journalist. What was that transition like? Did anything surprise you? Pelley : I’m surprised by how much I am enjoying the role of an independent journalist. In my media company, I am able to lead my team with integrity and return to the values I was taught in nearly 40 years at CBS News. I’m engaged in reporting, writing, documentary production and podcast development. I’m speaking all over the country on the indispensable role of press freedom in a democracy, and I’m lecturing at Columbia Journalism School. The opportunities are endless. Fu: What are your go-to news sources right now? What are you reading and/or watching? Pelley : I am a little old-fashioned in this. Every morning I read The New York Times, The Washington Post and The Wall Street Journal. I’ve frequently admired the Journal’s editorial page for insight into Trump administration policy. I’m watching some truly great documentaries, and I’m a fan of PBS’s “NewsHour” and “Frontline.” Fu: You’ve been very critical of CBS’ editorial decisions these past two years. Zooming out, how would you evaluate the media’s coverage of Donald Trump and key issues today? What is the industry overall doing well, or what is it missing in its coverage? Pelley : The investigative reporting into corruption in the Trump administration has been excellent, and some of it may, in time, become legendary. I am not seeing nearly enough coverage of the war with Iran, but that is largely due to Pentagon leaders who are hostile to the public’s right to know. As a profession, we can never do too much explanatory reporting on the unregulated frontiers of AI. There is great public service to be done by illuminating a technology that will transform civilization. This kind of journalism doesn’t fund itself. Poynter helps you understand what’s happening in the media industry and how it shapes the news you read every day.
