View it in your browser . Good afternoon!  Have you caught this week’s “Poynter Report Podcast” yet? CNN’s John King, of Magic Wall fame, spoke to host Tom Jones about last week’s historic midterm elections. And he didn’t hold back on the superlatives, calling the results “stunning” and saying MAGA and Trumpism “got whooped.” He also broke down what goes into his Magic Wall marathon ballet. Check it out. Here’s what else caught my attention this week. National news outlets landed the biggest stories of the 2026 campaign. That’s a problem. The scoops were ceaseless this election season. From the pile of allegations against Graham Platner in Maine to the pileup of Dan Sullivans in Alaska. From abuse allegations involving an Ohio congressman to a Kansas senator aggressively pursuing former patients over unpaid medical bills. It was a hell of a year for investigative reporting. But there was something unusual about all those scoops. Many came from national news outlets, not the local reporters who cover these politicians every day. In a column for Poynter, veteran media reporter Paul Farhi argues that this says as much about the state of local news as it does about the strength of national journalism. National journalists should absolutely be doing this work, but the local newsrooms that once broke these stories increasingly lack the resources to do it themselves. Read the story ▸ Here’s what a Democratic-controlled Congress could do to protect press freedom The press has been under near-constant attack since Donald Trump began his second term. Poynter has documented more than 100 actions by Trump and the federal government targeting journalists and news organizations. Now that Democrats have won control of both chambers of Congress, can they do anything to stop it? Poynter’s Angela Fu spoke with press freedom advocates about what the new Congress could accomplish. They see opportunities to investigate officials who have targeted the press, strengthen protections for journalists and push for greater government transparency. But with Trump still holding veto power, how much can Democrats actually get done? Read the story ▸ Scott Pelley says CBS has lost its credibility. A post-midterms about-face wouldn’t help. Of course, not every threat to press freedom comes from the government. Sometimes the pressure comes from the people who own the newsrooms. Just ask Scott Pelley, who was fired from “60 Minutes” earlier this year after publicly challenging the new leadership at CBS News. In an interview with Angela Fu, Pelley argues that the network sacrificed its credibility by putting editorial decisions in the hands of corporate executives rather than journalists. And he doesn’t think a change in political fortunes will fix that. Pelley will receive Poynter’s Medal for Lifetime Achievement in Journalism at our Bowtie Ball on Saturday. Read the story ▸ Behind the scenes at Poynter Our most-read story since my last newsletter was “As Democrats swept the midterms, news anchors struggled to find the words.” I’ve been Poynter’s managing editor since March 2020, just a few days before the pandemic struck. We’ve covered four major election nights since then, and though they were all pretty remarkable, none of them was quite like this one. We kept hearing one word in news coverage all night. results.pageTitle: The Washington Post Nears Breakeven After ‘Hundreds and Hundreds of Millions’ in Losses
results.pageDescription: In an interview at Web Summit in Lisbon, executive editor Matt Murray makes the case that The Post is poised for a rebound in 2027.
results.evidenceText: The Washington Post Nears Breakeven After ‘Hundreds and Hundreds of Millions’ in Losses Subscribe Sign In Agencies Brands Creativity Media TV Commerce Tech Healthcare Photo by Ramsey Cardy/Web Summit via Sportsfile By Mark Stenberg This story was originally published in On Background with Mark Stenberg, a free, weekly newsletter that explores the key themes shaping the media industry. You can sign up for it  here . After years of steep losses, layoffs, and leadership churn, The Washington Post is within striking distance of breaking even financially, according to executive editor Matt Murray.  In a conversation at the Web Summit conference in Lisbon, Murray argued that the publisher is poised to turn a corner in 2027. While that won’t be easy, The Post has recently begun rebuilding its commercial momentum, stacking up a handful of revenue wins alongside a string of editorial scoops. In the third quarter, direct advertising sales at The Post notched their strongest year-over-year growth since 2021, while programmatic revenue was up 48% year over year as of September, according to a company spokesperson. Meanwhile, the newsroom is hiring again, adding James Politi from the Financial Times, Nancy Cook from Bloomberg, and Ian Ward from Politico, among other additions.  The Post is also relaunching its Ben Bradlee award, an internal designation that honors the work of an outstanding reporter. On Tuesday, the award will go to Hannah Natanson, whose home the FBI raided in January, according to Murray. The Post will also be recognizing Heidi Levine, the photojournalist who was attacked by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank last month. In the Q&A below, Murray reflects on five years of turmoil at The Post, the first few months of the D’Onofrio era, and his plan to own post-Trump Washington. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Mark Stenberg: How did election night go? Matt Murray: We had a good night, and we wanted and needed that. This whole year has been about getting the layoffs behind us, but more than that, getting five years of turmoil behind us. The layoffs were terrible, but they were a kind of climax to a long stretch of buyouts and staff turnover. We hoped they would punctuate it, and that seems to be what happened. The rest of the year has been about stability, core coverage, and breaking scoops. Mark: You were recruited to The Post by Will Lewis, who left in February after much controversy. How does the leadership style of his successor, Jeff D’Onofrio, stack up? Matt: I’m cautious here. Will is a friend and somebody I’ve worked with for a long, long time, so I don’t want to make too much of a contrast. But we had some deep-seated challenges in how we were organized and how we understood our audience. We didn’t have great data. When I arrived two and a half years ago, too much of the newsroom was still oriented toward print. We had more foundational work to do than people realized. Jeff brings a low-drama, data-oriented focus on fundamentals. He’s very calm. He’s about the journalism, but he knows he’s not a journalist. He’s a business guy, and he relies on us. We haven’t had any clashes about that. Mark: Where does the business stand? Matt: I’ll be honest. We had years of losses, and steepening losses. That’s the truth. We’re a private company and don’t share the figures, but it was hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars. Now we’re within striking distance of break-even, and I expect next year will be our best year in seven years. We’ve done the right-sizing we needed, which was tough.  FOR Scoops, Sharp Analysis, and Insider Context On Background A direct line to ADWEEK’S senior media reporter, delivering scoops, sharp analysis, and insider context on how publishing, streaming, and advertising are changing. By submitting your email, you agree to our  Terms of Use  and  Privacy Policy  . You may opt-out anytime by clicking ‘unsubscribe’ from the newsletter or from your account. Email Subscribe Loading… Mark: Layoffs might reduce costs, but where do you see growth coming from? Matt: The Post has got to be about Washington, and I didn’t think we were dominant enough there in reach and comprehensiveness. We’ve had real successes this year: the ballroom , the Kennedy Center , the monuments . But how do we own post-Trump Washington? The whole city has been oriented to Trump for 10 years, and he’s still the center of the action. But last week was about millennials and Gen Z coming to the fore. I’m an older guy, and I’m trying to understand the world through their eyes. This is the first time in my lifetime that the boomers are receding and the next generations are rising. That’s the audience we want for news. Mark: What editorial changes are you making that will help drive new business? Matt: One thing we’re trying to do better is understand franchises. We suspended our daily podcast because costs overran the revenue, but now we can sell on the ad side, including through a partnership with Acast. The Post talked for years about [advice columnist] Carolyn Hax having a podcast. She has one now, and it’s taking off quickly. Personal finance reporter Michelle Singletary has one too. We’re reviving a version of the daily podcast, and we have at least half a dozen people for whom we can find that sweet spot of newsletter, podcast, and writing. Mark: People poke at The Post for not acquiring properties the way The Times does, which has recently set its sights on Letterboxd. How do you see that? Matt: The Times deserves enormous credit for how they reoriented the entire company and how it interacted with the newsroom. It took them many years. In hindsight, it seems inevitable, but it wasn’t. Our company struggled during that decade. We had successes in the more open internet age, like Facebook partnerships, and of course we had a Trump bump. We went from something like 35,000 subscriptions before Trump to 3 million. In the long run, we probably need our version of that model, with the journalism at the center. But we’re still getting the Post itself where it needs to be. Talking Heds City Casting Call (EXCLUSIVE): The cofounder and chief executive of City Cast, David Plotz, is stepping away from the nationwide network of city-based podcasts after six years, according to the company. As part of the transition, the publisher is naming cofounder and former chief creative officer Andi McDaniel as its new chief executive. Last October, I wrote about the recalibration afoot at City Cast , which was shuttering certain markets, expanding others, and tweaking its editorial strategy. At the time, it was generating around $5 million but had not yet reached profitability.  Continued : The leadership change comes at an intriguing moment: City Cast is backed by Graham Holdings, which also owns Slate. In late October, Slate named its editor in chief, Hillary Frey, as its new CEO, replacing Dan Check; then, last week, it laid off a small number of staff, according to an inside source. It would appear that some end-of-year housekeeping is underway at Graham, which—after selling The Washington Post to Jeff Bezos in 2013—has struggled with some of its media holdings. In 2023, after paying $348 million for the media company Leaf Group, which itself would shutter in 2025 , Graham Holdings president and CEO Timothy J. O’Shaughnessy admitted to investors that they had “overpaid” for the asset. “I screwed this one up,” he wrote in a shareholders letter at the time. AP Up (EXCLUSIVE): The Associated Press had a big week last week. In addition to penning a content licensing agreement with Anthropic , the first of its kind for the artificial intelligence firm, the publisher also grew elections revenue by more than 80% compared to the 2022 midterms, according to the company. The AP saw its highest traffic since the 2024 election, with over 23 million pageviews, a sixfold increase over election night in 2022.  Multimedia Brew: The New York Times veteran Nina Lassam joined Morning Brew Inc. as its first senior vice president of multimedia on Wednesday, MBI chief executive Robert Dippell shared on LinkedIn on Tuesday. Lassam worked at The Times for nearly a decade, where she helped build out its now robust audio and video offerings. The hire underscores just how seriously Morning Brew Inc. is taking its podcast, social video, and creator franchise efforts.  Quote/Unquote Louis Dreyfus is the chief executive officer of Le Monde, the largest news publisher in France. Under Dreyfus, whom I spoke with at the Web Summit conference in Lisbon, the Le Monde newsroom has grown from around 310 journalists to nearly 600 and now has 720,000 subscribers—620,000 of which are digital-only.  It stands out among European news publishers for its ongoing efforts to expand its subscriber base in the U.S., which I have written about in the past , as well as for its embrace of artificial intelligence. It was the first French publisher to sign with OpenAI, and it has since struck deals with Perplexity and Meta. In our conversation, Dreyfus shared a number of surprising elements, including the unlikely way in which the OpenAI deal originated, what Le Monde did with the licensing revenue it gained from the deal, and why it has avoided the fallout from Google Zero. This interview has been edited. Mark Stenberg: Le Monde was the first French publisher to sign with OpenAI. How did that happen? Louis Dreyfus: In fall 2023, I saw that Sam Altman was speaking at Station F, so I went. When they took questions from the room, I raised my hand and said: “I’m the CEO of Le Monde. Seventy-five percent of my revenue comes from readers. You need reliable data, and you give it to users for free. If you want Le Monde to keep publishing reliable news, we need to negotiate.” He said he knew Le Monde and would be happy to. Three months later, we had a deal. Mark: What have the partnerships actually delivered? Louis: First, a significant and sustainable revenue stream at a time when advertising in Western Europe is slow. Second, a new audience, as the readers click through far more than people coming from Facebook, and they convert to subscriptions. And I decided to redistribute a share of the licensing revenue from the deal to the newsroom, so every journalist at Le Monde gets an annual bonus from it. Mark: Anthropic has largely avoided these kinds of deals . Have you spoken with them? Louis: Our last conversation was almost a year ago. They said it was too early and that their focus was B2B, not general news. I believe that will change, though, as they prepare to go public and investors will ask whether their data is stolen or legitimate. results.pageTitle: US Prosecutors Ask Judge to Allow Bribery Evidence in South American Drug Trafficking Case
results.pageDescription: Ahead of a trial expected early next year, the U.S. Justice Department is asking a federal judge to admit intercepted messages and evidence of alleged payoffs made by Sebastián Marset to officials in Uruguay, Paraguay, Bolivia, and Venezuela.
results.evidenceText: US Prosecutors Ask Judge to Allow Bribery Evidence in South American Drug Trafficking Case | OCCRP Organized Crime • United States US Prosecutors Ask Judge to Allow Bribery Evidence in South American Drug Trafficking Case Ahead of a trial expected early next year, the U.S. Justice Department is asking a federal judge to admit intercepted messages and evidence of alleged payoffs made by Sebastián Marset to officials in Uruguay, Paraguay, Bolivia, and Venezuela. Banner: United States Drug Enforcement Administration/dea.gov | Mugshot of alleged South American drug trafficker Sebastián Marset. Reported by Kevin G. Hall OCCRP November 13, 2026 | 3 min read Share Article × Aa Text Settings × Text Size Small Medium Large Line Spacing Compact Normal Spacious American prosecutors want to introduce examples of encrypted communications and alleged bribery of government officials as part of their case against accused South American drug baron Sebastián Marset. In pretrial motions filed this week, the Justice Department argued the evidence is necessary to give jurors a full picture of Marset’s alleged global drug trafficking network ahead of a trial expected early next year. Prosecutors told District Judge Rossie Alston Jr. that the evidence will also show Marset engaged in a conspiracy to launder drug proceeds. Marset was arrested in a pre-dawn raid in Santa Cruz, Bolivia, in March and expelled to the U.S. with the assistance of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration. He was initially charged with money laundering counts, but was later indicted on drug trafficking and narco-terrorism charges. Marset’s lawyers argue that the initial charge of money laundering is invalid because it involved a single wire transfer between Portugal and China that did not involve the servers of a U.S. bank. They say Marset never trafficked drugs to the U.S., and the narco-terrorism groups were not designated as such at the time of his dealing with them. Prosecutors alleged in the new filings that “the defendant ran his organization in a ruthless, brutal manner, killing those that opposed him or cooperated with law enforcement. He also did not tolerate governments interfering in his criminal activity, employing a classic plata o plomo — silver or lead — model to coerce governments into acceding to his will.” “In practice, this meant that the defendant threatened, bombed, and even murdered those members of law enforcement whom he could not corrupt,” they wrote. In a key development as part of the filings, prosecutors asked Judge Alston to allow evidence of bribery in Uruguay, Paraguay, Bolivia, and Venezuela. They alleged that Marset “paid government officials in order to receive information and protection from law enforcement.” “These bribes allowed him to carry on his drug trafficking, money laundering, and terrorist activities without interference from law enforcement,” the prosecutors added. Videos from Marset’s arrest sparked a sweeping purge of high-ranking officials, just 48 hours after the U.S. State Department announced visa restrictions targeting Bolivian political and judicial officials over allegations of high-level corruption and illicit drug ties. The filing alleges that the “payments also allowed the defendant to receive drug trafficking files from Bolivian law enforcement, to evade capture operations, and to receive notice of DEA meetings with Bolivian officials.” Prosecutors want to allow witness statements showing a conspiracy to launder drug proceeds. They asked to introduce evidence statements from people including an unindicted co-conspirator and an undercover officer, describing how funds moved from Europe to South America. Prosecutors are also seeking to introduce encrypted messages sent to and from Marset on phones that were part of the Sky ECC network. A 2024 investigation by OCCRP and media partners showed how these phones from a Canadian company with servers in France were favored by criminal organizations in Serbia, Latin America, and elsewhere. The admissibility of Sky’s encrypted communications in court is an unsettled legal battle in several jurisdictions. In Marset’s case, prosecutors said they identified 12 personal identification numbers used by those in the alleged conspiracy. They alleged that three belonged to Marset, and contained messages and images showing his tattoos, his family, and other identifiers. The prosecutors note in the filing on Sky that “the defendant texted a picture of an individual he murdered, and the government has independent evidence that the defendant was responsible for the murder.” Defense attorneys filed their own motion asking the judge to withhold from the jury any reference to violent crimes that do not meet the definition of narco-terrorism, any reference to a drug seizure in international waters near Africa, all bank records not connected to the specific charges against Marset, and secondhand statements tied to the money laundering conspiracy. It is unclear when Judge Alston will rule on the seven new motions. He had pledged to rule by November 6 on several defense motions challenging the charges brought against Marset, but had not as of Thursday. The alleged trafficker’s defense last week withdrew a request to strike use of a seized cellphone as evidence after they said prosecutors committed to not use information from it. results.evidenceText: UK Arrests 349 in Nationwide Money Laundering Crackdown | OCCRP Money Laundering • United Kingdom UK Arrests 349 in Nationwide Money Laundering Crackdown November 12, 2026 | 1 min read Share Article × Aa Text Settings × Text Size Small Medium Large Line Spacing Compact Normal Spacious The UK's National Crime Agency (NCA) announced that 349 people had been arrested in a nationwide crackdown on businesses suspected of laundering criminal proceeds. During October, police inspected or raided 3,029 premises, including barbershops, vape stores and other cash-intensive businesses, seizing approximately $2.9 million in cash and obtaining court orders to freeze another $4.9 million in bank accounts. Authorities also identified or prevented an estimated $5.5 million in tax evasion and seized illicit goods worth nearly $9 million. The operation was the latest phase of Operation Machinize, a nationwide campaign targeting businesses used to conceal criminal profits. An earlier phase of the crackdown resulted in more than 900 arrests and inspections of over 2,700 businesses. The NCA estimates that at least $1.3 billion in criminal proceeds is laundered through such businesses in the UK annually. The agency said the campaign is increasingly focused on identifying the criminal networks behind the businesses rather than just individual premises. results.pageTitle: How Dan Hicks helped define an era of greatness
results.pageDescription: Dan Hicks contributed so much to the sports broadcasting world, but the highlights were Tiger Woods' and Michael Phelps' biggest moments.
results.evidenceText: How Dan Hicks helped define an era of greatness Skip to content Credit: Reuters/NBC, edit via Liam McGuire By Matt Yoder on 11/12/2026 11/12/2026 Less AI and more AA in your search results. Dan Hicks was a constant presence at some of the biggest sporting events in the world. After his sudden passing at the age of 64 following an acute illness, it’s almost unfathomable to imagine them without him. Hicks was a longtime fixture at NBC Sports, where he worked for well over 30 years. During that time, he called a number of marquee sporting events. The list includes, but is not limited to, NFL playoff games, Notre Dame football, the NBA on NBC, PGA Tour events and majors, and both the Summer and Winter Olympics. When you think of Dan Hicks as a broadcaster, the word “professional” immediately comes to mind. Hicks wasn’t one to overshadow any broadcast with his own personality — the game and the athletes on display were always the star. He hardly ever had a major moment go sideways. But if you ever tuned in to one of his broadcasts, you knew you were going to get a top-level performance because that’s what he did week in, week out, for decades. The scores of tributes from Hicks’ colleagues across the sports media show how respected he was by those inside the industry, both for his professionalism on the air and his life away from the cameras. But when looking back on Hicks’ impact as a broadcaster, it’s fitting that he will always be associated with two of the greatest athletes of the 2000s, as he provided commentary for so many famous triumphs of Michael Phelps and Tiger Woods. Dan Hicks called plenty of memorable games and moments at NBC Sports ranging from one of the greatest comebacks in NFL playoff history to countless gold medal events, major golf championships, and Ryder Cups. But decades from now, you will still hear his voice chronicling the otherworldly achievements of Woods and Phelps. “Expect anything different?” Perhaps the defining call of Hicks’ career came at the 2008 US Open at Torrey Pines . A clearly hobbled Tiger Woods was chasing his third US Open championship while battling a wrecked knee and a broken leg. On the 72nd hole, he needed to make a 12-foot birdie putt to force an 18-hole playoff with veteran pro Rocco Mediate. Woods would go on to win the playoff and his third US Open the next day. As the putt curled in, Hicks calmly and confidently delivered one of the most famous calls in golf history, “Expect anything different?” Dan Hicks was a master of unscripted play-by-play, voicing many of golf’s most famous moments over the last 30 years. Jimmy Roberts remembers his iconic call of Tiger Woods’ putt at the 2008 U.S. Open: “Expect anything different?” https://t.co/sIzzzJDt89 — Golf Channel (@GolfChannel) November 12, 2026 It was perfect for the moment because it wasn’t the most poetic call. It simply pointed to the absurd brilliance of Tiger Woods for the millions watching at home to marvel at. How could you not expect him to make that putt ? It was a message that we all were indeed watching a once-in-a-generation athlete simply willing himself to victory. It was prototypical Dan Hicks in that the moment wasn’t about his description; it was about lifting up greatness. Golf isn’t a sport that lends itself to many unforgettable calls because there’s rarely any live narration of the ball in play. You’re just watching to see where a ball ends up or if it falls into a hole in the ground. But Hicks’ call will live alongside “Yes sir!” “In your life!” and “Better than most!” as one of the most iconic in its history. “Unbelievable at the end!” Along with golf, Dan Hicks will be most fondly remembered for being the voice of swimming at the Summer Olympics. His time in the broadcast booth just so happened to correspond with the most decorated athlete in the history of the games, Michael Phelps. Hicks was there for all of Phelps’ record 23 gold medals and several world records. While Phelps’ heroics spanned four Olympic games, his peak also came in 2008 at the Beijing Olympics. Phelps broke Mark Spitz’s famous record by winning a combined eight gold medals in individual and team events. But the great irony is that Phelps’ most famous medal, and Hicks’ most famous call, came thanks to Team USA teammate Jason Lezak in the 4×100-meter freestyle relay . Phelps swam the first leg for the Americans, but by the time Jason Lezak entered the pool for the anchor leg, he was trailing the French team by a substantial margin. However, Lezak somehow swam a 46.06 split (almost 1.5 seconds faster than Phelps) and won in thrilling fashion. Dan Hicks’ call of the Michael Phelps-Jason Lezak relay from the 2008 Olympics will long live as one of the greatest ever. Rest in peace to a legend. https://t.co/6CZfqmfsU1 — Mark Harris (@itismarkharris) November 12, 2026 Forget Olympic history; that race and relay leg will stand the test of time as one of the most exciting moments in all of modern-day sports. And it got the treatment it deserved from the usually understated Hicks, who rose to the occasion and screamed in excitement and disbelief while nailing the call and even referencing Phelps’ quest for history staying alive. Most sports broadcasters can go an entire career without being privileged to call anything like that. But Dan Hicks got to call the peak performances of legendary figures at their very best within just a couple of months of each other. Of course, Hicks provided the soundtrack for many other stars from the golf course to the gridiron and from the warm waters of the Olympic swimming pool to the snowy mountains of alpine skiing. There was Katie Ledecky, Rory McIlroy, Andrew Luck, Lindsey Vonn, and many others. But many years from now, those two moments and those two calls will still be replayed for future generations to enjoy and be in awe. It was both the best of sports and the best of sports broadcasting. And that association is what fans will remember and appreciate most about Dan Hicks. He never needed to be the biggest personality in the broadcast booth, but when the biggest moments in sports happened, you were glad he was there to document them. results.pageDescription: Nick Wright recently exposed Clay Travis for fabricating political beliefs to arouse his following, and he’s willing to bet $1 million on it.
results.evidenceText: Nick Wright offers $1 million bet to expose Clay Travis Skip to content Credit: FS1, Sport & State By Brandon Contes on 11/12/2026 11/12/2026 Less AI and more AA in your search results. Nick Wright recently exposed Clay Travis for fabricating political beliefs to arouse his following, and he’s willing to bet $1 million on it. Wright joined Tim Miller on The Bulwark Daily podcast this week, where the FS1 host pulled back the curtain to reveal that Travis once admitted his beliefs and opinions are crafted for audience enrichment . According to Wright, Travis made the admission at a dinner about 11 years ago. Believing that’s worse than just having different political opinions, Wright told Travis he could not respect him, and claims to have left the dinner. Predictably, Travis fired back Wednesday night, attempting to dispute Wright by saying, “I guess this is what happens when you start voting Republican, people make up entire stories about you in their heads and share it with their far left wing friends.” Thursday morning, Wright had one final response to Travis, giving a detailed recount of the interaction 11 years ago and noting he has witnesses who will defend his side of the story before offering to bet $1 million to prove he’s telling the truth. I’m not going to go back and forth with you (it’s football season for God’s sake!), but I can’t believe you’re actually denying this interaction so I’ll jog your memory: August of 2016, during the Olympics, at the (now shuttered) Intercontinental hotel, a couple blocks from the Fox lot off Pico. We had just finished a night show that no longer exists where (among other things) we debated the Summer Olympics (it was a bad segment because we didn’t have rights to the footage, so we could only show still pictures of what we were talking about) & went to have a drink/meal with a colleague who was on the show with us. The exchange I discussed happened in the lobby bar, at a table with said colleague, and then after I said what I needed to say to to you I went outside and bummed a cigarette off a valet. We haven’t spoken in person since. You know as well as I do this is 100% true, and verifiable, by the colleague that was with us and/or our then bosses who contemporaneously heard the story. We actually also had the same agent at the time, and you and I both know he heard the story and could confirm it as well. So, I’ll pull a page out of your book; I’ll bet you $1,000,000 I’m telling the truth. I assume you’ll pretend you never saw this tweet & continue the grift. And that’s cool, but we both know what the facts are. Also, let this be a reminder that while you have found an amazing lane where you often are actually the smartest guy in the room, this ain’t that lane. So my advice would be to tread carefully. — nick wright (@getnickwright) November 12, 2026 “I’ll pull a page out of your book; I’ll bet you $1,000,000 I’m telling the truth,” Wright wrote. “Also, let this be a reminder that while you have found an amazing lane where you often are actually the smartest guy in the room, this ain’t that lane. So my advice would be to tread carefully.” Travis responded again by attempting to claim Wright just has a personal issue with him over Black Lives Matter. But in his response, which was surely meant to dunk on Wright, Travis claimed COVID broke him, leading him to vote for a Republican president for the first time in 2020. Travis then went on to say he would be willing to bet $1 million with Wright if a lie detector is involved so they can discuss transgender athletes, which has absolutely nothing to do with the bet Wright offered first. I can’t respond to @getnickwright’s post to me because he’s had me blocked on here since I said BLM was a total fraud and that LeBron faked the “hate crime” at his LA mansion. I was right, of course, about both of these things. I was a Democrat in 2015 — and 2016 — which he now says is the date of our dinner. He did not storm out of a dinner after telling me off. This is a very girly thing to brag about, but I’m pretty sure I would remember that because I would have found it funny. I don’t recall our dinner conversation from a decade ago, but I would presume it was similar to this private email I sent Nick that he posted on here back in 2017. You can read that if you wish. At the time I considered myself a radical moderate and felt alienated from the far left and far right. https://t.co/MKZnxUKEko Nick seems to spend a lot of time thinking about me since he’s now posted private emails and talked about private dinners from a decade+ ago. I’m flattered to be so memorable to him. I didn’t vote for a Republican for president until 2020. Covid radicalized me, as it did many people. As I’ve said and written for years, I didn’t leave the Democrat party, the Democrat party left me. If Nick wants to bet a million dollars on do I believe the things I say, I guess we can get a lie detector machine and fire it up. The first question can be, do you believe men pretending to be women should be allowed to play in women’s sports? I’m petty confident I will pass the test when I say hell no. Will you pass when you say yes, Nick? — Clay Travis (@ClayTravis) November 12, 2026 The bet Wright proposed was that his recall of Travis admitting he crafts political opinions for engagement 11 years ago was correct, and that Travis is now lying by claiming the conversation never happened. In the wake of their social media interaction, Wright has received strong support, with others sharing their own stories about when they learned Travis was a political grifter. the late, great ed aschoff told me a similar story in 2018. about how they were once cool but that he couldn’t fuck with travis after he revealed it was all an act. — Joel D. Anderson 🆓 (@byjoelanderson) November 12, 2026 I’m honestly surprised that people are surprised by this. It’s one of the worst kept secrets in our business that dude has been lying about his political beliefs for a long time. I also have some receipts, but I’ll keep those to myself. Make no mistake, he isn’t the only one. There’s a lot of people in our business who are cosplaying for clicks and views. It’s one of the most shameful and dishonest things that one can do. I applaud Nick for keep it real. — Jemele Hill (@jemelehill) November 12, 2026 An old clip of Pardon My Take’s PFT Commenter claiming Travis once admitted to him that he saw an open market for a right-leaning sports host also resurfaced. PFT has the same basic story as @getnickwright: “Clay’s such a fraud. He literally told me back in like 2015, ‘There’s no market out there right now for right wing sports, so I’m just going to start becoming a right wing sports [guy]’ – he told me what he was going to do.” https://t.co/eAUR8xRkJ5 — Elijah Cone (@ElijahCone) November 12, 2026 Interestingly, PFT said the interaction with Travis occurred in 2015, which aligns with the 11-year-old conversation Wright recalls having with the Sport & State founder. While Travis says COVID “radicalized me,” he previously described the 2015 protests at the University of Missouri as his “ red pill, ” which again matches the timing of the conversations he allegedly had with PFT and Wright. Travis has been open about previously identifying as a Democrat. He’s been open about not voting for Trump in 2016, and only voting for his first Republican presidential candidate in 2020. He’s been open about seeing an available market for right-leaning sports content. Everyone knows his background is not that of a lifelong conservative. So, what part of Wright’s story is Travis really contesting? About Brandon Contes Brandon Contes is a staff writer for Awful Announcing and The Comeback. (Photo provided by Laura Rodio, Nashville SUNN) By: Rhea Patney November 12, 2026 This article was originally published in the Student Press Report , a national news desk covering student media and journalism education in higher ed. On the day she was interviewed for this story, Sarah Nipper had a call scheduled with Ruby York, a 10th grader at Martin Luther King Jr. School in Nashville. York, who DJs on Teen Power Radio Hour at WXNA, had emailed a draft of an op-ed about teen radio. Instead of sending it back covered in Google Docs comments, Nipper, a Vanderbilt senior and the editor-in-chief of The Nashville SUNN, planned to walk the high schooler through it. “We’re going to talk through the developmental edits step by step instead of just commenting on them,” Nipper said. “That way, she can understand what goes into the structure of an op-ed.” York came to the publication with a love of music but no journalism training. These editing calls have changed how she writes. “I had no idea what I was doing when I first started writing, and it was kind of a mess,” York said. “(Nipper) completely helped teach me how to write, how to organize a piece, what to do during editing, how to make it longer and how to format it.” The Nashville SUNN bills itself as America’s first citywide, student-run newspaper. It launched in November 2025 with a network spanning 24 Nashville-area high schools. Most of its writers are teenagers, and its editors are all college students or recent grads. Amanda Little, a writer-in-residence at Vanderbilt University and former Bloomberg columnist, founded the Students United News Network, or SUNN, in 2024. The organization grew out of her work building youth civics programs. Its national publication, The SUNN Post , launched in March 2025 to showcase reporting from high school newspapers across the country. The Nashville SUNN, which works directly with student reporters across the city, is the network’s first local affiliate. Amanda Little holds a copy of the Nashville SUNN at Library Lab Aug. 29 at the Nashville Public Library. (Photo provided by Laura Rodio, Nashville SUNN) Little runs SUNN as an unpaid executive director, funded mostly by small donors and foundation grants. The organization is working to build out advertising, corporate partnerships and other consistent revenue streams. Since May, two Vanderbilt seniors have run the Nashville paper: Nipper and managing editor Manushree Navaneethakrishnan. Five to seven Vanderbilt students also serve as copy editors and fact-checkers, and the art director is a recent graduate of Belmont University, also in Nashville. Little said the college-led structure is intentional. “There’s no better way to motivate young talent than through college students who speak their language,” Little said. “A college student who’s doing amazing things as an undergraduate can be more exciting to the people we’re trying to reach.” From pitch to publication Stories come from existing high school newspapers, pitches from Nipper or Navaneethakrishnan, or, most commonly, the students themselves. About 20 writers contributed to the latest issue, the Nashville SUNN’s fourth, which officially came out Thursday. Recurring columns include Three Laws, a partnership with Tennessee’s youth governor that breaks down bills affecting students, and Thank You Mentor, where students thank a mentor. When writers pitch their own ideas, Nipper will typically call them and workshop the idea over the phone. The writer usually has about two weeks to draft. Nipper or Navaneethakrishnan does the developmental edit. Then the copy and fact-checking desks proofread, validate sources and add necessary links. Art director Laura Rodio, the Belmont graduate, finds student artists and photographers for each piece. The Nashville SUNN releases a new issue typically every other month during the school year. Stories, photos, op-eds, reviews and everything else the students produce run online and in print, to the tune of about 20 to 24 pieces an issue. Print copies are distributed through libraries, high schools and about 26 local businesses, some of them advertisers. About 6,000 copies are distributed, but Little is hoping to scale that up. “The print edition is really cool, and I think it’s helping us increase community involvement. If someone has a physical copy of something, they’re going to remember it,” Nipper said. “An English teacher can show students what the SUNN is.” The publication pays student writers between $50 and $125, depending on the assignment, and also compensates student artists and photographers. College editors are paid hourly for their work. The Tennessean, part of the USA Today Network, also republishes some Nashville SUNN stories in a regular Sunday feature in print and online. Tennessean opinion editor Tacuma Roeback picks which pieces run. More than 20 pieces have been published so far, and the newspaper pays $50 for each article, split between the student writer and the Nashville SUNN. Editing teenagers Submitted pieces go through significant edits, which focus mostly on structure. “My biggest fear isn’t that the piece won’t be good enough,” Nipper said. “It’s that they’ll be offended when I add to it or when they see all the red. The challenge is often that a student has a really unique voice and something cool to say but doesn’t understand journalistic standards or structure.” At the end of each edit, Navaneethakrishnan writes a paragraph about the piece’s strengths. “The first thing they’re going to think is, ‘Oh, my piece just isn’t good enough. My piece isn’t ready,'” Navaneethakrishnan said. “It’s comforting to know that someone didn’t just skim your piece. They genuinely read it and engaged with it.” Holding the operation together across two dozen schools takes legwork. Nipper recruits by emailing English teachers and advisers across the city, including at schools with no student newspaper, and gives new writers article templates and story guidance. “I think the biggest difficulty has been getting in contact with the high schoolers, because they’re high schoolers,” Navaneethakrishnan said. “They’re busy.” Saturday workshops at the downtown library help. College editors and local journalists, including people from NPR, the Tennessean and NewsChannel 5, meet with students. The sessions are free and open to any Nashville high schooler. Why the editors do it Nipper sees herself in the writers. “A big part of what I’ve liked about the job is meeting with high schoolers and walking them through the process of writing a journalistic piece step by step,” Nipper said. Nipper also said the startup-like operation has taught her a lot about accountability. She spends 10 to 15 hours a week on the paper. “There’s direct responsibility that I might not have in an entry-level internship. If I don’t send a text, no one else is going to do it. If I don’t send an email to get something done, it won’t get done,” Nipper said. “Honestly, my email response time is so much better now because I’ve had to learn that, which is going to be good for me after graduation.” The Nashville SUNN gave Navaneethakrishnan an opportunity to grow as an editor. In her role as opinion editor at the Hustler, Vanderbilt’s student newspaper, she edited pieces driven by personal anecdotes, where the writer’s own voice carried the argument. But for the SUNN, she is editing far more news stories. “Editing for Nashville SUNN was so interesting because it was so content-focused. The writers were really on top of things, fact-checking and making sure to corroborate information,” Navaneethakrishnan said. “It was … a very intellectual challenge for me, because I wasn’t just looking for the writer’s voice or personal perspective.” Tamyra Johnson, a Vanderbilt senior who fact-checks for the SUNN, said she has valued the network the project has brought her, particularly through those Saturday workshops. “I definitely think attending the events has been beneficial because it’s not just networking for the high schoolers,” Johnson said. “I can benefit from it, too. I met a journalist from NewsChannel 5 and we exchanged emails, and he told me to send him pieces if I want feedback.” The power of the local model The national SUNN Post draws on about 175 high school newspapers in 35 states, most of them established student publications. That network gives students at schools with strong journalism programs a wider audience for their work. The Nashville SUNN was designed to reach students who have fewer opportunities: those at schools with small or struggling journalism programs, or no publication at all. Its college editors help fill that gap through direct, in-person mentorship. “Mentoring lets us work with schools that have no journalism program, newspaper, broadcast, podcast or anything else. We can bring in students interested in debate, Model UN, youth in government or student council, or students who simply care about issues and want to amplify their voices,” founder Little said. “There are many ways to bring in students with tremendous potential as storytellers and journalists, even at schools without newspapers that we can’t currently reach through the national model.” That mentorship also shapes the college students doing the editing. On Saturdays at the library, Navaneethakrishnan shares lessons from her own path through college journalism with high schoolers just beginning theirs. The work gives her a chance to pass along guidance, while helping students build skills they can carry into any field. “You don’t have to want to be a journalist to do journalism,” Navaneethakrishnan said. “Genuinely, every single field can benefit from it because you’re having conversations with people. I owe so much to the SUNN — it truly is a facet of my identity and personality and has advanced my leadership in so many ways.” This kind of journalism doesn’t fund itself. Poynter helps you understand what’s happening in the media industry and how it shapes the news you read every day. View it in your browser . OPINION Longtime NBC Sports announcer Dan Hicks, dies suddenly. He was 64 NBC Sports announcer Dan Hicks. (Photo: NBC Sports) Horrible news from the sports world. NBC Sports play-by-play voice Dan Hicks has died after what his family said was an acute illness. Hicks was 64. The husband of longtime ESPN anchor Hannah Storm, Hicks was NBC’s lead play-by-play voice on its PGA Tour coverage since 2000, In addition, he has covered 16 Olympics and was the play-by-play announcer on the network’s coverage of Notre Dame football. In fact, according to a schedule released by NBC Sports earlier this week, Hicks was set to call this Saturday’s Notre Dame against Boston College. Storm said in a statement , “Our family is heartbroken by the sudden and unexpected passing of Dan following an acute illness. He was a devoted husband of over 30 years, loving father to our three daughters, and cherished friend to so many. His loss is immeasurable.” She continued, “Dan was truly one of a kind and, quite simply, the person everyone wanted to be around. When he walked into a room, he brought the energy, the laughter and the people together. He was endlessly kind, thoughtful and funny, and he made everyone feel like they mattered. Our three daughters and I are heartbroken. We are grateful for the love and support surrounding our family during this incredibly difficult time. These are simply no words to express how much he will be missed.” The news rocked the sports media world. Hicks was not only a smooth, professional and superb announcer, but he had a reputation for being easy to work with and someone who served as a mentor to younger broadcasters. NBC and Golf Channel analyst Roger Maltbie said on the air Thursday, “This is not losing a colleague and a nice guy; this is losing a pal.” Versant CEO Mark Lazarus said in a statement, “I am heartbroken by the sudden loss of our friend Dan Hicks. For decades, I had the privilege of working alongside Dan, but our friendship extended far beyond NBC Sports. Dan was one of the very best at what he did, but what I will remember most is the person he was: a loyal friend and a devoted husband and father. My family and I are thinking of Hannah, their children and the entire Hicks family. We will miss him.” Storm’s boss, ESPN chairman Jimmy Pitaro, said in a statement: “We are deeply saddened by the sudden passing of Dan Hicks, a respected voice in sports broadcasting and husband of ESPN anchor Hannah Storm. Hannah is a cherished member of the ESPN family, and our hearts are with her, their three daughters and all who knew and loved Dan, including his NBC colleagues, during this incredibly difficult time. We extend our deepest condolences and stand alongside Hannah and her family.” Hicks could call practically any sport, but he was best known for his golf announcing. Awful Announcing’s Drew Lerner wrote , “Hicks called any number of legendary moments throughout his career. Among them was his memorable call on the 72nd hole of the 2008 U.S. Open, when Tiger Woods rolled in a 12-foot birdie putt to tie Rocco Mediate and force a playoff the next day. ‘Expect anything different!?’ Hicks bellowed in a call that would live on forever.” The Athletic’s Brody Miller wrote , “Hicks understood how to make golf about the moment, and now those moments will feel a little more empty.” Hicks’ Olympic coverage was highlighted by calling Michael Phelps’ legendary run of eight gold medals in the 2008 Summer Games. The Athletic’s Andrew Marchand wrote , “His broadcasts were consistently strong and never about him. In an age of schtick, he delivered the goods with rare versatility, where his bosses could ask him to call play-by-play on a whim or host. Hicks’ ability to host and call the action made him perfect for golf, and he became synonymous with NBC’s coverage.” Marchand added, “It is an extremely sad day for the golf, Olympic and football communities with the news of Hicks’ passing. No words can make anything right for Storm and their three daughters. One day, maybe, they can find a little solace in the fact that Hicks left behind quite a legacy.” And Awful Announcing’s Matt Yoder put it perfectly when he wrote , “When you think of Dan Hicks as a broadcaster, the word “professional” immediately comes to mind. Hicks wasn’t one to overshadow any broadcast with his own personality — the game and the athletes on display were always the star. He hardly ever had a major moment go sideways. But if you ever tuned in to one of his broadcasts, you knew you were going to get a top-level performance because that’s what he did week in, week out, for decades.” Poynter honors Pelley Poynter will honor longtime former “60 Minutes” correspondent Scott Pelley with the Poynter Medal for Lifetime Achievement in Journalism this Saturday at Poynter’s Bowtie Ball in Tampa. Ahead of this weekend’s festivities, Pelley spoke with my colleague Angela Fu about a number of topics, including his leaving “60 Minutes,” the Skydance-Warner Bros Discover merger, his current media diet and what life is like as an independent journalist. Fu asked Pelley about his decision to confront new “60 Minutes” executive producer Nick Bolton, a confrontation that led to Pelley’s dismissal from the program, and, looking back, if he would have done anything differently. Pelley said, “No. I stood up for my colleagues. I stood up for integrity. I stand up for them today. If anything, the circumstances are more grave. With the closing of the Warner merger, Skydance is partly owned by the Saudi sovereign wealth fund. The fund is chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the kingdom’s de facto leader, who, according to U.S. intelligence, approved the operation that killed and dismembered Washington Post columnist Jamal Khashoggi. I cannot reconcile partial ownership of CBS News and CNN with the murder of a journalist. For this reason alone, I could not have remained at CBS News.” Shooter story A gunman in Washington, D.C. shot five people on Thursday, killing one, before dying of a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Police identified the shooter as Matt Lambert, 55. Authorities said he had been in an ongoing dispute with his condo association over maintenance issues and mold. The Washington Post’s Danielle Paquette, Douglas MacMillan, Paul Schwartzman and Aaron Schaffer have more details here . Now check out this story. The Washington Sun’s Michael Brice-Saddler wrote “What the Logan Circle Shooter Told Me.” Brice-Saddler wrote, “Lambert reached out to me in late 2025 when I was a reporter at The Washington Post, pitching a story about how his million-dollar Logan Circle penthouse had been rendered unlivable. I continued reporting the story into the new year, but the article was abandoned when I was laid off from the Post in early 2026.” Media news, tidbits and interesting links for your weekend review Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray tells AdWeek’s Mark Stenberg , “We had years of losses, and steepening losses. That’s the truth. We’re a private company and don’t share the figures, but it was hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars. Now we’re within striking distance of break-even, and I expect next year will be our best year in seven years.” The Associated Press’ Fernanda Pesce with “In Mexico, journalists face threats from attackers — and from the system meant to protect them, too.” The Atlantic’s Adam Kirsch with “The Last Trumpist Standing.” One day after a soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier admonished Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his entourage after someone in the group laughed loudly, Hegseth awarded the soldier with a commendation medal. Here’s more from The Washington Post’s Alex Horton and Tara Copp. Great to see the byline of former Washington Post media reporter Paul Farhi. He writes for Poynter: “National news outlets landed the biggest stories of the 2026 campaign. (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite) By: Angela Fu November 13, 2026 Less than 48 hours after it became apparent that Democrats would take both chambers of Congress, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) emailed the Federal Communications Commission, demanding records for an investigation into attacks on the First Amendment. That investigation, led by Democratic senators on a Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs subcommittee, was looking into how President Donald Trump’s and the FCC’s actions “erode and undermine freedom of speech and freedom of the press and bear on the laws governing media consolidation,” Blumenthal wrote in the email. It was a preview of the levers a Democrat-controlled Congress might pull next year to protect press freedom, which has been under severe attack by the second Trump administration. Armed with the power of oversight and investigation, Congress next term could push back against federal agencies that have gone after journalists and their First Amendment rights. Press freedom advocates are also eyeing several key pieces of legislation to support journalists that have received bipartisan support in the past. “The midterms and the results really create an opportunity to strengthen freedom of the press,” said José Zamora, the regional director for the Americas at the Committee to Protect Journalists. “What matters now is whether Congress turns that opportunity into action.” Critics have derided the current Republican-controlled Congress as unproductive. That could change come Jan. 3. The blue “tsunami” has buoyed Democrats, who appear eager to capitalize on the substantial majorities they gained in both chambers, which may increase even further as races continue to be called. On Election Night, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who will chair the House Oversight Committee next year, posted on X, “LAWYER UP.” Their priorities for the next two years are still coming into focus, and press freedom advocates have already set up calls with legislators to lobby for specific issues. Freedom of the Press Foundation chief of advocacy Seth Stern said that securing a free press can help Congress tackle other issues. For example, those who support healthcare legislation need a press that is able to expose abuses and inefficiencies in the current system. “I don’t think press freedom needs to come at the expense of other congressional priorities,” Stern said. “If anything, it’s complementary to all of those other priorities. A free and unencumbered press is only going to help reformers implement reforms because it helps them expose the needs for those reforms.” Investigations and oversight Congress members have a long list of people and issues they want to investigate. At the top of press freedom advocates’ list is FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. At least two groups have outright called for Carr’s impeachment. Under his leadership, the FCC — which is supposed to be independent — has opened investigations into numerous outlets that have faced criticism from conservatives. Egged on by Trump, the FCC’s dispute with ABC has been particularly contentious. ABC filed a lawsuit in August accusing the FCC of weaponizing its regulatory powers to censor and punish ABC for its speech. Carr himself has made thinly veiled threats against outlets, warning that the FCC can revoke their broadcast licenses. The FCC has also repealed a key broadcast ownership cap, paving the way for increasing media consolidation. Its oversight over the transfer of broadcast licenses means that companies pursuing mergers must get approval from the FCC. That power, critics say, has led to companies like Skydance — which is the result of two successive mergers between CBS-parent Paramount, Skydance Media and CNN-parent Warner Bros. Discovery — taking actions to curry favor with Trump. On Tuesday, during a Senate committee hearing on the nomination of Danielle Thumann to the FCC, Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) had a warning for Carr about what he can expect come January. “Mr. Carr, if you’re listening now, know you’re going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions, and you don’t have the protection of the gavel any longer.” Other major administration figures that Congress could investigate and question are Attorney General Todd Blanche and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, said Clayton Weimers, the executive director of Reporters Without Borders’ North American branch. Weimers said lawmakers should question Blanche about the FBI’s January raid of a Washington Post reporter’s home. Meanwhile, Hegseth has forced journalists out of the Pentagon, censored information about the war in Iran and is currently trying to turn the editorially independent Stars and Stripes newspaper into a mouthpiece for the Pentagon, Weimers said. Hegseth narrowly survived an impeachment effort Tuesday when the House voted 211 to 204 to refer eight articles of impeachment to committee. Only one Republican voted with Democrats. But next year, Democrats will have a majority if they choose to refile impeachment charges. If Congress decides to pursue investigations into the Trump administration next session, they should invest in reforming transparency laws like the Freedom of Information Act, said Lauren Harper, the Freedom of the Press Foundation’s Daniel Ellsberg Chain on Government Secrecy. FOIA processing times have been an issue for multiple administrations, but the situation has worsened under Trump. The Department of Government Efficiency’s cuts last year led to layoffs of FOIA staff at various agencies. Others have been fired for lawfully releasing documents over the objections of agency leaders. “It’s usually the same offices that play a role in responding to requests for information for both FOIA and for Congress,” Harper said. “So the capability, the software, the resources, the independence of FOIA offices is going to play a role with congressional inquiries.” Actions Congress could take include improving the statutory language of FOIA, funding FOIA offices and imposing financial penalties for officials or agencies who obstruct the release of documents, Harper said. Given the mass detentions of migrants initiated by the Department of Homeland Security and ICE over the past two years, Congress could also extend FOIA to include private prisons and detention facilities. FOIA has historically received bipartisan support, which would be important if Trump decides to veto any legislation Congress puts forth. Harper added that the near-unanimous support for the Epstein Files Transparency Act , which required the release of unclassified records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, also suggests that lawmakers from both sides of the aisle are interested in transparency legislation. “What Congress should do is basically take a lesson from what lawmakers did after Watergate,” Harper said. “After the Nixon administration and his resignation, Congress passed a bunch of transparency laws that really laid the foundation for modern oversight. … FOIA was passed in 1966, but it didn’t get real teeth in enforcement mechanism until 1974 after Watergate. “Watergate was the reason why Congress felt the need to actually do that.” Legislation Though Democrats will not have a veto-proof majority next year, press freedom advocates still see opportunity for Congress to advance legislation protecting journalists. A number of potential bills that have received bipartisan support in the past could be reintroduced. Their support may even grow as Republicans try to distance themselves from the unpopular policies and actions of the Trump administration that led to last week’s midterm results, Stern said. “I think a clear message was sent that the Trump administration’s abuses need to be reined in and stopped from happening again,” Stern said. The “lowest hanging fruit,” according to multiple experts, is the PRESS Act , which would prevent the government from forcing journalists to reveal their sources and protect their notes from seizure. Dozens of states already have a version of the law, and at the national level, the PRESS Act passed the House unanimously in 2024. It had bipartisan support in the Senate but did not advance after Trump won the election and told Republicans to kill it. Trump and his administration have spent his second term cracking down on media leaks, resulting in multiple journalists being subpoenaed and at least one being raided. While Trump would almost certainly oppose another attempt at passing the PRESS Act, the midterms have left him with less political clout, potentially paving the way for the bill to gain enough support to override a veto. “Democrats should at least try, and if they can’t, it’ll be clear why they can’t,” Stern said. The crackdown on media leaks also makes reform of the Espionage Act important, according to Stern. One attempt at doing that is the Daniel Ellsberg Press Freedom and Whistleblower Protection Act , which would help protect whistleblowers and prevent the government from using the act to go after journalists and publishers. Stern pointed out that the Espionage Act has been used to go after politicians and government officials ranging from former FBI director James Comey to Trump himself, so support for reform should be bipartisan. Anti-SLAPP legislation is another area in which state versions already exist, setting the stage for a federal version. Forty states — including many Republican-led states — have laws prohibiting meritless lawsuits. Those laws help protect journalists who often face groundless defamation lawsuits meant to silence and punish them by forcing them to spend time and money to fight back in court. Since taking office, Trump himself has filed several defamation lawsuits against media organizations whose coverage he dislikes, including the BBC , The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal . That makes passing anti-SLAPP protections at the federal level imperative, press freedom advocates said. Finally, Congress could pass the Right to Record Act , which would create financial penalties if a federal officer tries to threaten or stop a person peacefully recording federal law enforcement activity. It would also punish the seizure or destruction of such recordings. “People on the ground covering what the Trump administration has done these last two years, where ICE and the National Guard and the military are being deployed — those journalists often come under the most aggressive assault, scrutiny and attempts to criminalize their activities,” said Free Press senior counsel Nora Benavidez. She pointed to the examples of independent journalists Don Lemon and Georgia Fort, who were arrested in January after they filmed and livestreamed from an anti-ICE protest at a Minnesota church. Numerous other journalists across the country have been assaulted and detained while covering anti-ICE demonstrations and immigration operations. Press freedom advocates acknowledged that Congress cannot legislate a solution to every First Amendment issue currently facing journalists. Congress is part of just one branch of the government, and it is the executive branch that “has used every tool at its disposal to try to censor and silence the press,” Zamora said. In addition to physical assaults on journalists by federal officers, Zamora pointed to the White House’s and Pentagon’s continued efforts to limit press access and the Department of Homeland Security’s attempt to revise visa rules to restrict foreign journalists working in the U.S. Trump’s ability to veto legislation will also be a major issue. Still, there is value in pushing an agenda supporting press freedom for the next two years, Weimers said. “If nothing else, it sets you up to do it when there’s a new administration.” “My hope is that we get back to a place where press freedom is a nonpartisan American value that we can all get behind. We strayed away from that,” Weimers said. “Most of these things used to be common sense for just about every American. And I still think they are pretty common sense for the average American member of the public or voter. “But politicians need to realize this is our First Amendment rights. This really matters, and we can’t take it for granted.” This kind of journalism doesn’t fund itself. (AP Photo/Caleb Jones) By: Paul Farhi November 12, 2026 The two most important stories about the Senate race in Maine this year arguably involved revelations of alleged sexual misconduct by the Democratic candidate, Graham Platner, and allegations of corruption by the Republican incumbent, Susan Collins. The first story brought down Platner’s candidacy; the second may have contributed to Collins’ defeat at the polls last week. The striking thing about both stories is that neither one was published by a news outlet based anywhere near Maine. The New York Times and Politico did in Platner. ProPublica and The Intercept dug up the allegations against Collins. This wasn’t a fluke or a one-off. Some of the biggest and most consequential investigative work on the 2026 election came from reporters employed by national news organizations, parachuting in, as it were, to scoop the locals in their own backyards. The revelation that Democrats in Alaska surreptitiously recruited a Senate candidate named Dan J. Sullivan to stack the ballot against the incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan? That story was broken by a Times reporter, Kellen Browning, six days before Election Day. Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall’s aggressive pursuit of hundreds of former patients who owed him money for medical services? That was by another Times journalist, Sarah Kliff. Details about spousal and child abuse allegations involving Rep. Max Miller of Ohio? You didn’t see it first in Miller’s hometown paper; the story was a result of digging by a reporter at Mother Jones magazine, Abby Vesoulis. Another Mother Jones reporter, Noah Lanard, did the investigative pieces detailing Florida Rep. Cory Mills’ history of restraining orders, business issues and stolen-valor allegations. More than just counting scoops, the fact that out-of-towners consistently beat the local beat reporters suggests a serious underlying problem. For years, academics and others have been pointing to a growing crisis in local reporting — the hollowing out of newsrooms in towns and cities across the country. One consequence of this may have been on display during the 2026 election cycle, when the local news media was often the dog that didn’t, and perhaps couldn’t, hunt. Well-staffed regional newspapers — the Miami Herald, Chicago Tribune, Boston Globe, Baltimore Sun, among them — used to be the source of investigations, local and otherwise. The Globe’s Spotlight team broke the Catholic clergy abuse scandal in 2002; the Herald’s Julie K. Brown single-handedly revived the case against Jeffrey Epstein in 2018 with her series, “Perversion of Justice.” A few regional outlets did step up during the campaign, landing big stories. The San Francisco Chronicle’s Alexei Koseff and Sophia Bollag ended the political career of California Rep. Eric Swalwell, the leading candidate for governor, by reporting on a former Swalwell staffer’s allegation of sexual assault. The San Antonio Express-News and The Texas Tribune dropped bombshells nearly simultaneously in February, disclosing Rep. Tony Gonzales’ relationship with a staffer who later committed suicide by lighting herself on fire. Swalwell and Gonzales resigned from Congress. But years of declining advertising and waning subscriptions have sapped the investigative muscle, as well as routine reporting, of local news organizations. A growing number of American counties have turned into news deserts, with no professional news reporting at all. The parlous financial state of local news weighs against the time and expense necessary for sustained reporting. A particularly aggressive bit of reporting or a devastating scoop can even backfire, eliciting charges of bias and demands to cancel subscriptions. Steve Greenlee, the former editor of the Portland Press Herald in Maine, told the Columbia Journalism Review last week that he would often hear from readers who were angry that the paper’s reporting didn’t match the opinions expressed on talk radio or Fox News. The fear, he said, is that subscriptions would drop so much “that you won’t have a newspaper anymore.” Hence the drift toward the “nationalization” of deep political reporting by outfits with both deeper pockets and few local ties. “The big players in D.C. and New York City are taking on an oversized role in investigative journalism with local ramifications,” said Michael Socolow, a journalism professor at the University of Maine. National news organizations are stepping in where diminished newspapers and local TV stations “don’t have the investment or protection anymore.” Socolow watched the Platner and Collins stories unfold in his home state. He noted its antecedents: The Bangor Daily News had the first whiff of Collins’ questionable relationship with a defense contractor in February 2022. The conservative Maine Wire, meanwhile, had inklings about Platner in May, including screenshots from dating apps that suggested problematic personal behavior. But the big picture behind both stories remained hidden until reporters from national outlets showed up. The Times’ Katie Glueck and Lisa Lerer reported in late May that Platner’s wife had warned campaign officials that Platner had been sending sexual messages to as many as a dozen women while married. A few days later, Glueck and Lerer reported on Platner’s troubling behavior with women, including a former girlfriend’s accounts of physical altercations. The final beat: Politico’s Jessica Piper and Adam Wren broke the most serious allegations , leading to Platner’s withdrawal from the race two days later (it surely helped that Piper is an alum of the Bangor Daily News and maintained her local connections). The failure, or mere inability, of local outlets to nail the larger story was reminiscent of the coverage of former Rep. George Santos’ campaign in 2022. A small newspaper, the North Shore Leader, reported oddities and anomalies in Santos’ biography before Election Day, and opined that he was “sketchy.” But the breadth of Santos’ fabrications didn’t emerge until the Times’ Grace Ashford and Michael Gold spent weeks looking into Santos’ claims. By then, however, Santos had already been elected. One of the obvious advantages of a national news organization is its reach and prestige; sources may be more willing to divulge sensitive information to an outlet with the mammoth impact of the Times than one that circulates in one town or region. But Big Media’s structural advantage over its local brethren goes beyond staff size, circulation and bankroll. National reporters don’t live in the communities they wade into, which immunizes them and their employers from social pressure, political retaliation and advertiser boycotts that could paralyze a smaller newsroom. Further, a news organization with a strong presence in Washington ensures sources and connections that don’t exist on the local level. Local news organizations used to have bureaus in Washington; these have been gutted, too. The good news is that reporters still dug up important stories during the campaign. As Socolow put it, “investigative journalism still matters in 2026.” But out-of-town journalism isn’t a substitute for the local kind. Scandals and corruption don’t just occur with every election cycle, and they don’t just happen in Washington. They’re down the street and across town. The big scoops by national reporters are, in some ways, evidence of failure, suggesting that the media system works at the top but is crumbling at the foundation. Rigorous and probing news reporting “takes money, time, credibility, relationships, and independence,” Socolow said. Unfortunately, “those are much more difficult to secure in local newsrooms today.” This kind of journalism doesn’t fund itself.
