Novos ângulos para assuntos do dia Brasis nov 13, 2026 6 1 Partilhar 🔸 O ministro Flávio Dino, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), autorizou que empresas distribuam a jornada semanal de 42 horas em cinco dias de trabalho, com até 8 horas e 24 minutos diários, sem pagamento de horas extras pelos minutos excedentes à oitava hora. A medida vale para empresas que não firmarem acordo coletivo até 15 de dezembro e poderá ser aplicada durante a fase de transição para o fim da escala 6x1, até dezembro de 2027. O Jota detalha a decisão do ministro, que estabelece parâmetros para a implementação da emenda constitucional aprovada em outubro. Dino também permitiu que os dois repousos semanais remunerados sejam distribuídos por negociação coletiva, sem a exigência de que ocorram na mesma semana, desde que garantidos oito dias de descanso por mês. O ministro determinou ainda a manutenção dos salários após a redução da jornada e proibiu a contratação de novos funcionários com remuneração inferior em razão da mudança. 🔸 O presidente Lula (PT) afirmou que o Brasil tem a “obrigação moral” de sediar uma edição da Conferência sobre a Transição para Longe dos Combustíveis Fósseis. “Vou fazer, temos a obrigação moral”, afirmou ontem, durante encontro com representantes da sociedade civil na COP31, na Turquia. Segundo a eixos , apesar do protagonismo internacional, o Brasil enfrenta contradições na definição de sua própria estratégia de transição energética. O governo ainda elabora um mapa nacional para reduzir a dependência dos combustíveis fósseis, que deve ficar para a COP32, em 2027, e deverá preservar espaço para a exploração de petróleo e gás. Embora as emissões brasileiras estejam em queda desde 2023, graças à redução do desmatamento, o setor de energia continua sendo um desafio, sobretudo pelo aumento do consumo de diesel nos transportes. Obrigada por ler a Brasis. Gostou do conteúdo? Assine e compartilhe. Subscrever 🔸 A propósito: o roteiro internacional apresentado pela presidência brasileira da COP30 propõe que os países produtores de petróleo, gás e carvão comecem a reduzir a oferta desses combustíveis entre 2031 e 2033, acompanhando a queda prevista na demanda mundial. A proposta, porém, contrasta com os planos do governo Lula (PT) de ampliar a exploração de petróleo na margem equatorial, especialmente na Bacia da Foz do Amazonas. A Petrobras anunciou a descoberta de três depósitos de petróleo no bloco 59, na costa do Amapá, onde a produção poderá começar em cerca de dez anos, justamente quando o consumo global deverá estar em declínio. A Sumaúma destrincha as contradições entre os compromissos climáticos defendidos pelo Brasil e a expansão da atividade petrolífera. O país já concedeu 51 blocos para exploração em alto-mar na margem equatorial. 🔸 Falando em meio ambiente… O governador de São Paulo, Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos), nomeou o ex-ministro do Meio Ambiente Ricardo Salles para a Secretaria de Justiça e Cidadania do estado, cargo que assumirá em janeiro de 2027. A nomeação seria resultado de um acordo eleitoral: segundo a CBN, Tarcísio ofereceu o posto em troca da desistência de Salles de disputar o Senado. Uma semana antes das eleições, o ex-ministro retirou sua candidatura. A Agência Pública relembra que Salles é réu, desde 2023, em uma ação penal sobre contrabando de madeira da Amazônia para os Estados Unidos e a União Europeia. O processo tramita no STF. Durante sua gestão no Ministério do Meio Ambiente, entre 2019 e 2021, Salles enfraqueceu a fiscalização ambiental e ficou conhecido por defender que o governo deveria “ir passando a boiada” para flexibilizar normas ambientais enquanto a imprensa concentrava sua atenção na pandemia de Covid-19. 🔸 O Dia do Pantanal, celebrado nesta quinta-feira, chamou a atenção para as ameaças à maior planície de inundação do planeta. Dados do MapBiomas, divulgados nesta semana, mostram que o planalto da Bacia do Alto Paraguai perdeu 6,7 milhões de hectares de vegetação nativa entre 1987 e 2025, enquanto a planície pantaneira perdeu 1,8 milhão de hectares. No mesmo período, a expansão da agropecuária transformou a paisagem da região: as pastagens avançaram 6,9 milhões de hectares e a agricultura cresceu 304% entre 1985 e 2025. O #Colabora explica que a redução da vegetação nativa, associada às mudanças climáticas, tem alterado o regime de cheias do Pantanal. Entre 2015 e 2025, a área alagada média diminuiu 53%, de 5,99 milhões para 2,79 milhões de hectares. A região também enfrenta secas mais intensas e mudanças na dinâmica dos incêndios. Nos últimos sete anos, as chuvas ficaram abaixo da média. Entre 1985 e 2025, o fogo atingiu pelo menos uma vez 61% do território pantaneiro, o equivalente a 9 milhões de hectares. 📮 Outras histórias Uma história repetida há décadas em Propriá, no norte de Sergipe, conta que Dom Pedro II teria passado uma noite no atual Hotel Imperial durante sua viagem pelo rio São Francisco, em 1859. O proprietário, José Oscar Vieira Soares, mantém viva a versão e mostra aos visitantes o quarto 12, onde o imperador supostamente dormiu, e um armário que teria sido utilizado por ele. A história, porém, não tinha comprovação documental. O Meus Sertões explora o mistério e, a partir dos diários de Dom Pedro II, disponibilizados pelo Museu Imperial, esclarece o que aconteceu durante a passagem do monarca pela cidade. Os registros revelam que a visita a Propriá durou apenas três horas e 45 minutos. O imperador conheceu igrejas, escolas e autoridades locais, almoçou na residência de um juiz e seguiu viagem. Naquela noite, dormiu na Casa de Câmara e Cadeia de Traipu, em Alagoas, e não no hotel sergipano. 📌 Investigação Uma mancha esverdeada provocada pela proliferação de cianobactérias potencialmente tóxicas avançou pelo rio Bacajá, no Pará, e chegou ao rio Xingu, após percorrer cerca de 55 km desde 24 de outubro. A InfoAmazonia confirmou o avanço da contaminação por meio de imagens de satélite e teve acesso a laudos obtidos pelo Ministério Público Federal (MPF), que identificaram três gêneros de cianobactérias em concentrações até quatro vezes superiores ao limite estabelecido pela legislação ambiental. O fenômeno, inicialmente detectado por indígenas, provocou mudanças na cor da água e mortandade de peixes, além de ameaçar a saúde das comunidades da região. Na Terra Indígena Arara da Volta Grande do Xingu, em Anapu (PA), as 52 famílias da aldeia Terrã Wãngan deixaram de pescar e enfrentam dificuldades para obter alimentos. “A gente não pode mais sair para caçar, por ser uma distância longa. Não teria água suficiente, porque não pode consumir do rio”, afirma o cacique Adauto Arara. Quase três semanas depois da primeira detecção, as causas da proliferação das bactérias ainda não haviam sido esclarecidas. 🍂 Meio ambiente O desmatamento, a ocupação desordenada e a abertura de estradas sem planejamento provocaram o surgimento de mais de 200 voçorocas na bacia do rio Cabaçal, em Mato Grosso. São grandes erosões que podem atingir o lençol freático, despejam toneladas de sedimentos nos cursos d’água que abastecem o Pantanal e, assim, ameaçam o equilíbrio da maior planície alagável contínua do planeta. O Eh Fonte acompanha a mobilização de moradores, pesquisadores e organizações ambientais que, há mais de 15 anos, buscam recuperar áreas degradadas na região. Em Reserva do Cabaçal (MT), moradores relatam a transformação de córregos antes cristalinos em cursos d’água assoreados, com redução dos peixes e impactos sobre comunidades ribeirinhas. “O assoreamento foi acabando com o peixe, acabando com tudo. Não ficou ninguém”, conta Elson Santana de Carvalho, de 50 anos, cuja família viveu da pesca por quatro gerações. 📙 Cultura Celulares erguidos durante shows, conversas em voz alta nos teatros, gritaria nas salas de cinema e espectadores que se comportam como se estivessem sozinhos. Na revista piauí , o jornalista Gilberto Porcidonio parte de experiências pessoais em apresentações de Jorge Drexler, Caetano Veloso e Maria Bethânia para discutir a deterioração das regras de convivência nos espaços culturais. Ele lembra episódios de conflitos entre artistas e plateias, como o tapa que Mateus Solano deu no celular de uma espectadora durante uma peça, e conversa com profissionais da cultura sobre a crescente dificuldade do público de se concentrar nas apresentações. O ator Antônio Fagundes, que transformou a questão em tema da peça “Sete Minutos”, afirma que a capacidade de atenção dos espectadores diminuiu drasticamente. “O teatro é o último resquício de humanidade na comunicação”, diz. 🎧 Podcast “Tem um monte de piada que eu ganho porque eu gaguejo, porque eu sei contar essa história ; e a piada que eu perco, eu faço piada porque perdi.” Foi assim que o comediante Gui Albuquerque transformou a gagueira, que o acompanha desde a infância, em matéria-prima para seus espetáculos de stand-up. No primeiro ato do “Rádio Novelo Apresenta”, produção da Rádio Novelo , ele conta sobre o espetáculo “Eu Gago e Ando”, que apresenta no Rio de Janeiro, no qual faz piadas sobre as dificuldades de comunicação, os constrangimentos e as estratégias que desenvolveu para lidar com as palavras. “Eu esqueço que eu sou gago. Isso não me define, ao mesmo tempo. Ao mesmo tempo que sou muito eu, né, que eu sou muito em cima disso, que eu sou formado em cima disso, isso não me define também, sabe? Eu posso tantas outras coisas”, afirma. No episódio, ele conversa com Mariana Leão, editora de som da Rádio Novelo que também é gaga e passou boa parte da vida tentando esconder essa característica. 💆🏽‍♀️ Para ler no fim de semana A rotina de trabalho da produtora cultural e DJ Germana Nobre, de Juazeiro do Norte (CE), é dividida entre reuniões, apresentações e os cuidados com as duas filhas. Como microempreendedora individual, ela encontra na flexibilidade de horários uma forma de conciliar as atividades, mas enfrenta a instabilidade dos contratos, os atrasos nos pagamentos e a sobrecarga doméstica. “Você investe duas, três horas se inscrevendo. Se for um edital longo, um mês todo. Porque não é só sentar no computador, tem vida acontecendo, no meu caso, são duas crianças chamando: ‘mamãe, mamãe, mamãe’”, conta, ao descrever as dificuldades para participar de editais culturais. O Nonada ouviu artistas e produtoras culturais de diferentes regiões do país sobre os obstáculos para conciliar a maternidade com o trabalho na cultura. Entre elas está Caroline Holanda, de Fortaleza (CE), que chegou a ser desencorajada a disputar uma vaga em uma escola de artes na França por estar grávida. Mãe solo, ela afirma que precisa acumular funções nos projetos para garantir seu sustento e o da filha: “Então essa é a condição para que eu continue sendo artista: a sobrecarga”. The Free Press prints a racist lie to fit a prefab narrative; Israel authorizes 34 settlements under cover of condemnations. Apr 12, 2026 159 12 27 Share Note to readers: I’ve recently taken the plunge into full-time writing and reporting, leaving behind the work that’s paid my bills for the past fifteen years. It’s both exciting and unnerving—journalism isn’t exactly a gold mine these days, and every bit of my reporting is self-funded. I travel with no crew, no security team—just me. But, at the risk of sounding sentimental, I’ve never felt more certain of my purpose. Infinite Jaz exists because I believe reporting on Israel-Palestine, and the systems of power that shape it, should not be filtered through the priorities of billionaires and politically biased, risk-averse institutions. But it cannot continue without your support. If my work has mattered to you, please consider becoming a paid subscriber—you’ll gain access to the full archive of subscriber-only reporting and help cover my upcoming reporting trips to the West Bank. For a limited time, I’m offering 20% off for an annual commitment—just over $5 per month: Get 20% off for 1 year Subscribe A very funny and ridiculous but also not-funny and ominous thing happened on the internet this past week. Olivia Reingold of The Free Press —owned by CBS’s Bari Weiss—covered a much-talked-about political rally, in which Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed stumped with the popular left-wing streamer Hasan Piker. The announcement of the event had already generated a three-week news cycle, in which Piker—a proud anti-Zionist who is doing more than anyone to combat the real antisemitism festering in dark corners of the internet—was smeared as antisemitic. As Trump threatened to end a 3,000-year-old civilization, prominent pundits and Democrats lined up to criticize El-Sayed for sharing a stage with Hasan Piker. A Newsmax-level chyron on CNN. During the actual event, footage of an exchange between Reingold and El-Sayed—coming after he had already fielded a barrage of hostile questions from her—went viral. The internet, which has recently caught on to the fact that the question of whether “a state has a right to exist” doesn’t actually mean anything, was quick to point out that Reingold froze when asked to define what she herself had asked. Here is how Reingold characterized the interaction the following day (the same language was used in her Free Press article, Michigan Gets Its Own Mamdani ): It starts with “Abdul El-Sayed, who is Muslim,” and only goes downhill from there. You may have noticed that Reingold, who is Jewish 1 , misquoted El-Sayed, something that The Free Press later corrected: But there’s another, more telling detail they failed to correct. To see it, you have to set aside, for a moment, the awful prose of “he retorted, narrowing his eyes”—young writers, please note that “he said” was right there —and focus instead on its accuracy: Do you see any narrowing of his eyes? Of course not. If anything, El-Sayed’s expression is extraordinarily warm, given the rhetorical game he’s being subjected to—and the constant defamations he’s forced to respond to. In my culture, we’d say that he’s acting here like a mensch. After I pointed this out on X, many people had fun with it. A few of my favorites: One more, since I really couldn’t help myself: Okay, now that the jokes are out of the way, it’s worth being precise about what exactly happened here: Olivia Reingold, a star reporter for what is effectively a CBS-affiliate, fabricated a detail in her story from whole cloth to portray El-Sayed as a nefarious, antisemitic Muslim. For actual reporters, this is not trivial. It is, in fact, a very big deal: lying to advance your narrative is a cardinal sin in our field. These are the details that make stories come to life, and Reingold’s lie that El-Sayed “narrowed his eyes” is a perfect one to go alongside the relentless Islamophobic characterization of men with names like Hasan Piker and Abdul El-Sayed. I’ve had many true details cut from stories by editors on the grounds that I couldn’t prove without a shadow of a doubt that they actually happened—through visual evidence, corroborating witnesses, or confirmation from the subject themselves—even though the editors believed me. Serious publications observe an abundance of caution to avoid having to issue corrections. Reingold, for her part, attended Columbia Journalism School, where she presumably learned the same cautionary tales I did at NYU, about reporters like Jayson Blair and Stephen Glass, whose careers ended in disgrace after they were exposed as serial fabulists. This is apparently not a concern when working at The Free Press . The fact that the publication left this fabrication in—despite a viral video that readily disproves it—suggests that Bari Weiss, who has rapidly become one of the most powerful figures in American media, is willing to sideline the truth when it conflicts with a prefab narrative. The irony is hard to miss coming from a reporter and outlet that accused the media of lying about the Gaza famine by profiling starving children with preexisting conditions. This child died days after Reingold’s article cited him as an example to cast doubt on the Gaza famine, pointing to his rickets—a condition typically associated with deficiencies in vitamin D, which is obtained from foods like milk, fortified cereals, and fatty fish. The episode is a good microcosm of the broader antisemitism hysteria since October 7. On the journalism front, Adam Johnson made a good point about how writers like Reingold have boxed themselves into a corner with their own delusional narratives, leaving them reliant on imagined details that inevitably read as flowery and unreal. But I am being optimistic—the general news-following public is not reading lines like this and immediately recognizing them as unreal, but instead taking them at face value. Such distortions have flourished for decades in the mainstream media, calcifying racist narratives into conventional wisdom. Which leads me to the even graver issue—and please bear with me through this moderate leap—of Israel’s ethnic cleansing of the West Bank, and the way it is routinely obscured through toothless condemnations of settler violence. For years, I’ve written about how ritual condemnations of settler violence serve as a pressure release valve for Israel’s broader project of ethnic cleansing in the occupied West Bank. When footage grows bad enough and international outrage builds, Israeli officials and their allies step out to placate their critics— Yes, we agree with you, this is bad, but they’re just a few bad apples! —quarantining the supposed “fringe youth” who commit the violent acts. The more “liberal” among the tsk-tskers, like NYC Congressmen Dan Goldman and Richie Torres, call on the Israeli government to prosecute the violent settlers, obscuring the basic fact that this is the same government that funds, arms, and protects them. The call, in other words, is for the foxes to get serious about henhouse security. The violence has been so bad over the past month that even some settler leaders joined in on the condemnations: The event was called, “Yes to the Land of Israel. No to Violence,” begging the question: How do they propose to take over the ‘Land of Israel,’ where three million Palestinians live, without violence? Well, they can’t, and that’s where the Israeli government comes in: as the condemnations calm the outrage and attention fades, the cabinet quietly rewards the settlers by authorizing their illegal gains, approving new settlements on the land they’ve violently emptied of Palestinians. This is why the settlers are known to their supporters as “Jewish pioneers,” pushing the frontiers of the Land of Israel—and why settler leaders roll their eyes and accuse their pro-Israel critics of hypocrisy, knowing they’re simply doing the state’s dirty work when they terrorize defenseless Palestinians. This is, quite literally, the opposite of the truth. Well, here it is playing out in plain sight. Amid the explosion of settler violence during the war on Iran and the ensuing wave of condemnations, the Israeli cabinet quietly approved a record-breaking number of new settlements, including many that began as bases of settler terror in the northern West Bank, the epicenter of the past few weeks’ pogroms . These 34 new settlements will now be fast-tracked for state support, with access to funding, public utilities, municipal services, building permits, and more. It’s the largest batch ever authorized at one time, bringing the total under the current government to 103. By contrast, in the three decades between the Oslo Accords and the establishment of the new government in late 2022, six new settlements were formally approved. Translates to: “The settlements that the cabinet approved for establishment.” At a ceremony for one of the new settlements, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich congratulated the “twelve core families of pioneers,” a reference to the settlers who broke Israeli law to establish an illegal outpost and waited out the clock for the government’s rubber stamp, which had finally come. He also promised that the settlement movement would push into Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria. Elisha Yered, the Hilltop Youth settler leader accused of murder (whom I write about often), celebrated the announcement as a “historic” breakthrough—not just for the number of settlements approved, but for their strategic placement deep in the northern West Bank, the same region where he’s led a campaign of terror in recent weeks. He described it as evidence that the government recognizes that the settlers are nearing completion of the takeover of Area C, and are now preparing the ground for the next phase: pushing settlements into Areas A and B. Yes to the Land of Israel! “The order of the hour is to storm the next goal of the settlement,” Yered wrote. “To abolish the Oslo Accords with your feet!” On Thursday, Israel’s Minister of Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism, Amichai Chikli, concurred, visiting an infamously violent outpost deep in Area B and declaring that it was “time to wean off” the Oslo Accords. (I think I can speak for Jews across the diaspora in saying: thank you, sir, for combating antisemitism.) And Haaretz reported that the new chief of the Shin Bet—the agency ostensibly responsible for cracking down on settler violence—does not refer to attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank as “Jewish terror,” but rather as “cases of friction” between Jews and Palestinians. Notably, he’s using the exact same euphemism as Elisha Yered, who has openly described their violent incursions into Palestinian villages as attempts to “generate friction.” So my question is this: Will Dan Goldman, Richie Torres, and even those “respected settler leaders” clamoring for a “peaceful takeover” of the Land of Israel—all of whom condemned settler violence last month—acknowledge that the Israeli government, rather than heed their calls to crack down on the perpetrators, has responded by rewarding them for their acts of terror? Doubtful! YNet reported that “According to two officials familiar with the matter, the approval of the new settlements was kept under wraps during the war at the request of the United States.” This is, of course, the reason Israel is undertaking a de facto annexation in the first place: Jewish control of the West Bank continues expanding unabated without crossing the “red line” of formal annexation set by the U.S., Europe, and several Gulf states. The hollow condemnations can be swatted away with no fear of material consequences . The full statement, from Friday, read: “As President Donald Trump has made clear, he does not support the annexation of the West Bank by Israel.” That oughta do it! I want to revisit the viral CNN moment from last month, which has become a neat case study in how all this works. First, a refresher: In the middle of the night on March 26, settlers stormed the Palestinian village of Tayasir, beating 75-year-old Abdullah Daraghmeh while he slept, breaking his skull and several bones in his face, and knocking several of his teeth out. By morning, the settlers had set up a new outpost. The following day, as CNN’s Jeremy Diamond visited Tayasir to report on the attack, he and his cameraman were accosted by IDF soldiers. The soldiers told him, in no uncertain terms, that they were seeking revenge for the death of a young settler , that they believed Jews are entitled to the whole West Bank, and that they were working to help turn the illegal outpost into a legal settlement—the exact process I have just described that culminates in a formal government authorization. After the footage went viral, the IDF quickly condemned the comments, saying they do not represent the IDF, and announced the suspension of the battalion. They also said that the outpost had been evacuated. Here’s what happened when the cameras stopped rolling: The next day, settlers returned to the evacuated outpost to rebuild it and terrorize Tayasir once again, wounding four Palestinians and torching homes and cars. Soldiers were nowhere to be found—except days later, when they joined the settlers in their outpost rebuilding efforts. Attacks on Tayasir continued. On April 7, during a settler incursion backed by the IDF, a soldier shot and killed a young man, Alaa Khaled Sbiah, who had come out to defend his village. Step six has not happened yet, but a question for the future: If (and when) this outpost is formally authorized as a settlement, will the media connect it to its history of violence? The article quotes a settler council calling the event a “terror attack and murder attempt.” Centrist and right-wing media in Israel were quick to label the murder near Tayasir as a foiled terror attack—quite a way to describe a response to an armed invasion. But, again, this is precisely the point of these settler incursions or “ land patrols ”: to “generate friction.” To Israeli authorities, the Palestinian response to this “friction” is known as “terrorism,” which then serves as justification for additional state and military resources. IDF chief Eyal Zamir admitted as much during the meeting in which 34 new settlements were approved, reportedly telling the cabinet that “he was ‘raising 10 red flags’ over the IDF’s manpower levels, arguing that the military would need additional personnel to meet its expanding operational demands, including those stemming from settlement expansion.” From my piece, Good Settler, Bad Settler , in November: Just this week, the Knesset advanced a bill granting major new tax breaks to West Bank settlements deemed “under threat,” a designation made by the IDF Central Command, inseparable from the dynamics of encroachment that produce those threats: The deeper a settlement pushes into Palestinian land, the more “dangerous” its surroundings become, manufacturing the “insecurity” that then entitles it to further state support. The irony here—and what Zamir may be hinting at—is that many people believe the devastating effectiveness of the October 7 attack was, in part, a consequence of the IDF being stretched thin protecting West Bank settlements rather than stationed along the Gaza border. And October 7, of course, led to the annihilation of Gaza, which has quietly transitioned into a process of resettling it. That is to say, October 7 has proven to be a boon for the settlement movement across the Land of Israel. “But Jasper,” you might ask, suspiciously, “do you really think that all of this—the provocations, the violence, the condemnations—is meant to expand the settlement project?” “At the end of the day,” I retort, narrowing my eyes, “all roads in Israel lead to settling.” If you found this piece of journalism valuable, consider upgrading to a paid subscription so I can keep doing this work. It tells to me, they only see their identity with Judaism when they get to be thee victim and use their victimhood. It’s a shallow reading of Judaism and so irritating. Submit Sign In | Membership News Training Ethics Fact-Checking Media Literacy AI Events Future of Public Media Newmark Ethics Center IFCN MediaWise PolitiFact Donate About Us Press Freedom Watch The Poynter 50 Podcasts Artificial Intelligence Business & Work Reporting & Editing Fact-Checking Ethics & Trust Local News Journalism, Media & Communication Training Poynter Membership Categories Consulting & Coaching For ACES Members For Local News Funders All Categories Broadcast & Visual Journalism Business & Work Ethics Fact-Checking & Media Literacy Leadership Reporting & Editing Writing Poynter ACES Introductory Certificate in Editing Poynter ACES Intermediate Certificate in Editing Poynter ACES Advanced Certificate in Editing Workshops and Coaching Tools for Funders Ethics Ethics Training Ethics Articles AI Ethics Public Editor Project Get Ethics Advice Fact-Checking Articles IFCN IFCN Grants International Fact-Checking Day Teen Creator Network PolitiFact MediaWise Media Literacy Resources AI Literacy Ambassadors Teen Creator Network Research & News International en Español MediaWise Training All Events The 2026 Poynter Journalism Prizes A free press is the bedrock of American democracy, vital enough to be enshrined in the Bill of Rights. It informs citizens, holds leaders accountable and preserves democratic principles. After decades of relative freedom, the press now faces a precarious future. Since January, President Donald Trump and his administration have taken actions that have hindered the media’s ability to cover the government, including cutting funding, investigating outlets and detaining writers. Some actions appear tied to broader strategies, such as Project 2025, the 900-page conservative roadmap for reshaping government. Others focus on outlets that Trump has repeatedly singled out for criticism. To document these developments, Poynter is compiling a list of federal actions affecting journalists, including lawsuits, policy changes, investigations, funding cuts, firings and detentions. The list will be updated periodically and does not include verbal attacks, threats or media companies’ anticipatory compliance. For tips or suggestions, email Poynter reporter Angela Fu at afu@poynter.org or contact her on Signal at angelafu.74. Detention and Violence Funding Cuts Government-Funded Media Intimidation of Sources Investigations and Harassment Loss of Access News Suppression Public Broadcasting Wire Outlets Two Congress members bar reporters from election night events November 3, 2026 Source: Democrata Journalists reported issues accessing election night events held by Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) and Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R-N.J.). Lawler banned Bloomberg News from his event shortly after the outlet published a story revealing that his campaign was facing a lawsuit by canvassers who alleged that they had been discriminated against and had not been properly paid, according to Semafor . Kean, meanwhile, banned all press from his event, Politico reported. Pentagon fires top general for leaking to media October 28, 2026 Source: Axios The Pentagon fired Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia and referred him for criminal prosecution after he admitted to speaking to reporters at The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal, according to Axios. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said his department has “zero tolerance for the intentional, unauthorized disclosure of classified information.” Axios reported that an internal report had found that Sylvia began speaking to reporters without permission in the fall of 2025, giving information about Ukraine and Iran. During the second Trump administration, the Pentagon has made investigating media leaks a priority, implementing mass polygraphs and punishing those found to have spoken to the press without authorization. Government contractor arrested by FBI for leaking to media October 23, 2026 Source: Department of Justice The FBI arrested Ian Brinksman, a federal contractor, for allegedly leaking classified national defense information to his girlfriend, independent journalist Aída Chávez. Brinksman had worked for a company providing services to the CIA. An affidavit of an agent involved in the case included quotes matching posts on Chávez’s politics and foreign policy Substack, Capital & Empire. The second Trump administration has made it a point to investigate and punish media leakers, which press freedom advocates say chills and hurts speech. The Independent blocked from White House pool October 22, 2026 Source: The Independent The White House removed The Independent’s Andrew Feinberg from the pool of reporters set to travel with President Donald Trump to a rally in South Dakota. Feinberg had drawn the White House’s ire two days before when he questioned Trump and Vice President JD Vance about a new initiative to award whistleblowers. Trump called Feinberg a “sick person,” and a White House X account later called him a “M******** Moron,” using a slur for people with disabilities. The next day, Feinberg was told that although he had been scheduled to serve as the print pooler for the South Dakota trip, he was being removed from the trip. Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.) tells officials to take journalist’s camera October 14, 2026 Source: The Baltimore Banner During a press scrum following an election debate, Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.) tried to have a journalist’s camera taken away. The reporter, Cat Murphy, was a student journalist working for Capital News Service. Murphy, along with multiple other journalists, were trying to question Harris while recording him. Harris singled Murphy out, however, and demanded that she stop recording him even though he was in a public space. He called out for an officer and said someone needed to take her camera away. Though Harris tried to cite Maryland’s wiretapping law that requires that all parties consent before recording a private conversation, the law does not apply to public forums, such as the press scrum. Pentagon appoints public affairs official as acting publisher of Stars and Stripes October 13, 2026 Source: Military.com The Department of Defense appointed one of its public affairs officials to serve as interim publisher of the Stars and Stripes newspaper. Though Stars and Stripes is owned and partially funded by the department, it has historically enjoyed editorial independence. The new publisher, public affairs executive director and principal adviser Christian Devine, will continue to serve in his Pentagon job. Military.com pointed out that means there will be “a single official inside both the office that shapes the military’s message, and the newsroom charged with covering it independently.” Stars and Stripes’ previous publisher, Max Lederer Jr., was fired in August, along with the paper’s editor-in-chief and a reporter, for “insubordination.” The editor-in-chief and reporter both said they were fired for speaking out in favor of the paper’s independence. Lederer was fired for not agreeing to terminate them. More from Poynter: A diminished Stars and Stripes is bad for the US military and bad for America Department of Justice investigates major TV networks October 9, 2026 Source: The New York Times The Department of Justice opened an investigation into five major television networks — ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC — for allegedly violating antitrust laws, The New York Times reported. All five are part of the primary TV White House pool, the rotating group of journalists that report on President Donald Trump’s activities. After Trump kicked CNN out of the pool in mid-September, the other four networks refused to participate in the pool, leaving him without TV coverage. That boycott is at the center of the Justice Department’s Antitrust Division’s investigation. Press freedom advocates and legal experts have denounced the investigation, stating that the outlets have the First Amendment right to engage in protests such as the boycott. More from Poynter: What’s behind Trump’s White House media ban — and what happens next The White House has a workaround when networks refuse to replace CNN Politico banned from Air Force One October 4, 2026 Source: CNN The White House banned Politico from traveling on Air Force One as part of the press pool responsible for covering President Donald Trump. Normally, Politico and other outlets rotate through the travel pool — a system necessary given the size constraints of Air Force One. But the White House has left Politico off the rotation on days when Trump is taking the presidential plane. The move follows a more extensive ban that had barred Politico (along with CNN and MS NOW) from White House grounds entirely. That ban was temporarily blocked by a federal judge, but the White House has argued that Air Force One is a more exclusive space over which it has greater control. CNN has similarly been barred from participating in the pool on days that Trump travels on Air Force One. More from Poynter: President Trump’s losing streak versus the press continues Trump banned three news outlets. A judge let them back in. Then things got weirder. What’s behind Trump’s White House media ban — and what happens next White House bans CNN from Air Force One September 25, 2026 Source: CNN Starting Sept. 25, the White House banned CNN from traveling with President Donald Trump on Air Force One as part of the White House pool, the rotating group of journalists that cover Trump’s activities each day. The move follows a more expansive Sept. 18 ban by Trump barring CNN, Politico and MS NOW from White House grounds. A court order forced the administration to let the three outlets back onto White House grounds, but the administration has argued that the Air Force One (and the Oval Office) are separate, more exclusive spaces over which the administration has greater control in access. As a result, the White House has left CNN off the pool rotation on days that Trump is scheduled to take Air Force One, leaving him to travel without mainstream television coverage. More from Poynter: The White House has a workaround when networks refuse to replace CNN Trump banned three news outlets. A judge let them back in. Then things got weirder. President Trump’s losing streak versus the press continues What’s behind Trump’s White House media ban — and what happens next Trump bans CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists from the White House September 18, 2026 Source: Donald Trump President Donald Trump announced via Truth Social that he would ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” He added that outlets should not be able to report “FICTION and LIES” in their political coverage and that he would ban more news outlets in the future. The next day, several reporters and photographers from the three outlets had their White House press passes deactivated. The White House has previously banned The Associated Press from certain presidential spaces after the AP refused to call the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America.” However, AP reporters had some of their access restored after the outlet sued the administration over the ban. More from Poynter: What’s behind Trump’s White House media ban — and what happens next From absurd to disturbing as Trump White House bans AP from important media events Pentagon polygraphs Joint Staff employees in media leak investigation August 31, 2026 Source: The New York Times The Pentagon polygraphed 50 military officers and civilian employees on the Joint Staff as part of a media leak investigation, The New York Times reported. The investigation came after media outlets reported that the U.S. was running low on important munitions due to the Iran war. One expert told the Times that he had “never seen polygraphs employed this broadly or at this seniority level.” The executive branch under President Donald Trump has ramped up its use of polygraphs as part of a crackdown on media leaks, despite the tool’s unreliability. In addition to the Defense Department, the Department of Homeland Security and the FBI have polygraphed employees to identify the sources of media leaks. Treasury Department denies several journalists press credentials for G20 meeting August 29, 2026 Source: The New York Times The Department of the Treasury refused to grant press credentials to several reporters for The New York Times, Bloomberg News and The Wall Street Journal to cover a Group of 20 meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, the Times reported. A different reporter from the Times was given a press credential, and a Treasury Department spokesperson said that “nearly 300 members of the media” from various outlets including NPR and The Washington Post had received credentials to cover the meeting. Last year, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatened to withhold access from Bloomberg over its reporting about his decision to list two homes as his “primary residence.” Bessent appeared to follow through with his threat as he stopped granting interviews to Bloomberg TV, according to Semafor. US Central Command press office blacklists journalists August 24, 2026 Source: The Intercept After making several calls to the U.S. Central Command, The Intercept reporter Nick Turse was told by a public affairs official that he could be put on a “list of people to disregard” for calling too often. The official, Richard Allee, confirmed that such a list existed after further questioning by Turse. CENTCOM later denied having a blacklist of journalists in an emailed statement to The Intercept. Other departments of the executive branch — including the Treasury Department and Department of the Interior — have previously blacklisted certain publications over negative coverage. Pentagon fires Stars and Stripes editor, publisher and reporter August 21, 2026 Source: Slavin v Parnell lawsuit complaint Stars and Stripes editor-in-chief Erik Slavin and Middle East reporter Lara Korte said they were fired by the Department of Defense for saying in media interviews that they were committed to providing independent journalism to their readers in the military. Specifically, both had given interviews to “CBS Sunday Morning” for a piece about changes the Defense Department — which contributes half of the Stars and Stripes’ funding — had made to the paper as part of an effort to exert more control over the editorially independent publication. Korte was quoted as saying she worked for the paper, “not for the Pentagon, not for any administration, not for any policymaker.” Meanwhile, Slavin said a “redline” he would not cross would be if the Pentagon told him not to run a certain news story and instead run a prewritten press release. Several weeks later, the Pentagon instructed Stars and Stripes publisher Max Lederer to terminate Slavin and Korte. Lederer refused and resigned instead. In response, the Pentagon also issued a notice of separation to Lederer. In all three notices, the Department of Defense cited “insubordination.” More from Poynter: A diminished Stars and Stripes is bad for the US military and bad for America Defense Department accuses former Air Force secretary of disclosing classified information, revokes security clearance August 7, 2026 Source: Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced on X that former Secretary of the Air Force Frank Kendall’s security clearance had been revoked. (It is relatively common for officials to retain their clearance even after leaving their jobs to allow them to advise the government or work as contractors.) Parnell accused Kendall of disclosing classified information about Air Force One to a media outlet. Kendall denied doing so in a statement to the AP, saying he had not been told what classified information he allegedly disclosed. Kendall had given on-the-record interviews to media outlets, including The New York Times, about security concerns surrounding the airplane donated by Qatar, which President Donald Trump is using as the new Air Force One. The Justice Department later subpoenaed four Times reporters over their reporting, though it later dropped the effort. More from Poynter: How Air Force One became a press freedom story More Entries

results.pageTitle: Nick Wright claims Clay Travis fabricates political beliefs for clicks
results.pageDescription: Nick Wright of 'First Things First' joined Tim Miller on 'The Bulwark Daily' and ripped his colleagues grifting with fake political personas.
results.evidenceText: Nick Wright claims Clay Travis fabricates political beliefs for clicks Skip to content Credit: The Bulwark, USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect By Megan Armstrong on 11/12/2026 11/12/2026 Less AI and more AA in your search results. Nick Wright has become a sports media superstar on FS1’s First Things First and his own eponymous podcast, and as he recently explained to Andrew Marchand , his lifelong dream had always been to parlay his sports broadcasting fame into a career in politics. The past decade of American politics, Wright told Marchand, left him feeling “beaten down” and changed his mind about formally entering the political arena. However, in the aftermath of “ The Blue Tsunami ” in the midterm elections, Wright is slowly reclaiming his rightful place in political and social commentary. Wright called out Stephen A. Smith for his grift-adjacent persona as a fair-weather political pundit before delivering a 32-minute analysis of the midterms on What’s Wright? With Nick Wright and burying Matthew Yglesias for baseless critiques of newly elected Sen. Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.). On Wednesday, Tim Miller of The Bulwark welcomed Wright on his The Bulwark Daily podcast to “ lib out .” Ben Stiller loved it , but Clay Travis presumably did not. .@getnickwright tells @Timodc why a private admission from Clay Travis 11 years ago destroyed his respect for him: “If what you’re saying is true, that you don’t really believe what you’re saying, it’s just for audience and enrichment, I actually think that’s worse.” https://t.co/EPnCJq8eih — The Bulwark (@BulwarkOnline) November 12, 2026 “I’ve always been an unapologetic, you know, I’m a liberal Democrat,” Wright said. “And in my field, what is frustrating to me is—everyone’s allowed whatever politics they are. I really, really don’t like the folks who have the opposite politics of mine who pretend they’re centrists or independents. They’re a lot of folks in my space, the tell is, if they make a big mistake or a fact error or tell a story that’s not true accidentally, it’s always because it was fed from the right-wing ecosystem. Those guys who claim they’re down-the-middle neutral never tell a crazy, zany left-wing falsehood that they stumbled upon because all they’re stumbling upon is the right-wing crazy stuff.” Smartly, Miller asked whether Wright had anyone specific in mind. “One of my first TV things ever was with Clay,” Wright said. “And then we went to dinner after, and he told me, he was like, ‘You know I worked for Obama, and I just do this’ or whatever. Luckily, there was a third person at this dinner, so if he disputes it, I have a witness. I told him, I was like, ‘I want to be very clear. If what you’re saying is true—that you don’t really believe what you’re saying, it’s just for audience and enrichment, I actually think that’s worse, and it is impossible for me to ever respect you.’ And I left. That was the last time I ever talked to him. That was 11 years ago.” Late Wednesday night, Travis responded to Wright. “Eleven years ago I was still a Democrat so this entire story is completely made up,” Travis tweeted. “I guess this is what happens when you start voting Republican, people make up entire stories about you in their heads and share it with their far left wing friends.” Eleven years ago I was still a Democrat so this entire story is completely made up. I guess this is what happens when you start voting Republican, people make up entire stories about you in their heads and share it with their far left wing friends. — Clay Travis (@ClayTravis) November 12, 2026 Hopefully, the anonymous third person who attended the dinner breaks the tie, but no word yet. Travis founded OutKick in 2011 and sold it to Fox in 2021. This June, Travis officially departed OutKick , and by August, he launched Sport & State , for which he interviewed President Donald Trump in late September. He also hosts The Clay Travis Show , which airs on FS1, and The Clay Travis & Buck Sexton Show . This is not the first time Wright has called out Travis for fabricating his public persona. In June 2017, Travis and Wright got into it over the Black Lives Matter movement. Wright tweeted , “Here’s @ClayTravis when he’s not in character, performing for the masses. Careful who you call a liar, Clay. Folks keep receipts these days.” The tweet included two screenshots of emails from Travis: Here’s @ClayTravis when he’s not in character, performing for the masses. Careful who you call a liar, Clay. Folks keep receipts these days https://t.co/gmP4sizMV7 — nick wright (@getnickwright) June 4, 2017 Here’s the year old tweet that references @ClayTravis that he seems to be so bothered by at the moment. https://t.co/0OhcpVtdrY — nick wright (@getnickwright) June 4, 2017 Clay is now saying that my tweet is a “lie”. Here’s some photographic evidence, which evidently he yearns for in all cases. https://t.co/QKx7HAzhaQ — nick wright (@getnickwright) June 4, 2017 On The Bulwark Daily , Wright didn’t stop at Travis. “Listen, the biggest name in my space, Stephen A., has more than flirted with politics,” Wright said. “And I just would like him to actually be honest with himself and the audience about what his politics are, and so be it.” “That he’s pro-Trump, you mean?” Miller interjected. “Yeah, I mean, pretty obviously,” Wright said. “And so, pretending like, oh, I’m just calling balls and strikes, like, no you’re not. In my field, the job is not to be unbiased. The job, however, is to be honest with your audience about your biases, and then let them call it how they see it.” Miller asked Wright to estimate “how many of those guys are faking it,” and while Wright didn’t keep naming names or put a specific number to it, he expertly demystified the grift. “It is so much easier to get an audience and make money [by] appealing to the lowest common denominator of the MAGA-sphere than it is to do it in sports,” Wright said. “Like, I’m going to sound like an a**hole here, but actually achieving at a high level in daily sports talk, it’s a very competitive space. And you have to get lucky, but you also really gotta be on it. “And so, I think it’s a lot of folks who are like I wasn’t good enough. I wanted to do commentary about X—pop culture, entertainment, sports—I’m not good enough at that. But I’m comfortable talking into a camera or a microphone, and I can con these people. I do think there’s an element of that.” Last week, Awful Announcing’s very own Sean Keeley pondered whether the historic Democratic victories in the midterms forecast “ a sports media blue wave .” If that indeed comes to fruition, Wright won’t be alone in poking holes in the red MAGA balloon that has hovered over media and society for 10-plus years.
